lessons.title: The Cell, Properties of Life and Cell Theory
lessons.notes_html:
The cell is the structural and functional unit of living organisms. Some organisms are made of only one cell (unicellular), such as Euglena, Amoeba, Paramecium and Plasmodium, while others are made of many cells (multicellular), such as plants and animals. The study of the cell is called cell biology or cytology. An adult human contains more than 37.2 trillion cells.

1.1 Properties of Life

Because cells are the basic unit of life, they carry out all the fundamental functions of life:

  • Movement — Change in shape and position of a body part. Cells use cilia, flagella, pseudopodia and contractile proteins, with energy from mitochondria.
  • Respiration — Breakdown of glucose and other nutrients to release energy in the form of ATP.
  • Homeostasis — Maintaining a stable internal environment, such as pH, temperature and ion concentration, helped by transport proteins in the plasma membrane.
  • Growth — Increase in size and number of cells by cell division; DNA controls growth and ribosomes synthesize protein for growth.
  • Reproduction — Producing offspring of their own kind and passing on genetic material; binary fission, mitosis and meiosis make genetic continuity possible.
  • Excretion — Removal of metabolic wastes such as CO₂ and urea.
  • Nutrition — Obtaining food: plant cells absorb minerals and make food by photosynthesis; animal cells absorb digested nutrients from the blood stream.

1.2 Cell Theory

  • All organisms are composed of one or many cells.
  • The cell is the structural and functional unit of life.
  • All cells come from parent (pre-existing) cells.
  • The cell contains hereditary information, transferred from parental cells to daughter cells.

Validation of Cell Theory

Robert Hooke first described cells in 1665 while examining cork under a self-built microscope. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek observed the first living cells and called them animalcules. In 1838, Matthias Schleiden stated that plants are made of cells, and one year later Theodor Schwann said the same about animals and found that animal cells lack a cell wall. Rudolf Virchow (1855) observed that all cells come from pre-existing cells. Culturing cells in the laboratory also supports the theory. In the 1880s, Louis Pasteur sterilized chicken broth by boiling and showed that living organisms do not spontaneously reappear; life returned only after exposure to pre-existing cells.

Exceptions to Cell Theory

  • Multinucleated cells of striated muscle, fungal hyphae and some giant algae, whose cytoplasm is not divided into separate cells.
  • Viruses, prions and viroids are not formed of cells and cannot perform the functions of life on their own; they are not capable of autopoiesis.
  • Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells of plants lack nuclei, so they cannot divide to form new cells.
  • Protozoans are acellular, that is, not divided into cells.

Key Points

  • The cell is the structural and functional unit of life; its study is called cytology.
  • The seven properties of life are movement, respiration, homeostasis, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition.
  • Cell theory: organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, cells arise from pre-existing cells, and cells carry hereditary information.
  • Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow and Pasteur validated the cell theory.
  • Viruses, prions, viroids, mature RBCs and sieve tube cells are exceptions to the cell theory.

lessons.title: Light and Electron Microscopes and Cell Ultrastructure
lessons.notes_html:
Cells and their subunits are microscopically small, so microscopes with high magnification and resolution are needed. Resolution is the ability of a microscope to view two close objects as separate from each other; the resolution of the naked human eye is 0.1 mm. Magnification power is the ability to view an object by enlarging it from its real size.

Measuring Size and Magnification

In decreasing order of size are cells, organelles, bacteria, viruses, membranes and molecules. Actual size can be worked out from the diameter of the field of vision, measured with a micrometer or a simple ruler. Magnification = size of image / size of specimen. Example from the book: an image of 50 mm of a subject 5 micrometres long has a magnification of 10000x. Scale bars on a micrograph also show actual size.

Light Microscope and Electron Microscope

The first light microscope was invented by Hans and Janssen in 1590. Light microscopes use light passing through living or dead specimens to form an image; stains may be used to see details. Electron microscopes use electrons passing through a dead specimen and give the greatest magnification and resolution; they were invented by Knoll and Rusk in the 1930s.

Light MicroscopeElectron Microscope
Illumination is bulb light or sunlightIllumination is a beam of electrons
Eyepiece, objective and condenser lenses are made of glassAll lenses are electromagnetic
Specimens are stained by coloured dyesSpecimens are coated with heavy metals to reflect electrons
Preparation takes minutes to hours; live or dead specimens may be seenPreparation usually takes a few days; only dead or dried specimens are seen
Low resolving power (0.25 to 0.3 micrometre); magnification 500X to 1500XHigh resolving power (0.001 micrometre), about 250 times higher; magnification more than 1000,000X
Image is seen by eyes through the ocular lensImage is produced on a fluorescent screen
Inexpensive and easy to operateExpensive and needs training to operate

Types of Electron Microscope

TEMSEM
Electron beam passes through a thin sample on a TEM gridElectron beam scans over the surface of the sample, mounted on an aluminium stub
Image is shown on a fluorescent screenImage is shown on a TV monitor
Image is a two-dimensional projectionImage is a three-dimensional projection

TEM is the Transmission Electron Microscope and SEM is the Scanning Electron Microscope, so SEM is best suited to get the 3D surface view of an object.

1.4 Ultrastructure of Animal and Plant Cells

Animals and plants are eukaryotes. A eukaryotic cell generally ranges in diameter from 5 to 100 micrometres, and the nucleus is usually the most prominent structure in the cytoplasm. Organelles are subcellular structures that carry out specific functions, a bit like organs in multicellular organisms. Different types of cells may have different organelles.

Key Points

  • Resolution separates two close objects; magnification enlarges from real size.
  • Magnification = size of image / size of specimen.
  • Light microscope: light and glass lenses, 500X to 1500X. Electron microscope: electron beam and electromagnetic lenses, more than 1000,000X.
  • TEM gives a 2D image through a thin sample; SEM gives a 3D surface image.
  • Eukaryotic cells are 5 to 100 micrometres across, with the nucleus as the most prominent organelle.

lessons.title: Cell Wall and Plasma Membrane
lessons.notes_html:
Every cell is bounded by the living plasma membrane, which controls what enters and leaves. Plants, algae, fungi and prokaryotes also have a nonliving cell wall outside it; animal cells do not.

1.5 Cell Wall: Structure and Composition

The cell wall is the outermost nonliving covering, secreted by the protoplasm. The plant cell wall has three layers:

  • Primary cell wall — Formed in developing cells, present in all plant cells; some cells (leaves, storage cells) have only this wall. It is made of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin (pectin has around 200 galacturonic acid molecules). In the epidermis it is impregnated with cutin and wax, forming the plant cuticle. Cellulose microfibrils lie criss-cross, held by hydrogen bonds, giving high tensile strength; the wall is thin and slightly flexible.
  • Middle lamella — The first layer deposited at cell division between two adjacent cells, of sticky, gel-like magnesium and calcium salts that stick neighbouring cells together.
  • Secondary cell wall — A thick layer formed between the primary wall and plasma membrane when the cell is fully grown, of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, inorganic salts and waxes; such cells are rigid, as in sclerenchyma and collenchyma.

Plant cells communicate through microscopic channels in the wall called plasmodesmata. The wall provides structural support and shape, protects the cell from mechanical damage and pathogens, protects it from bursting by withstanding turgor pressure, and is porous, allowing water, gases and small molecules to pass between cells.

1.6 Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic Model

The plasma membrane is the outermost living boundary of animal cells; in plant cells it lies beneath the cell wall. Membranes are 60 to 80% proteins, 20 to 40% lipids and a small amount of carbohydrates, and the membrane is about 7.5 to 10 nm thick. The fluid mosaic model (Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson, 1972) describes it as a fluid mosaic of proteins floating within a bilayer of phospholipid and cholesterol.

  • Each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails; tails face each other, heads face the water inside and outside the cell. The lipid part controls fluidity, which depends on unsaturated fatty acids.
  • Cholesterol in the interior makes the membrane less permeable to water-soluble substances and provides stability.
  • Proteins are extrinsic (surface) or intrinsic (embedded in the bilayer); they give the membrane its mosaic nature.
  • Carbohydrates form glycoproteins (with proteins) and glycolipids (with lipids). The three classes of amphipathic lipids are phospholipids, glycolipids and sterols.

The fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it.

1.7 Functions of Plasma Membrane

  • Glycoproteins and glycolipids are receptor sites for hormones and nerve impulses and recognition sites for antigens — cell surface markers, like a signboard on a shop.
  • Channel proteins and carrier proteins pass molecules across; some proteins act as enzymes, and others as receptors that bind only the correct hormone.
  • It secretes useful substances such as enzymes and hormones, removes wastes such as ammonia, urea and uric acid, and keeps a constant favourable ionic concentration.

1.8 Techniques Used to Study Plasma Membrane

High-resolution microscopes, most importantly the electron microscope, plus x-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance, cell fractionation, membrane isolation and western blotting.

Key Points

  • The plant cell wall has three layers: primary wall, middle lamella and secondary wall; it is mainly cellulose.
  • The wall gives support and shape, protects the cell, and resists turgor pressure.
  • The plasma membrane is 60 to 80% protein and 20 to 40% lipid, about 7.5 to 10 nm thick.
  • The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) describes proteins floating in a fluid phospholipid bilayer.
  • Glycoproteins and glycolipids act as cell surface markers and receptor sites.

lessons.title: Membrane Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis, Endocytosis and Exocytosis
lessons.notes_html:
All living cells need nutrients, water and oxygen, and must remove wastes such as CO₂ and excess water. Substances cross the plasma membrane by passive transport, which does not require energy (ATP), and active transport, which does.

1.9 Passive and Active Transport

In passive transport, a substance moves from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, aided by a concentration gradient. In active transport, the substance is moved against the concentration gradient, so energy must be spent and a membrane protein must be involved. This allows a cell to keep interior concentrations different from the exterior: animal cells have much more potassium inside and more sodium outside, maintained by pumping potassium ions in and sodium ions out.

Diffusion

Diffusion is passive transport in which particles (except water) move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration; for example, oxygen gas moves from outside the cell to inside.

  • Simple diffusion — Substances move between phospholipid molecules or through protein molecules that possess channels.
  • Facilitated diffusion — Diffusion with specific carrier proteins that combine with the substance and change shape to aid its movement, without using energy. It is very specific: glucose, sodium ions and potassium ions pass through the membrane using carrier proteins.

Osmosis

Osmosis is passive transport along a concentration gradient involving only the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane. Entry of water into the cell is endosmosis; exit of water from the cell is exosmosis.

1.10 Endocytosis and Exocytosis

Endocytosis is the ingestion of material by the cell through the plasma membrane, by infolding. It covers three processes: phagocytosis (cell eating, solid particles), pinocytosis (cell drinking, small molecules) and receptor-mediated endocytosis (ions and macromolecules). All require energy, so they may be regarded as forms of active transport.

In exocytosis (cell vomiting), a vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and extrudes its contents to the surrounding medium. Exocytosis removes undigested residues, secretes substances such as hormones and enzymes, and transports a substance completely across a cellular barrier, for example across the wall of a blood vessel.

1.11 Simple Diffusion and Facilitated Diffusion Compared

Simple DiffusionFacilitated Diffusion
Unassisted diffusionAssisted diffusion
Occurs through the phospholipid bilayerOccurs through transmembrane carrier proteins
Transports small, non-polar particlesTransports large or polar particles
Takes place directly through the cell membraneTakes place through specific molecules
Example: diffusion of gases across the respiratory membraneExample: counter-transport of chloride and bicarbonate in renal tubular cells

Key Points

  • Passive transport moves substances down a concentration gradient without ATP; active transport moves them against the gradient using ATP.
  • Facilitated diffusion uses specific carrier proteins but needs no energy.
  • Osmosis is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane: endosmosis in, exosmosis out.
  • Endocytosis takes material in (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated); exocytosis expels material out.
  • Simple diffusion carries small non-polar particles; facilitated diffusion carries large or polar particles.

lessons.title: Cytoplasm and Organelles: ER, Ribosomes, Golgi Complex and Lysosomes
lessons.notes_html:
The living contents of a eukaryotic cell are divided into the nucleus and the cytoplasm; together they are known as protoplasm.

1.12 Cytoplasm

Cytoplasm is the liquid substance inside the cell membrane and outside the nucleus, containing amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, nucleotides, vitamins, salts and dissolved gases. Its soluble part is cytosol, about 90% water. Small molecules form a true solution; large molecules form a colloidal solution (starch in plant cells, glycogen in animal cells), as a sol or a gel. The cytoplasm stores vital materials, for example glycogen in liver cells, and is the site of glycolysis. The cytoskeleton maintains the shape of the cell and moves organelles; its microfilaments are mostly made of actin. Non-living materials in the cytoplasm are called cell inclusions.

1.13 Cytoplasmic Organelles

Membranous organelles are made of phospholipid bilayer with embedded protein (ER, Golgi bodies, mitochondria, plastids, lysosomes). Non-membranous organelles include ribosomes, centrioles and the cytoskeleton.

1.13.1 Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of channels extending between the nuclear membrane and the cell membrane. Its components are cisternae (long, flattened units in a stack), vesicles (oval membrane-bounded structures) and tubules (irregular, branched tubes). It divides the cell into luminal and extra-luminal compartments. Rough ER bears ribosomes; Smooth ER does not. The ribosome-rich rough ER is also called ergastoplasm.

  • It gives mechanical support and transports material within the cell.
  • Rough ER helps protein synthesis; proteins leave in vesicles from transitional ER, called transport vesicles. The RER is the membrane factory of the cell.
  • Smooth ER synthesizes cholesterol and phospholipid and detoxifies drugs, pollutants, steroids and other toxins.
  • ER membranes increase surface area, contain enzymes such as sucrases and glucose 6-phosphatase, and help form the nuclear membrane during cell division.

1.13.2 Ribosomes

Ribosomes are granular, non-membranous organelles first observed by George Palade in 1953, present in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (except mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells) and also inside chloroplasts and mitochondria. They are ribonucleoprotein particles: in prokaryotes rRNA is 60% and protein 40%; in eukaryotes protein is 60% and rRNA 40%. A common eukaryotic cell has about half a million ribosomes, free or attached to the RER. Many ribosomes on one mRNA strip form a polysome, giving many copies of the same polypeptide in less time. Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis, so they are called the factory of protein synthesis.

  • Eukaryotic ribosome: 80S = larger subunit 60S + smaller subunit 40S. S is the Svedberg unit (sedimentation rate); the subunits are held by magnesium ions and salt bonds.
  • Prokaryotic ribosome: 70S = 50S + 30S.
  • Subunits are made in the nucleolus and reach the cytoplasm via nuclear pores, so the nucleolus is the factory of ribosomes.

1.13.3 Golgi Complex

The Golgi complex was discovered by Camillo Golgi in 1898; in plants it is called a dictyosome. It is a stack of smooth, flattened, fluid-filled sacs or cisternae (3 to 7 in most animals, up to 30 in lower organisms) with tubules and vesicles. The outer convex face near the nuclear membrane is the cis-Golgi (forming face); the inner concave end is the trans-Golgi (maturing face), where cisternae break up into vesicles. It is the post office of the cell, collecting and dispatching protein products from the ER.

  • Cell secretion is the main function: secretions are processed, packed in membranes and exported, so Golgi bodies are abundant in secretory cells.
  • In plant cells its vesicles fuse at the equator to form the cell plate or phragmoplast.
  • It forms primary lysosomes, glyoxysomes and peroxisomes, the acrosome in spermiogenesis and the vitelline membrane of the egg, and conjugated molecules like glycoproteins and lipoproteins.

1.13.4 Lysosomes

Lysosomes (lyso: splitting, soma: body) are sac-like, single-membrane organelles that break macromolecules, first reported by Christian de Duve in 1949. They occur in almost all eukaryotic cells except mammalian RBCs; in plants the central vacuole functions as a lysosome. They contain about 40 types of hydrolytic enzymes (acid phosphatases, carbohydrases, lipases, nucleases, proteases) and are 0.1 to 0.8 micrometres across, largest (0.8 to 2 micrometres) in phagocytic WBCs.

  • Enzymes from the RER are processed in the Golgi and budded off as primary lysosomes. A primary lysosome fused with a food vacuole (phagosome) forms a secondary lysosome (digestive vacuole); what remains is a residual lysosome, kept as lipofuscin granules in multicellular organisms.
  • Digestion of foreign material is heterophagy; digestion of old organelles and stored food during starvation is autophagy; digestion of excess secretory granules, such as excess hormones, is crinophagy.
  • If all lysosomes of a cell burst, the cell dissolves, so they are called suicidal bags; this autolysis removes old WBCs, platelets and epithelial cells and the tadpole's tail.

Key Points

  • Cytosol is the soluble part of cytoplasm, about 90% water; glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.
  • Rough ER bears ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs and toxins.
  • Ribosomes are the factory of protein synthesis: 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes, 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes.
  • The Golgi complex processes, packs and secretes products, and forms lysosomes and the cell plate.
  • Lysosomes contain about 40 hydrolytic enzymes and are called suicidal bags because of autolysis.

lessons.title: Organelles: Mitochondria, Plastids, Microbodies, Centrioles, Vacuoles and Nucleus
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson covers the remaining organelles: mitochondria, plastids, microbodies, centrioles, vacuoles and the nucleus.

1.13.5 Mitochondria

Mitochondria (mitos: thread, chondrion: granules) are self-replicating organelles, 0.2 to 1 micrometre in diameter and 1 to 4.1 micrometres long, from a few to many thousands per cell; all together they are the chondriome. Altman (1890) called them bioblasts; the term was given by C. Benda (1898). Like bacteria, they have circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, so they are believed to have an endosymbiotic origin from a prokaryotic cell.

  • The outer membrane is smooth, with porins, so it is freely permeable; if it is removed, the rest is called a mitoplast.
  • The inner membrane is folded into cristae, which bear pin-head oxysomes (F0-F1 particles) containing ATP synthetase, which makes ATP.
  • The inner fluid, the matrix, contains enzymes of aerobic respiration, 70S ribosomes, RNA and circular double-stranded DNA (1% of the cell's total DNA).
  • The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain occur here and most ATP is produced here, so mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell.

1.13.6 Plastids

A plastid (plastos: formed, molded) is a double-membrane organelle of plant cells for manufacture and storage of chemical compounds. All plastids form from a precursor, the proplastid.

  • Chloroplasts — Green plastids, the site of photosynthesis. Disc-like thylakoids stack in groups of 25 to 50 to form a granum (plural grana); about 40 to 60 grana occur in a chloroplast and up to 40 chloroplasts in a cell. The fluid around them is the stroma (the matrix of the chloroplast), with enzymes for the dark reactions, including Rubisco (about 16% of the chloroplast), plus DNA, RNA and 70S ribosomes, so it is semiautonomous. Grana are joined by lamellae. Light reactions occur in the grana, dark reactions in the stroma.
  • Chromoplasts — Pigmented plastids in petals and fruit coverings; they help cross-pollination and seed dispersal.
  • Leucoplasts — Colourless plastids of roots and woody stems storing food: amyloplast stores starch, elaioplast stores lipid, proteinoplast stores protein.

A chloroplast: grana of stacked thylakoids in the stroma, joined by lamellae, inside a double membrane.

1.13.7 Microbodies: Peroxisomes and Glyoxysomes

  • Peroxisomes — Single-membrane vesicles rich in oxidative enzymes (peroxidase, catalase), 0.6 to 0.7 micrometres across, 70 to 100 per cell, first isolated by de Duve and co-workers in 1965. They form and decompose hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂): catalase breaks H₂O₂ into H₂O and O₂. In plants they also take part in photorespiration.
  • Glyoxysomes — Found only in plants, mostly in lipid-rich seeds (soybean, sunflower) and seedlings. Their enzymes convert lipids into sugar (through succinate) by the glyoxylate cycle, used until the seedling can photosynthesize.

Together, peroxisomes and glyoxysomes are called microbodies; they are not part of the endomembrane system and are smaller than lysosomes. Unlike a lysosome, a glyoxisome does not carry out general intracellular digestion.

Centrioles

Centrioles are non-membranous organelles, two in number near the nucleus, found in animal cells and lower plants but absent in higher plants (Beneden, 1883; Boveri, 1895). With the surrounding centrosphere they form the centrosome. Each is a cylinder of nine microtubules of triplet tubules, the two lying at right angles. They replicate before division, migrate to opposite sides of the nucleus, and spindle fibres form between the pairs. The centriole is present only in animal cells among the organelles of this chapter.

1.13.9 Vacuoles

Vacuoles are membrane-bounded storage sacs. In animal cells they are small and temporary (food vacuoles in Amoeba and Paramecium). In mature plant cells the vacuole occupies about 90% of the cell volume, pushing the nucleus to the boundary. Its membrane is the tonoplast and it holds cell sap: sugars, amino acids, proteins, minerals (such as K⁺ and Cl⁻) and wastes such as anthocyanin and alkaloids. Vacuoles maintain osmotic pressure, store toxic by-products, give turgidity and rigidity, and protect the plant from herbivory.

1.13.10 Nucleus

The nucleus (karyon: central commander), discovered by Robert Brown in 1831 in an orchid cell, controls all cellular metabolism and contains the genetic information. Usually one nucleus occurs per cell; Paramecium has two (meganucleus and micronucleus) and striated muscle cells have many, while mature sieve tube elements and mammalian RBCs have none. In a non-dividing cell it has four parts:

  • Nuclear membrane (envelope) — Two membranes with a perinuclear space of 10 to 50 nm; the outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores (with the protein nucleoporin) regulate RNA and ionic exchange with the cytoplasm.
  • Nucleoplasm — The ground substance (nuclear matrix or karyoplasm), with histone and non-histone proteins and enzymes such as DNA and RNA polymerases.
  • Nucleolus — A non-membrane-bound body attached to chromatin at the nuclear organizer region (NOR), visible only in interphase; its fibrillar area has 85% proteins, 10% rRNA and 5% DNA. It forms the ribosomal subunits, so it is the ribosome factory of the cell.
  • Chromatin and chromosomes — Chromatin (DNA, histone and non-histone proteins, a little RNA) condenses into chromosomes during division; they are best studied at metaphase, when shortest. The number is definite for each species (karyotype study): human 46, pea 14, maize 20, frog 26, chimpanzee 48, fruit fly 08. Each metaphase chromosome has two sister chromatids joined by a centromere, with a kinetochore disc where spindle fibres attach. Chromosomes carry the genes from parent to daughter cell.

Key Points

  • Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell: Krebs cycle and ETC occur in them, and ATP is made on the oxysomes of the cristae.
  • The chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis: light reactions in the grana, dark reactions in the stroma.
  • Peroxisomes break down hydrogen peroxide; glyoxysomes, only in plants, convert lipids into sugars by the glyoxylate cycle.
  • The membrane enclosing the vacuole is the tonoplast; the nucleolus is the factory of ribosomes.
  • Chromosomes are the hereditary material, best studied at metaphase; the human body cell has 46 chromosomes.

lessons.title: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells, and Cell Signaling
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson compares the two basic types of cells and then explains how cells communicate by cell signaling.

1.14 Comparison Between Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cell

Prokaryotic CellEukaryotic Cell
Primitive cellEvolved cell
No prominent nucleus: nuclear material is not bounded by a nuclear membrane; nucleolus absentDistinct nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane; nucleolus present
Found only in bacteria and cyanobacteriaFound in protists, fungi, plants and animals
Membranous organelles are absentMembranous organelles are present
Mesosomes are presentMesosomes are absent
70S ribosomes80S ribosomes
Single circular chromosome of only DNATwo or more linear chromosomes of DNA, protein and a little RNA
Cell wall contains peptidoglycanCell wall of cellulose (plants, algae) or chitin (fungi); absent in animal cells
Divides by binary fission: no mitosis or meiosisDivides by mitosis; germ line cells divide by meiosis

1.15 Cell Signaling

Cell signaling is the process by which a cell communicates with itself, other cells and the environment; it is a fundamental characteristic of all cellular organisms and may be intercellular or intracellular. A signal process involves three components: the signal, the receptor and the effector. Most signals are chemical, though some are physical cues such as temperature, pressure, light and voltage. Chemical signal molecules are called ligands: they may be ions (sodium, calcium, potassium) or hormones (steroid, prostaglandin, insulin, glucagon), nucleic acids and proteoglycans, and they bind and activate specific receptors.

1.16 Protein Signaling or Fixed Membrane Pathway

Peptide and protein hormones are water-soluble and cannot pass through the plasma membrane. They attach to receptors on the plasma membrane of the target cell and start a series of steps inside. The membrane enzyme adenylate cyclase converts ATP into the second messenger, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP); the hormone itself is the first messenger. The cAMP triggers changes such as activation of enzymes (for example glycogen breakdown) and gene activation. The whole process is also called signal transduction.

Steroid Signaling or Mobile Pathway

Steroid and amino-acid-derivative hormones are lipid-soluble and pass easily through the plasma membrane. Their receptors lie inside the target cell, in the cytoplasm or nucleus. Hormone and receptor form a hormone-receptor complex, which travels to a particular gene and acts as a transcription factor. The gene is transcribed into messenger RNA, which is translated into a polypeptide (protein) in the cytoplasm, so the activities of the target cell are modified by altered gene expression. This pathway is also called gene or signal modulation.

Protein SignalingSteroid Signaling
Hormone is water-soluble and cannot cross the membraneHormone is lipid-soluble and passes through the membrane
Receptor is on the plasma membrane (fixed)Receptor is inside the cell (mobile)
Acts through a second messenger, cAMPHormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor
Activates enzymes already presentChanges gene expression and produces new proteins

Key Points

  • Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus, no membranous organelles, 70S ribosomes and a single circular chromosome; they divide by binary fission.
  • Eukaryotic cells have a distinct nucleus, membranous organelles, 80S ribosomes and linear chromosomes.
  • Peptidoglycan is present in the bacterial cell wall.
  • Cell signaling involves a signal (ligand), a receptor and an effector.
  • Protein signaling works through a membrane receptor and cAMP; steroid signaling works through an intracellular receptor that changes gene expression.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Stem Cell and Cell Cycle

lessons.title: Stem Cells and Their Advantages
lessons.notes_html:
Stem cells are undifferentiated cells with the ability to renew themselves and become specialized. There are different types of stem cells, such as totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent. Cell division is the sequence of events in cell growth and division, and it is crucial for the development, growth and repair of organisms.

2.1 What Is a Stem Cell?

A stem cell is a cell that can divide and produce new cells that can differentiate into many kinds of specialized cells. Groups of cells within an organism retain their ability to divide to form more daughter cells, which either become new stem cells or specialized cells of various types. So a stem cell has two key abilities: self-renewal and differentiation. A stem cell is defined by this ability to divide and differentiate into various cell types.

Advantages of Stem Cells

  • They may be used to replace cells and tissues that have been damaged or lost due to diseases.
  • Stem cell therapy has benefited the treatment of diseases like diabetes type 1, Parkinson's disease, stroke, Alzheimer's disease, burns and cancer.
  • They help to test new drugs safely before using them on humans.
  • They help scientists to learn how the body grows and develops.
  • They are required for growth, development and the repair of damaged tissue.

Stem Cells in Plants

Plants contain such cells in meristematic tissues, which occur near root and stem tips and are composed of rapidly reproducing cells. These cells produce new cells capable of becoming various types of tissues within the root or stem. Gardeners take advantage of these cells when they take cuttings from stems or roots and use them to propagate new plants.

Key Points

  • Stem cells are unspecialized cells that can self-renew and differentiate into specialized cells.
  • Stem cells can replace damaged or lost cells and tissues, and help treat diabetes type 1, Parkinson's disease, stroke, Alzheimer's disease, burns and cancer.
  • Stem cells are used to test new drugs safely and to study growth and development.
  • In plants, meristematic tissues at root and stem tips act like stem cells and are used for cuttings.

lessons.title: Categories of Stem Cells
lessons.notes_html:
Stem cells are categorized in two ways: by their source and by their potency, their potential to differentiate into other types of cells.

Types of Stem Cells by Source

In animal embryos, the cells of the blastocyst stage are the best source of stem cells; stem cells can also be obtained from the umbilical cord after childbirth. The three main types by source are:

  • Embryonic stem cells — They have the most potent role, able to become every type of cell in the body.
  • Adult stem cells — They supply new cells as an organism grows and replace cells that get damaged. They are multipotent: they can change into only some specific cells in the body, not all types. They occur in tissues such as bone marrow and skin.
  • Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) — Stem cells that scientists make in the laboratory; they can develop into any cell type.

Categories by Potency

  • Totipotent — Can differentiate into all possible cell types and give rise to all parts of the body. The first few cells that appear as the zygote starts to divide are totipotent; they can form a complete organism, including the placenta.
  • Pluripotent — Can turn into almost any cell except the extra-embryonic membrane and placenta; each such cell can develop into over 200 types. Cells from the early embryo are pluripotent.
  • Multipotent — Can differentiate into a closely related family of cells. Adult hematopoietic (blood) stem cells, for example, can become RBCs, WBCs and platelets.
  • Oligopotent — Can differentiate into a few different cell types, for example adult lymphoid or myeloid stem cells.
  • Unipotent — Can only produce cells of one kind, their own type; for example, adult muscle stem cells can renew themselves. This is the most limited kind of stem cell.

The stem cell hierarchy: potency decreases from totipotent to unipotent.

Key Points

  • By source, stem cells are embryonic, adult and induced pluripotent stem cells.
  • By potency, stem cells are totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent, oligopotent and unipotent.
  • Totipotent cells can form a complete organism; pluripotent cells can form almost all body cell types but not the placenta.
  • Multipotent blood stem cells form RBCs, WBCs and platelets; unipotent cells form only one cell type.

lessons.title: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells: Advantages, Disadvantages and Ethics
lessons.notes_html:
Scientists create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) in laboratories from skin cells and other tissue-specific cells, by directly reprogramming adult cells. They were first described by Shinya Yamanaka and his colleagues at Kyoto University (Japan) in 2006 and were awarded the Nobel Prize in 2012. Induced pluripotent stem cells are not natural; they are made artificially.

Advantages of Using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells

  • They behave like embryonic stem cells, so they can give rise to almost any type of desired cell and could be used to develop a range of therapies.
  • Blood stem cells have been introduced routinely into humans to replace the damaged bone marrow of some leukemia patients (cancer of white blood cells). In the future, iPSCs will also be used in research to treat diseases like cancer, diabetes and nerve paralysis.
  • They are taken from the patients themselves, so they could be used to grow new organs with a lower risk of being rejected.
  • They avoid the ethical problems of embryonic stem cells, and can be used to model diseases and test drugs.

Disadvantages of Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells

  • If the sample cells are contaminated by viruses, the virus could be transmitted into the patient; retroviruses are usually used to introduce the reprogramming genes, and retroviruses may cause cancer.
  • There is a risk of tumour formation if the cells are not properly controlled after transplantation; uncontrolled stem cells can form tumours and may differentiate into the wrong tissue.
  • There may be immune rejection unless the cells are matched or modified.
  • There are chances of incomplete differentiation and genetic instability due to genetic mutation during culture.

Ethics of Using Stem Cells

  • Embryonic stem cells — Always morally objectionable, because the human embryo must be destroyed to harvest its stem cells; this is the ethically controversial type.
  • Embryonic germ cells — Morally objectionable when fetal tissue from elective abortions is used, but morally acceptable when material from spontaneous abortions (miscarriages) is used with the parents' informed consent.
  • Umbilical cord stem cells — Morally acceptable, since the umbilical cord is no longer required once delivery is completed.
  • Placentally-derived stem cells — Morally acceptable, since the afterbirth is no longer required after delivery.
  • Adult stem cells — Morally acceptable.

Stem cells must also be chosen carefully: if a person needs liver cells, a unipotent liver stem cell (or a cell directed to become liver) is preferred over a general pluripotent cell, because the more specialized the stem cell, the lower the risk of forming unwanted tissues.

Key Points

  • iPSCs are adult cells reprogrammed in the laboratory (Yamanaka, 2006; Nobel Prize 2012) to act like embryonic stem cells.
  • Advantages: made from the patient's own cells, so lower rejection risk; almost any cell type can be produced; no embryo is destroyed.
  • Disadvantages: retroviruses used in reprogramming may cause cancer; risks of tumour formation, incomplete differentiation and genetic instability.
  • Ethics: embryonic stem cells are controversial because the embryo is destroyed; cord, placental and adult stem cells are morally acceptable.

lessons.title: The Cell Cycle and Mitosis
lessons.notes_html:
The cell cycle describes the behaviour of cells as the cell grows, replicates its DNA and divides, producing two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell. Cell division is essential for growth, repair, reproduction and replacement of old or damaged cells. Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows it. Karyokinesis can occur without cytokinesis, giving a multinucleate cell, but normally the two follow each other.

2.4 Phases of the Cell Cycle

  • Interphase — Not part of mitosis; the period between two consecutive divisions. Its preparatory phases are G1 (cell growth: the cell grows, makes RNA, proteins and organelles, and decides whether to divide again), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation: the cell grows a little more, makes what division needs, and checks the copied DNA for errors). So G1 comes before DNA replication and G2 after it. Cells which do not divide and remain out of G1 constitute the G0 phase.
  • Mitosis or M phase — The actual nuclear division: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.

The cell cycle: interphase (G1, S and G2) prepares the cell, and the M phase divides it.

2.4.1 Mitosis Cell Division

Mitosis is asexual cell division in eukaryotic cells producing two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same 2n chromosome number as the parent; a human skin cell dividing by mitosis gives daughter cells with 46 chromosomes. It serves growth and development, tissue repair and regeneration, asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms, and replacement of old and damaged cells, and it occurs in somatic (body) cells.

  • Prophase — Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each of 2 sister chromatids joined at the centromere. The nuclear envelope breaks and spindles appear.
  • Metaphase — Chromosomes align at the equatorial plate; spindles attach to centromeres via kinetochores.
  • Anaphase — Sister chromatids separate at the centromere and are pulled to opposite poles; each chromatid becomes an individual chromosome. So metaphase lines chromosomes up, anaphase pulls them apart.
  • Telophase — Chromosomes decondense into chromatin, the nuclear envelope reforms, spindles disappear and two nuclei appear. It is called the reversal of prophase, because everything done in prophase is undone.

Cytokinesis

Cytokinesis starts at the end of telophase. In animal cells, which have centrioles and asters, a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two. In plant cells, which have no centrioles or asters, the cell plate (phragmoplast) forms and divides the cell; the phragmoplast is the structure which divides the plant cell.

Mitosis and Cancer

Sometimes cells multiply so rapidly that they form a solid mass of cells called a tumour; this disease state is cancer. When mutations in the genes controlling the cell cycle make a cell lose its orderly pattern of division, it divides again and again without stopping, and if the cells invade other tissues the cancer spreads.

Key Points

  • The cell cycle is interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation) plus the M phase.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells for growth, repair, regeneration and replacement.
  • Metaphase lines chromosomes on the equator; anaphase pulls sister chromatids to opposite poles.
  • Cytokinesis is by a cleavage furrow in animal cells and by a cell plate (phragmoplast) in plant cells.
  • Loss of control of mitosis leads to tumours and cancer.

lessons.title: Meiosis: Reduction Division
lessons.notes_html:
Meiosis occurs only in reproductive cells (germ cells): in animals during gametogenesis (formation of gametes, egg or sperm) and in plants during sporogenesis (formation of spores). The chromosome number is reduced in the daughter cells, diploid to haploid, or half, which is why meiosis is important for sexual reproduction: fertilization restores the number.

Two Divisions of Meiosis

Meiosis has two consecutive divisions after a single interphase (a single replication of DNA) and produces four daughter haploid cells: meiosis I (reduction division) and meiosis II (just like mitosis). A human somatic cell is diploid (46 chromosomes) and its mitotic daughters are identical to it; a human gamete is haploid (23 chromosomes) and genetically different because of crossing over and independent assortment. Mitosis and meiosis are similar: both begin with DNA replication and pass through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, ending with cytokinesis.

Meiosis I: The Reduction Phase

In meiosis I the chromosome number becomes haploid, because homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I; meiosis II only separates sister chromatids and does not reduce the number further. Meiosis I has Prophase-I, Metaphase-I, Anaphase-I and Telophase-I.

Prophase-I and Its Five Sub-Stages

Prophase-I is very lengthy and differs from mitotic prophase because homologous chromosomes pair up — one from the father, the other from the mother — and crossing over occurs.

  • Leptotene — Chromosomes become visible, and shorten and thicken by condensation of chromatin fibres. The nucleus enlarges and homologous chromosomes start coming closer to form pairs.
  • Zygotene — Pairing of homologous chromosomes, called synapsis, begins; it is highly specific, point to point, like a zipper. The paired homologue is called a bivalent or tetrad.
  • Pachytene — Each bivalent has two centromeres and four chromatids (a tetrad) wrapped around each other. Non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata: this is crossing over, and the reshuffling of genetic material produces recombination. Crossing over therefore occurs during prophase-I.
  • Diplotene — Desynapsis begins: the chromosomes repel each other, but separation is incomplete and each pair remains joined at at least one point of chiasmata.
  • Diakinesis — Desynapsis completes, the homologues still united at one point, and condensation is maximum. The nucleoli disappear and the nuclear membrane breaks down.

Metaphase-I, Anaphase-I and Telophase-I

  • Metaphase-I — Homologous pairs align at the centre; spindle fibres attach to each chromosome from both poles.
  • Anaphase-I — Homologous chromosomes are pulled apart to opposite poles; sister chromatids stay together.
  • Telophase-I — Two haploid cells form and chromosomes start uncoiling.

Meiosis II

  • Prophase-II — Chromosomes condense again and spindles form.
  • Metaphase-II — Chromosomes line up in the centre.
  • Anaphase-II — Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
  • Telophase-II — Chromosomes uncoil, nuclear membranes reform, and cytokinesis follows, so four genetically different haploid cells are formed.

Significance of Meiosis

  • It forms the haploid gametes required for sexual reproduction.
  • It introduces genetic recombinations, leading to variations and evolution.
  • Haploid gametes unite at fertilization, so the chromosome number is restored.
  • In plants, spores are formed due to meiosis.

Key Points

  • Meiosis occurs in germ cells, halves the chromosome number, and produces four genetically different haploid cells.
  • Meiosis I is the reduction division; meiosis II is like mitosis and separates sister chromatids.
  • Synapsis occurs in zygotene and crossing over in pachytene of prophase-I.
  • Homologous chromosomes are chromosomes with the same sequence of genes.
  • Meiosis forms gametes and spores, creates variation, and restores the chromosome number at fertilization.

lessons.title: Biochemistry, Chemical Bonds and Biological Molecules in Protoplasm
lessons.notes_html:
Biological molecules are essential chemical compounds that form the basis of life, maintain cell structure and function, and include proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids.

3.1 Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

Biochemistry is the study of biological molecules, their processing and significance for living organisms. It is important for understanding biological systems, agriculture, pharmaceutical and food industries, genetics and biotechnology. Molecular biology deals with the structure and function of macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, and explains gene expression, DNA replication, transcription and translation.

3.2 Chemical Bonds

Chemical bonds are forces of attraction holding atoms or ions together, formed through electron interactions so atoms achieve stable configurations.

  • Hydrogen bond — weak attraction between hydrogen and a negatively charged atom such as oxygen, chlorine or fluorine, with no sharing of electrons. Shown as a dotted line; intermolecular or intramolecular. Weak alone, but in large numbers in water, proteins and DNA it creates a strong attraction.
  • Covalent bond — two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, e.g. oxygen shares with two hydrogens in water. Examples: carbon-carbon, carbon-hydrogen, peptide bond and glycosidic bond in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
  • Ionic bond — one atom donates electrons to another, creating positive and negative ions that attract, e.g. sodium and chloride. Less common in biological molecules, but important between some amino acids in proteins, in the phosphate group of DNA, and in enzyme-substrate interaction.
  • Hydrophilic — water-loving: polar or charged substances that dissolve in water and form hydrogen or ionic interactions with it, e.g. salts, sugars, some amino acids. Hydrophobic — water-repelling: nonpolar, uncharged substances that do not dissolve; water forms an ordered structure around them so they cluster together, involving van der Waals forces, e.g. oils, fats. In the plasma membrane phospholipid heads are hydrophilic and face water; tails are hydrophobic and face away.

3.3 Biological Molecules in Protoplasm

Living organisms are composed of 25 elements, only 16 essential for life. The six most common — hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and phosphorus — are about 99% of living mass. In the human body: oxygen 65%, carbon 18.5%, hydrogen 9.5%, nitrogen 3.3%. Macromolecules are made of many repeating monomer units and have high molecular weight; micromolecules are individual units with low molecular weight. A mammalian cell is about: water 70%, protein 18%, carbohydrate 4%, lipids 3%, RNA 1.1%, DNA 0.25%, other organic substances 2% and inorganic ions 1%.

The four fundamental molecules: carbohydrates (C, H, O) provide fuel, store reserve food, and cellulose and chitin are structural; proteins (units: amino acids) are the most abundant organic compounds in protoplasm — enzymes, haemoglobin carrying O₂, myoglobin storing O₂, hormones and antibodies; lipids are hydrophobic, store food and build organelles and plasma membranes; nucleic acids (unit: nucleotide) — DNA is hereditary material and RNAs synthesise proteins under its instructions.

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies biological molecules; molecular biology studies macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids.
  • Hydrogen bonds are weak and dotted; covalent bonds share electrons; ionic bonds transfer electrons.
  • Hydrophilic substances dissolve in water; hydrophobic substances cluster away from water.
  • H, C, O, N, S and P make about 99% of living mass.
  • The four fundamental molecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

lessons.title: Condensation, Hydrolysis and Properties of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Polymers are made and broken by two opposite reactions, condensation and hydrolysis. Water is the most abundant component of protoplasm — bodies contain about 70–90% water — and without it life cannot exist.

3.4 Condensation and Hydrolysis

  • Condensation (dehydration synthesis) — small molecules join to form a large molecule or polymer; water is released and energy is used. An OH is removed from one monomer and an H⁺ from the other. Example: disaccharides and polysaccharides from monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose).
  • Hydrolysis (hydration) — breakdown of a polymer into monomers; water is used, one monomer gets H⁺ and the other OH⁻, with the help of enzymes, and energy is released when a bond is broken.

Condensation joins monomers and removes water; hydrolysis uses water to split polymers.

3.5 Properties of Water

  • High polarity — sharing of electrons is fairly equal in a nonpolar bond (O₂, N₂) but not in a polar covalent bond. Water is polar: hydrogens carry a slight positive charge, oxygen a slight negative charge (angle 104.5°). It is a universal solvent for polar substances, ionic compounds, electrolytes and molecules with charged groups, such as sugar.
  • Hydrogen bonding — attraction between hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (oxygen, nitrogen, fluorine) and another polar group. Each water molecule can form four hydrogen bonds. Water is liquid at suitable temperature, boils at 100°C and freezes at 0°C.
  • High specific heat — heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C (15°C to 16°C) is one calorie or 4.18 joules per gram per degree. Most energy is used breaking hydrogen bonds, so temperature changes slowly; body and environmental temperature stay stable — water is a thermostabilizer. Bone and seed contain only 20% water, brain 85%, blood 88% and jellyfish 99%.
  • High heat of vaporisation — heat to convert 1 ml of liquid to vapour without changing temperature; for water 574 kcal/kg, due to hydrogen bonds. Important in sweating, panting and transpiration, and in moderating environmental temperature.
  • Cohesion and adhesion — cohesion is attraction between similar molecules, adhesion between dissimilar molecules. Water molecules stick together and flow together, and stick to walls such as the xylem wall, due to hydrogen bonding and polarity.
  • Hydrophobic exclusion — contact area between water and hydrophobic substances is reduced; oil drops on water join into a single drop. This maintains the integrity of the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes.
  • Ionization — a molecule gains or loses electrons to form ions. Water releases equal H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, which take part in metabolism and maintain pH. H⁺ exists as hydronium (H₃O⁺), a hydrogen ion bound to a water molecule; hydronium controls pH, enzyme activity and energy production.
  • Lower density of ice — density decreases below 4°C, so ice is lighter than water and floats; water is the only substance whose solid is less dense than its liquid, because it has maximum hydrogen bonds. Ice insulates water below and increases survival in winter.

Key Points

  • Condensation joins monomers, releases water and uses energy; hydrolysis splits polymers, uses water and releases energy.
  • Water is polar, forms four hydrogen bonds per molecule, boils at 100°C and freezes at 0°C.
  • High specific heat and heat of vaporisation keep temperatures stable and cool the body.
  • Ice is less dense than water, floats, and insulates water below it.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates and Monosaccharides
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:2:1, general formula Cn(H₂O)n, so they are called hydrated carbon. Their source is green living things — plants, cyanobacteria, algae and many bacteria.

3.6 What Carbohydrates Are

Some molecules have the same ratio but are not carbohydrates, e.g. lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃) and acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂), and some carbohydrates do not fulfil the formula, e.g. rhamnose (C₆H₁₂O₅) and deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄). So: carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Aldehydes have a carbonyl group (C = O) at the end of a chain, bonded to hydrogen and an R-group (in glucose, ribose); they are easily oxidised and are powerful reducing agents. Ketones have the carbonyl group within the chain, bonded to two R-groups; such sugars are ketose sugars.

MonosaccharideOligosaccharidePolysaccharide
One sugar; simplest, cannot be hydrolysed; highly soluble, sweetest; glucose, ribose, fructose2–10 sugars; less soluble, less sweet; maltose, sucrose, lactoseMore than 10 sugars; complex, insoluble or sparingly soluble, tastes less; starch, glycogen, cellulose

3.7 Monosaccharides

Monosaccharides (mono: one, saccharide: sugar) are the simplest carbohydrates, cannot be hydrolysed further, contain 3 to 7 carbons, and are building blocks of complex carbohydrates. They are very sweet and easily soluble. All carbons except one have a hydroxyl group; the remaining carbon has an aldehyde group (aldo sugar) or ketone group (keto sugar), so they are reducing sugars. An asymmetric carbon bonds with four different atoms or groups — in glucose, galactose and mannose, carbons 2, 3, 4 and 5 are asymmetrical.

  • Trioses (C₃H₆O₃) — glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone. Tetroses (C₄H₈O₄) — erythrose, erythrulose. Pentoses (C₅H₁₀O₅) — ribose, deoxyribose, ribulose. Hexoses (C₆H₁₂O₆) — glucose, mannose, fructose, galactose; glucose is the most common monosaccharide and the starting respiratory substrate. Heptoses (C₇H₁₄O₇) — glucose-heptose, sedoheptulose.

The molecular formula of a hexose is C₆H₁₂O₆; a structural formula shows the arrangement of atoms. Pentoses and hexoses usually form rings in water: a six-member ring is pyranose (glucopyranose), a five-member ring is furanose (ribofuranose). If the OH on carbon 1 is below the ring plane it is alpha-glucose; if above, beta-glucose. Different forms of the same chemical are isomers.

3.8 Isomers and Stereoisomers of Glucose

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structure. Structural isomers have atoms and functional groups joined in different ways, e.g. glucose and fructose. Stereoisomers have the same bond structure but different positioning in space, e.g. D-glucose and L-glucose. Alpha and beta glucose have 16 stereoisomers in three groups:

EnantiomersDiastereoisomersEpimers
Non-superimposable mirror images; D and L glucoseH and OH differ at more than one asymmetrical carbon; D-glucose and D-altroseH and OH differ at only one asymmetrical carbon; D-glucose and D-mannose

Laboratory left-handed (L) sugars (tagatose, sucralose) taste like D-glucose and help diabetic and obese patients, but are expensive and overuse causes diarrhoea. They are not digested — the body makes no enzymes or receptors for them — and are not converted into fats.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, general formula Cn(H₂O)n.
  • Monosaccharides have 3–7 carbons, are sweet, soluble reducing sugars and cannot be hydrolysed further.
  • Hexoses are C₆H₁₂O₆; glucose is the most common monosaccharide.
  • Enantiomers are mirror images, diastereoisomers differ at more than one carbon, epimers at only one.

lessons.title: Oligosaccharides, Glycosidic Bonds and Polysaccharides
lessons.notes_html:
Monosaccharides join by glycosidic linkage to form oligosaccharides and polysaccharides — the transport, storage and structural forms of carbohydrate.

3.9 Oligosaccharides and Disaccharides

Two to ten monosaccharides joined by glycosidic linkage form oligosaccharides (disaccharides, trisaccharides, tetrasaccharides). The most common are disaccharides — condensation products of two monosaccharides, general formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, less sweet and less soluble than monosaccharides. The bond may break on hydrolysis, yielding two monosaccharides again.

  • Maltose (malt sugar) — two alpha glucose. In fruits and in the digestive tract as a breakdown product of starch by amylase; used in brewing to synthesise alcohol. Produced from barley starch by amylase — this process is malting.
  • Lactose (milk sugar) — galactose-beta-1,4-glucose; energy source for young mammals, 4 to 6 percent in cow milk and 5–8 percent in human milk. Hydrolysis gives glucose + galactose.
  • Sucrose (cane sugar) — most abundant disaccharide in nature; hydrolysed to glucose + fructose. From sugar cane or sugar beet, also in pineapple, sorghum and sweet fruit; the main transport sugar in plants.
  • Cellobiose — present in traces; released during digestion of cellulose by cellulase of microorganisms.

3.10 Glycosidic Bond

A glycosidic bond is the bond between two monosaccharides, formed by condensation. It normally joins carbon 1 to carbon 4 of the neighbouring unit; in sucrose it joins carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose; in branched chains a 1–6 glycosidic bond forms.

3.11 Polysaccharides

Polysaccharides have more than 10 monosaccharides linked by glycosidic linkage, branched or unbranched, tasteless and insoluble or sparingly soluble, and are the most abundant carbohydrates in nature. Homopolysaccharides are made from one kind of monosaccharide (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin); heteropolysaccharides from different kinds (agar, hemicellulose, pectin, peptidoglycan). They store food and energy and give structure. Their large size makes them insoluble, so they exert no osmotic or chemical influence in the cell, fold into compact shapes, and convert easily to sugars by hydrolysis when required.

PolysaccharideStructure and role
StarchPlant storage polymer of glucose. Amylose 15–20%: straight chain, 1–4 linkage, soluble in warm water. Amylopectin 80–85%: branched, 1–6 linkage at branches, insoluble
CelluloseMost abundant carbohydrate in nature; structural, main constituent of plant and algal cell walls. Humans lack cellulase and cannot digest it; herbivores can, because gut microorganisms (bacteria, yeast, protozoans) secrete cellulase
GlycogenAnimal starch: highly branched polymer of glucose, stored in liver and muscles, also in fungi; insoluble, converted back to glucose when needed
ChitinNitrogenous structural homopolysaccharide related to cellulose; in fungal cell walls (fungal cellulose) and arthropod exoskeletons. Second most abundant organic molecule on Earth; derivative of N-acetyl glucosamine, a modified beta glucose

Iodine test: potato turns dark blue (starch present); glycogen solution turns red (glycogen present); cellulose solution remains unchanged (no starch or glycogen).

Key Points

  • Disaccharides (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) form by condensation and split by hydrolysis.
  • Maltose = glucose + glucose; lactose = glucose + galactose; sucrose = glucose + fructose.
  • Glycosidic bonds normally join carbon 1 to carbon 4; branches use 1–6 bonds.
  • Starch and glycogen store energy; cellulose and chitin give structure.

lessons.title: Proteins: Amino Acids, Peptide Bonds and Roles
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are the most complex and important organic compounds in food, found in all plants and animals. The word comes from the Greek proteios, meaning primary or of prime importance.

3.12 Proteins and Amino Acids

Proteins are essential components of protoplasm, form the structural framework of cells, and are linked with cell division and heredity. Enzymes, hormones, antigens and antibodies are proteins. They are polymers of amino acids containing C, H, O and N; most also contain sulphur and phosphorus, a few iron, copper and iodine. Protein is the most abundant organic compound in cells.

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. About 170 types are discovered, 25 are involved in protein synthesis, and most proteins are made of 20 types. Each has a central alpha carbon with an NH₂ (amino group) on one side, a COOH (carboxyl group) on the other, hydrogen on the third side, and a different R (radical) group on the fourth. Nine are essential (indispensable) — adults cannot synthesise them, so they are required in diet: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine. The rest are non-essential (dispensable) — the body can synthesise them, e.g. alanine, glycine, serine, tyrosine.

3.13 Peptide Linkage

Amino acids link to form a polypeptide chain by a peptide (amide) linkage, formed by condensation between the amino group (N-terminal) of one amino acid and the carboxyl group (C-terminal) of another, releasing water. One or more polypeptide chains unite to form a protein.

3.14 Significance of the Sequence of Amino Acids

Each protein has a unique, specific arrangement of amino acids, essential for its function; if any amino acid is out of place the protein fails. Example: sickle cell anaemia. Normal red blood cells are disc-shaped; haemoglobin has two alpha chains of 141 amino acids and two beta chains of 146 amino acids. In sickle cell anaemia, amino acid 6 of the beta chain is valine instead of glutamate; haemoglobin carries insufficient oxygen and red blood cells become sickle-shaped.

3.15 Classification and Levels of Structure

Fibrous proteinsGlobular proteins
Chains in fibrils; insoluble in water; non-crystalline, elastic; structural. Keratin (nails, hair), fibrin (blood clot), myosin (muscle), silk fibres, collagen (skin, bones, ligament, tendon)Spherical or ellipsoid by multiple folding; soluble in water, salt solution, acids, bases or alcohol; disorganised by environmental changes. Enzymes, antibodies, many hormones, haemoglobin, myoglobin

Levels: primary — linear sequence of amino acids; secondary — hydrogen bonding of the backbone folds the chain into alpha helix and pleated sheet; tertiary — three-dimensional folding from side-chain interactions; quaternary — more than one polypeptide chain.

3.16 Role of Proteins

  • Structural — keratin in feathers, horns, beaks, hair; collagen in bones and cartilages; histone arranges DNA into chromosomes; elastin in tendons and ligaments.
  • Functional — enzymes catalyse all cellular reactions; transport — haemoglobin transports oxygen and CO₂, myoglobin stores oxygen in red muscles (as named in the book); defence — fibrinogen and prothrombin clot blood; hormones regulate metabolism; storage — ovalbumin (egg white) and casein (milk); contractility — actin and myosin, and tubulin helps chromosome movement in anaphase; nucleoproteins form genes and chromatin.

Biuret test: biuret solution added to food changes from blue to violet if protein is present.

Key Points

  • Each amino acid has NH₂, COOH, H and a different R group on a central alpha carbon; nine are essential in diet.
  • A peptide bond joins amino acids by condensation, releasing water.
  • In sickle cell anaemia valine replaces glutamate at position 6 of the beta chain.
  • Fibrous proteins are insoluble and structural; globular proteins are soluble, folded and functional.

lessons.title: Lipids: Acylglycerols, Phospholipids, Terpenes, Waxes, Steroids and Prostaglandins
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are a heterogeneous group of organic compounds, insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as alcohol, ether, chloroform, acetone and benzene, with a greasy or oily consistency — fats, oils, waxes and cholesterol.

3.17 Nature of Lipids

Lipids contain C, H and O, but with a lower percentage of oxygen than carbohydrates, so they are lighter and much less soluble in water. Being hydrophobic they form membranes, act as storage compounds, and give double the energy of carbohydrates due to a high proportion of C–H bonds: 1 gram of carbohydrate gives 4.1 Kcal, protein 4.6 Kcal, and lipid 9 Kcal.

3.18 Classes of Lipids

Classified by solubility and hydrolysis products into acylglycerols, phospholipids, terpenes and waxes.

  • Acylglycerols (neutral fats) — esters of fatty acids and glycerol, the most abundant lipids. An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a fatty acid, releasing water; here the alcohol is glycerol, a three-carbon compound with an OH on each carbon. A fatty acid is a long straight chain of even-numbered carbons (2–30) with a carboxyl group at the end. With one, two or three fatty acids the molecule is a monoglycerol, diglycerol or triglycerol; triglyceride is most common. About 30 fatty acid types exist, e.g. acetic acid (2 carbons), stearic acid (18 carbons). Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds (palmitic acid, spelled palmatic in the book): solid at room temperature, more energy, mostly from animals. Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds (oleic acid): liquid, less energy, usually from plants.
  • Phospholipids — major components of all cell membranes, forming bilayers because they are amphiphilic. One molecule has two hydrophobic fatty acid tails and a hydrophilic head (glycerol backbone + phosphate group): fatty acids attach to carbons 1 and 2 of glycerol, phosphoric acid to carbon 3, and sometimes choline, serine or ethanolamine attaches to the phosphate. Heads face outward to water, tails inward away from water. Most common is phosphatidylcholine (lecithin). Too much fat in diet causes obesity and cardiovascular disorders such as high blood pressure and heart attack.
  • Terpenes — large, diverse compounds from plants and some insects, built from the isoprene unit, a five-carbon unsaturated hydrocarbon, C₅H₈ — also the basic unit for steroids, vitamins A, E, K and rubber. Two units: monoterpene (menthol); four: diterpene (vitamin A); six: triterpene (ambrein, from gums and resin); eight: tetraterpene (carotenoid); rubber is a polyterpene.
  • Waxes — long alkyl chains, completely water insoluble, generally solid at room temperature. Beeswax is the most common animal wax; plants have epicuticular waxes. They protect, act as a water barrier and prevent abrasive damage. Cutin on leaves and fruits and suberin in roots are waxes; waxes also store energy in microscopic aquatic plants and animals.

A phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic heads face water, hydrophobic tails face each other inside.

3.19 Steroids and Prostaglandins

  • Steroids — non-fatty-acid lipids with a core of 17 carbon atoms in 4 interlocked rings (three six-sided, the fourth five-sided); types vary by functional groups on the fourth ring. Cholesterol is structural in cell membranes and brain tissue; sex hormones (estrogen, progesterone, testosterone), vitamin D (calcium metabolism) and bile salts (emulsify fats) are steroids.
  • Prostaglandins — named from the prostate gland, first isolated from seminal fluid in 1935; hormone-like lipids found in almost every tissue, derived from fatty acids, each with 20 carbons including a 5-carbon ring. Aspirin-like drugs inhibit their synthesis (found in 1971). They dilate and contract smooth muscle, aggregate and disaggregate platelets, regulate inflammation and hormones, control cell growth, sensitise pain neurons, and regulate fever and menstrual cramping. Synthetic prostaglandins induce parturition and treat peptic ulcer.

Key Points

  • Lipids are hydrophobic and give 9 Kcal per gram.
  • A triglyceride is glycerol + three fatty acids joined by ester bonds.
  • Phospholipids are amphiphilic and form membrane bilayers; lecithin is most common.
  • Terpenes are built from isoprene (C₅H₈); steroids have 17 carbons in 4 rings; prostaglandins have 20 carbons.

lessons.title: Nucleic Acids, DNA, RNA, Central Dogma and Conjugated Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides: DNA carries hereditary information and RNA helps in, or controls, protein synthesis. They were first isolated in 1869 by Friedrich Miescher (spelled Fredrick in the book) from pus cells and salmon sperms as nuclein; Jones in 1920 proved there are two types, DNA and RNA. Partial hydrolysis yields nucleotides or nucleosides; complete hydrolysis yields bases, pentose sugars and phosphate ions.

3.20 Nucleotide, Nucleoside and Bases

  • Nucleoside — a nitrogen base linked to a pentose sugar by an N-glycosidic bond. Nucleotide — a nucleoside + phosphoric acid, existing as mono-, di- or triphosphate esters. DNA is made of deoxyribonucleotides, RNA of ribonucleotides.
  • Pyrimidine bases — single six-corner ring: thymine, cytosine, uracil. Purine bases — two rings: adenine, guanine.
  • Pentose sugars — deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄, in DNA) and ribose (C₅H₁₀O₅, in RNA); deoxyribose has one oxygen less at carbon 2. Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) forms an ester linkage with the OH group of the sugar.

3.21 ATP and 3.22 NAD

ATP is a mononucleotide: adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups. Adenine + ribose forms the nucleoside adenosine; adding one, two or three phosphoric acids by condensation gives AMP, ADP and ATP. ATP is the energy currency of the cell — its hydrolysis releases energy for muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses and protein synthesis. When two nucleotides join they form a dinucleotide: NAD has one nucleotide with a nicotinamide base and one with adenine, linked by their phosphates, and is derived from niacin (vitamin B). NAD carries electrons in redox reactions: NAD⁺ accepts two electrons and a proton to become NADH, a reducing agent. FAD is another dinucleotide coenzyme, becoming FADH₂.

3.23 Phosphodiester Linkage

This covalent bond forms the backbone of DNA and RNA, linking the 3rd carbon of one pentose to the 5th carbon of the next through a phosphate group. In formation, nucleoside triphosphates (ATP, GTP) are used; the 3-OH of the growing chain attacks the phosphate of the incoming triphosphate, the bond forms, and the other two phosphates are released as pyrophosphate (PPi), whose hydrolysis to two Pi is highly exergonic and makes the reaction effectively irreversible.

3.24 DNA: Watson and Crick Model

In 1951 Chargaff found adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine (purines : pyrimidines = 1:1). In 1953 Watson, Crick, Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin worked out the double helix; Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962, and Franklin provided X-ray diffraction evidence. DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose, phosphate and a base (purines adenine, guanine; pyrimidines thymine, cytosine). Two strands twist into an antiparallel double helix like a circular ladder — sugar and phosphate make the sides, bases make the rungs. Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and cytosine with guanine (three), so strands are complementary. Diameter is 2 nm, a full turn every 3.4 nm, with 10 base pairs per turn. DNA amount is fixed for a species; germ cells have half the DNA of somatic cells.

DNA double helix: antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones with A–T and G–C pairs inside.

3.25–3.26 RNA and Its Types

RNA is a single, unbranched chain of ribonucleotides with bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil; only Reovirus RNA is double-stranded. Some RNA coils into hair-pin loops by hydrogen bonds (A = U, G = C) within the same molecule. It is made in the nucleus from one DNA template strand, is mostly in the cytoplasm, helps DNA in protein synthesis, and is hereditary material in some animal and all plant viruses. The three types are made by transcription:

TypeRole
mRNA (3–4%)Carries information from DNA to ribosomes; its coding sequence determines the amino acid sequence
tRNA (about 15%)About 80 nucleotides; transfers a specific amino acid to the growing chain; at least 20 types per cell, about 45 kinds in humans
rRNA (about 80%)Catalytic component of the ribosome, a platform for protein synthesis; largest and most abundant RNA, made in the nuclear organizer region

3.27 Central Dogma and 3.28 Conjugated Molecules

Central dogma: genes in DNA are copied into mRNA by transcription, and mRNA is converted into polypeptide chains by translation at ribosomes; proteins link genotype (DNA) to phenotype. DNA replication is DNA to DNA by DNA polymerase. Conjugated molecules combine two classes of molecules: lipoproteins (lipid + protein, in cell, mitochondrial, endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes); nucleoproteins (nucleic acid + protein, e.g. ribosomes and chromosomes); glycolipids (glucose + lipid, in cell membranes, joined by a glycosidic bond); glycoproteins (glucose + protein, functioning as hormones, transport and structural proteins and receptors; blood group antigens contain glycoproteins).

Key Points

  • A nucleotide = base + pentose sugar + phosphate; a nucleoside is base + sugar only.
  • Purines have two rings; pyrimidines have one ring.
  • ATP is a mononucleotide energy currency; NAD is a dinucleotide redox coenzyme.
  • DNA is an antiparallel double helix, 2 nm wide, 10 base pairs per turn, A–T with 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C with 3.
  • Central dogma: DNA to RNA by transcription, RNA to protein by translation.

lessons.title: Enzymes: Biological Catalysts and the Active Site
lessons.notes_html:
Thousands of chemical reactions take place in the body of a living organism. The sum of all these reactions is called metabolism. A special group of chemicals responsible for facilitating and speeding up these reactions is called enzymes. They catalyse almost all metabolic reactions in the body, e.g. in the digestive tract.

The term enzyme was derived from a Greek word enzymon, meaning leavened. The first enzyme was discovered by Payen and Persoz from germinating barley seeds in 1833 and named diastase. The term enzyme was introduced by Wilhelm Kuhne in 1877. Enzymes are biological polymers that catalyse chemical reactions. They are thermolabile biocatalysts: mostly protein in nature, specific in function and coded by DNA.

Enzymes work both inside and outside the cell. The substance on which an enzyme acts is called the substrate. When an enzyme combines with the substrate it forms an enzyme-substrate complex. After the reaction, product is formed and the enzyme itself remains unchanged, so it can be used again. A few catalytic RNA molecules called ribozymes can also catalyse a specific substrate, e.g. peptidyl transferase controls polypeptide elongation during translation.

4.1 Active Site of Enzyme (Structure)

Enzymes are generally globular proteins: a linear chain of amino acids which gives rise to a three-dimensional structure. The sequence of amino acids specifies the structure of the active site, which determines the catalytic activity of the enzyme. The active site is a specific, charge-bearing, three-dimensional cavity. Its shape is designed according to the reactant (substrate), so it is specific for a particular substrate, although some related reactants can also bind to it. An enzyme may have one or more active sites.

  • Binding site — Where the substrate attaches by non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions).
  • Catalytic site — Where catalysis of the substrate takes place, i.e. conversion of substrate into products. It is a very small portion, comprising a small number of amino acids, usually ranging from 3 to 12.
  • Allosteric site — Another site an enzyme may contain; binding here causes conformational changes that increase or decrease enzyme activity.

The active site of an enzyme: the binding site holds the substrate, the catalytic site changes it, and the allosteric site controls activity.

Chemical Nature of Enzymes

Each enzyme has its own specific structure, which is required for its proper functioning. A complete functional enzyme is called a holoenzyme. It consists of two parts: the apoenzyme, the proteinaceous part of the enzyme (mostly inactive), and the cofactor, the non-proteinaceous part. Some enzymes are composed only of protein, with no cofactor attached, e.g. lipase.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are thermolabile biocatalysts: mostly proteins, specific in function, coded by DNA, and unchanged after the reaction.
  • The active site is a charge-bearing 3D cavity with a binding site and a catalytic site of only 3 to 12 amino acids.
  • Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (protein part) + cofactor (non-protein part).
  • Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules, an exception to the protein nature of enzymes.

lessons.title: Enzyme Cofactors: Inorganic Ions, Coenzymes and Prosthetic Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Enzyme cofactors are non-protein molecules or ions that help an enzyme function properly. Without these cofactors, many enzymes cannot catalyse reactions. Cofactors help enzymes in different ways, like binding the substrate, stabilizing the enzyme structure, and participating in the chemical reactions.

Types of Cofactor

A cofactor can be an inorganic metal ion, or an organic compound like flavin or haeme. The three types are compared below.

TypeHow it attachesExamples and work
Inorganic metal ionsLoosely attached activators, easily separatedFe, Mg, Zn, Ca, Cu, K and Co ions. They help in making the enzyme-substrate complex, by moulding the active site or the shape of the substrate.
CoenzymesOrganic, detachable and loosely attached; released from the active site during the reactionNADH, NADPH, FADH₂ and ATP. Most vitamins are coenzymes or components of coenzymes, which is why vitamins are needed in our daily diet.
Prosthetic groupsTightly bound, hence a permanent part of the enzymeHaeme in haemoglobin and myoglobin, biotin, flavin and ubiquinone.

Examples from the Book

  • Metal ion as activator — ATP + Glucose + Hexokinase + Mg → ADP + Glucose 6-phosphate. The Mg ion activates hexokinase.
  • Coenzyme in action — Ethyl alcohol + Alcohol dehydrogenase + NAD → Acetaldehyde + NADH₂. The coenzyme NAD carries hydrogen during the reaction.
  • Prosthetic group — Haeme stays permanently bound in haemoglobin and myoglobin.

So the apoenzyme alone is mostly inactive. It becomes a working holoenzyme only when the correct cofactor joins it, and the kind of attachment — loose or permanent — separates metal ions and coenzymes from prosthetic groups.

Key Points
