  • Cofactors are the non-protein part of an enzyme; they help in binding substrate, stabilizing structure and taking part in reactions.
  • Metal ions are loosely attached inorganic activators, e.g. Mg with hexokinase.
  • Coenzymes are loosely attached organic molecules, often from vitamins, e.g. NAD, NADH, NADPH and FADH₂.
  • Prosthetic groups are tightly and permanently bound, e.g. haeme.

lessons.title: Mechanism of Enzyme Action: Lock and Key and Induced Fit
lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes must bind their substrate before they can catalyse any chemical reaction. To understand the mechanism of enzyme action, two models have been proposed.

a) Lock and Key Model

This model was developed by the German chemist Emil Fischer in 1894. The specific action of an enzyme with a single substrate can be explained using a lock and key analogy: the lock is the enzyme and the key is the substrate. Only the correctly sized key, the substrate, fits into the key hole, which is the active site of the lock, the enzyme. The same enzyme can be used to catalyse hundreds of the same substrates.

The enzymes which work on this mechanism are called non-regulatory enzymes, because they are specific in their action and each enzyme can carry out only one particular reaction. When one enzyme can catalyse only one substrate, this is called absolute specificity, e.g. lipase, amylase, sucrase, maltase and urease. Example: Urea + Water —urease→ Ammonia + CO₂. This model explains the specificity of enzymes, but it does not say anything about the change in the active site.

b) Induced Fit Hypothesis (Model)

In 1958, Daniel Koshland suggested a modification to the lock and key model. According to the induced fit model, the active site of an enzyme is a flexible structure. Enzyme molecules are in an inactive form; to become active, enzymes must undergo slight conformational changes in structure to accommodate the substrate. This flexibility of the active site allows more than one type of related substrate to be attached in the active site.

A suitable analogy is that of hand and gloves: the hand corresponds to the substrate and the glove to the enzyme, shaped by insertion of the hand. Enzymes which follow the induced fit mechanism are called regulatory or allosteric enzymes, e.g. hexokinase and carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic anhydrase works in two steps: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, and it also helps haemoglobin load oxygen: Hb + 4O₂ → Hb4O₂ (oxyhaemoglobin).

4.4 Enzyme Catalysis

Catalysis is a phenomenon in which the rate of a reaction is altered with the help of a substance called a catalyst. The catalyst does not participate in the reaction; its concentration and composition remain unchanged. The catalysis in which enzymes act as catalysts is called enzyme catalysis. For example, lyases catalyse the lysis of a substrate without water or oxygen; ligases catalyse the joining of two substrates, often by the elimination of water, e.g. two glucose molecules unite to form maltose; isomerases catalyse the rearrangement of a single substrate; and hydrolases break polymers into monomers by the addition of water.

Enzymes are denatured by heat but not by cold, so enzymes stored below 0°C are able to function again. Luciferase is the enzyme in fireflies responsible for their light.

Key Points

  • Lock and key (Fischer, 1894): the active site is rigid, the substrate fits exactly, and the enzyme shows absolute specificity.
  • Induced fit (Koshland, 1958): the active site is flexible and changes shape slightly when the substrate binds — like a glove shaped by the hand.
  • Lock and key enzymes are non-regulatory; induced fit enzymes are regulatory or allosteric, e.g. hexokinase and carbonic anhydrase.
  • In enzyme catalysis the catalyst speeds the reaction and remains unchanged in concentration and composition.

lessons.title: Energy of Activation and Factors: Temperature, pH and Enzyme Concentration
lessons.notes_html:
4.5 Energy of Activation (EA)

All chemical reactions need energy to start. This minimal amount of energy required to start a reaction is called activation energy, denoted by EA and measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol) or kilocalories per mole (kcal/mol). Hundreds of reactions go on continuously in the cell, and all of them need activation energy — but such a huge amount of energy is not present in living organisms. Living organisms possess enzymes which lower the activation energy: with an enzyme, less activation energy is required to convert a substrate into product.

An enzyme lowers the activation-energy barrier between reactants (e.g. CO₂ + H₂O) and products (H₂CO₃).

The rate of an enzyme reaction can be determined by measuring the amount of substrate used or product formed during a period of time.

4.6 Temperature

Heat increases molecular motion: as temperature rises, substrate and enzyme molecules gain kinetic energy, successful collisions increase, and the rate rises. For every 10°C rise, the rate of enzyme activity doubles approximately.

  • Optimum temperature — The specific temperature at which enzyme catalytic activity is fastest. For enzymes found in humans it is around 37°C. After this point the rate decreases, and at 45–50°C enzyme activity stops, as the enzyme binding site denatures at this temperature.
  • Thermophilic bacteria — Some bacteria live in hot springs; the optimal temperature of thermophilic bacterial enzymes is approximately 75°C. Such enzymes are used in biological washing powders and detergents, which is why cloth washing needs lukewarm water, not too hot. Taq polymerase also has a higher optimal temperature, being adapted to extreme heat.
  • Low temperature — Molecules move slowly, so enzyme-substrate complexes form with difficulty. Near or below freezing, enzymes are inactivated but do not denature; on warming they regain activity. The temperature at which an enzyme becomes active again is called the minimum temperature.

4.7 pH

Every enzyme needs a specific pH for its proper functioning. The pH at which an enzyme works maximum is called its optimum pH. Some enzymes work best in an acidic medium, e.g. pepsin; some in a neutral medium, e.g. amylase; and others in an alkaline medium, e.g. lipase and alkaline phosphatase (in liver, intestine and kidneys). However, most enzymes in our body work in the range of pH 6–8. Some enzymes may work in both acidic and alkaline media, e.g. the papain enzyme in green papaya.

A change in pH alters the ionic charge of acidic and basic groups, disrupting the ionic bonding that maintains the enzyme's specific shape — so the shape changes and the active site may denature.

EnzymeOptimum pH
Pancreatic lipase7.4–7.8
Pepsin2.0
Trypsin7.8–8.7
Maltase6.1–6.8
Arginase9.0–9.5
Sucrase5.5

4.8 Enzyme Concentration

Enzyme concentration is directly proportional to enzyme activity: if substrate is kept high and pH and temperature are constant, more enzyme gives more activity, and less enzyme gives less. In natural conditions substrate is usually higher than enzyme; when the enzyme becomes saturated as compared to the substrate, the rate will not increase further — the saturation point.

A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments; in bacteria it provides defence against invading viruses.

Key Points

  • Activation energy (EA) is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction; enzymes lower it, so reactions run at body temperature.
  • Rate roughly doubles per 10°C rise up to the optimum (37°C in humans, about 75°C for thermophilic bacteria); at 45–50°C human enzymes denature, while cold only inactivates them.
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH (pepsin 2.0, sucrase 5.5, arginase 9.0–9.5); pH change disrupts ionic bonding and the shape of the active site.
  • Enzyme activity is directly proportional to enzyme concentration until the saturation point is reached.

lessons.title: Enzyme Inhibition: Irreversible, Reversible, Competitive and Feedback
lessons.notes_html:
4.9 Enzyme Inhibition

The term enzyme inhibition means to stop an enzyme from its functioning, usually by enzyme inhibitors or due to a change in temperature or pH. Such molecules or substances which stop enzyme activity are called enzyme inhibitors, such as drugs, toxins and products of enzymes. Some poisons are enzyme inhibitors, which is why a person exposed to poison may die. On the other hand, there are enzyme activators which bind to an enzyme to increase enzyme activity.

Cyanide irreversibly binds to and inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, a key enzyme of the electron transport chain, blocking cellular respiration and oxygen utilization. Enzymes which catalyse a reaction again and again are called regulatory enzymes, e.g. phosphofructokinase.

Types of Inhibitors

  • a) Irreversible inhibitors — These stop enzyme activity permanently, either by destroying (denaturing) the active site of the enzyme or by occupying the active site by making a covalent bond with it. Irreversible inhibitors often contain reactive functional groups, e.g. aldehydes and alkenes; these electrophilic groups make covalent bonds with amino acid side chains. They may be natural or artificial, e.g. poisons and the venom of snakes.
  • b) Reversible inhibitors — These attach to enzymes with non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and ionic bonds. They generally do not undergo chemical reactions when bonded to the enzyme and are easily removed from enzymes. Reversible inhibitors are of two types: competitive and non-competitive.

4.10 Competitive and Non-competitive Reversible Inhibitors

  • a) Competitive inhibitors — These have a similar shape to the substrate molecule, hence they compete with the substrate to occupy the active site. The process of inhibition depends on the concentration of substrate and inhibitors: with a high concentration of inhibitors, the chances of inhibition are also high.
  • b) Non-competitive inhibitors — These do not possess structural similarities with the substrate molecule, therefore they attach to the allosteric site of the enzyme rather than the active site. The attachment of the inhibitor changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate cannot bind with the active site. Such inhibitors are not affected by substrate concentration, and they lower the maximum rate (V-max) of the reaction.

4.11 Feedback Inhibition

The production of enzymes, hormones and other products should be in limit to maintain homeostatic conditions; the overproduction of any product in the body may prove fatal. The mechanism through which the production of different products is controlled in the body is known as the feedback mechanism.

Many reactions run in biochemical pathways, in which the product of the first reaction becomes the substrate of the next, until the desired end product is synthesized. To regulate that product, the pathway needs to be shut down — done by the feedback mechanism, an automatic system. Example: aspartate changes into threonine through five enzymatic reactions. When threonine becomes sufficient, it accumulates on the allosteric site of the first enzyme (E₁), changes the shape of the active site, and threonine production stops.

Key Points

  • Enzyme inhibitors stop enzyme activity; they include drugs, toxins and poisons such as cyanide, which blocks cytochrome c oxidase.
  • Irreversible inhibitors bind covalently and destroy the active site permanently; reversible inhibitors bind weakly by non-covalent bonds and can be removed.
  • Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete for the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind the allosteric site, change the active site shape and lower V-max.
  • Feedback inhibition: the end product (e.g. threonine) binds the allosteric site of the first enzyme of its pathway and switches the pathway off.

lessons.title: Classification of Enzymes and Their Importance in Homeostasis
lessons.notes_html:
4.12 Nomenclature of Enzymes (Classification of Enzymes)

The name of an enzyme is often formed by adding ase to the name of the substrate. Enzymes are also named for the action they perform, e.g. lipase breaks down lipids and cellulase breaks down cellulose. Enzymes are also named by taking into consideration both the substrate acted upon and the type of reaction catalysed, e.g. DNA polymerase, or according to the type of reaction they catalyse, e.g. oxidases and reductases.

1. Classification on the Basis of Reaction Types or Functions

The International Union of Biochemistry in 1961 gave a nomenclature system for enzymes. According to this system, enzymes are classified into six groups:

ClassReaction catalysed and examples
OxidoreductasesCatalyse oxidation-reduction reactions — removing or adding electrons or hydrogen ions. Sub-classes: oxidases (remove hydrogen), oxygenases (incorporate oxygen) and peroxidases (break H₂O₂ into H₂O and oxygen).
TransferasesTransfer a group from one molecule to another — amino group, carboxyl group, methyl and carbonyl group. Example: hexokinases transfer a phosphate group from ATP to glucose: Glucose + ATP → Glucose-6P + ADP.
HydrolasesBreak down proteins, fats and carbohydrates by adding water: lipase (lipids into fatty acids and glycerol), sucrase (sucrose into glucose and fructose), maltase (maltose into two alpha glucose), cellulase (cellulose into beta glucose), proteinase (protein into amino acids).
LyasesCatalyse the breakdown of a specific covalent bond and removal of a functional group without hydrolysis, e.g. decarboxylases add or remove a carboxyl group, and deaminases add or remove an amino group.
IsomerasesBring about intramolecular rearrangement within a molecule, e.g. phosphohexose isomerase changes glucose 6-phosphate to fructose 6-phosphate, and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) changes into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P).
LigasesResponsible for the formation of a bond between two substrates, e.g. polymerases join monomers into polymers, such as joining mononucleotides into a dinucleotide or polynucleotide by DNA polymerase or RNA polymerase.

4.13 Classification on the Basis of Substrate

  • Proteases — These break down proteins. These proteolytic enzymes are produced by all organisms, e.g. pepsin and renin in the stomach, and trypsin in the pancreas.
  • Lipases — These enzymes break down fats, e.g. pancreatic lipase and lingual lipase.
  • Carbohydrases — These enzymes break down carbohydrates like starch, cellulose and maltose, e.g. amylase, cellulase and maltase.
  • Nucleases — These enzymes cleave the phosphodiester bond between nucleotides of nucleic acid, e.g. endonucleases and RNases.

4.14 Importance of Enzymes in Maintaining Homeostasis and Its Disturbance

Homeostasis means the maintenance of the internal environment at a nearly constant state. Enzymes regulate metabolic reactions such as digestion, respiration and DNA replication, help to regulate body temperature and pH, and are also involved in signalling pathways and tissue repair.

When enzyme activity is disturbed due to enzyme inhibitors, homeostasis is affected, leading to various disorders. For example, Tay-Sachs disease is due to a lack of the enzyme hexosaminidase, which leads to the accumulation of lipids in nerve cells. A deficiency of insulin leads to the improper functioning of enzymes, causing a high blood glucose level.

Germinating seeds have enzymes which convert insoluble stored food into simpler soluble substances: the enzyme amylase digests starch and converts it into maltose.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are named by adding ase to the substrate, by the action performed, or by both substrate and reaction type.
  • The six reaction classes (IUB, 1961) are oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases.
  • By substrate, enzymes are proteases, lipases, carbohydrases and nucleases.
  • Enzymes maintain homeostasis by regulating digestion, respiration, DNA replication, temperature and pH; their disturbance causes disease, e.g. Tay-Sachs disease.

lessons.title: Bioenergetics: Role of Light, Carbon Dioxide and Water in Photosynthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Bioenergetics is an interdisciplinary field of biochemistry, cell biology and physiology which deals with the study of the processes by which cells use, store and release energy. The quantitative study of energy relationships in a biological system is called bioenergetics. A central component is energy transformation, the conversion of energy from one form to another. Biological energy transformations obey the laws of thermodynamics, and energy is necessary for growth and reproduction — we cannot exhibit any characteristic of life without energy.

Photosynthesis is the biological process that captures light (solar) energy and converts it into chemical energy, i.e. organic molecules, e.g. glucose. It takes place in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Photosynthesis is a redox process which links the non-living world to the living world: it involves the reduction of carbon dioxide into sugars and the oxidation of water into molecular oxygen. (Redox: oxidation is the loss of electrons by a molecule; reduction is the gain of electrons.) The overall reaction is:

6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ (in sunlight, with chlorophyll)

5.1.1 Role of Light in Photosynthesis

Light is electromagnetic energy. Solar radiations consist of photons — separate packets of energy (Greek Phos = light) that travel in waves; short waves contain more energy than long waves. The full range of radiation from the Sun is the electromagnetic spectrum; visible light (380–750 nm) is only a small part of it.

Photons of visible light have enough energy to promote electrons to a higher electron shell in atoms. Leaves absorb only 4–10% of the total light which falls on them; the rest is reflected. Only 1–2% of the total absorbed light is converted into chemical energy through photosynthesis. This energy is used in the synthesis of ATP from ADP or AMP — called phosphorylation, an endergonic reaction: ADP + Pi + energy → ATP. The formation of ATP during photosynthesis is called photophosphorylation. Blue light is highly absorbed by chlorophyll and red light is also very effective for photosynthesis; violet and orange are moderately effective; green light is poorly absorbed and mostly reflected, which is why plants appear green.

5.1.2 Role of CO₂ in Photosynthesis

CO₂ is a raw material, along with water, for photosynthesis in plants and algae. Air contains about 0.03 to 0.04% CO₂. Terrestrial plants use this CO₂, while aquatic plants use dissolved CO₂, bicarbonates and carbonates present in water as a source of carbon. CO₂ acts as the carbon source for the synthesis of organic compounds (glucose), and plants use it in the Calvin cycle. An increase in CO₂ concentration in the environment increases the rate of photosynthesis, but when CO₂ concentration rises above 1%, the rate rapidly slows down due to stomatal closing.

5.1.3 Role of Water in Photosynthesis

Water is also a raw material of photosynthesis. A film of water present around the mesophyll cells of the leaf helps to absorb CO₂. The water molecule is broken down into hydrogen and oxygen by P680 during photolysis. The hydrogen combines with CO₂ to form organic food, and molecular oxygen is released into the atmosphere.

Earlier it was thought that the released oxygen comes from CO₂. Van Neil (1931) first observed that water splits during photosynthesis: its hydrogen is used to synthesize glucose, while O₂ is released as a by-product. Robin Hill (1940) supported this with oxygen-18 isotope experiments: algae grown in isotope water evolved isotope oxygen, while isotope CO₂ gave oxygen without the isotope — proving the source of the evolved oxygen is water.

An exergonic reaction is a spontaneous chemical reaction that releases energy (a catabolic reaction); an endergonic reaction is an anabolic chemical reaction that consumes energy.

Key Points

  • Bioenergetics studies how cells use, store and release energy; photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy (glucose).
  • Visible light is 380–750 nm; leaves absorb only 4–10% of falling light and convert only 1–2% of it into chemical energy. ATP formed in photosynthesis is by photophosphorylation.
  • CO₂ (0.03–0.04% of air) is the carbon source for glucose; above 1% CO₂ the rate falls because stomata close.
  • Water is split by photolysis at P680; Van Neil (1931) and Robin Hill (1940) proved the released O₂ comes from water, not CO₂.

lessons.title: Photosynthetic Pigments, Absorption Spectra and Photosystems
lessons.notes_html:
5.2 Photosynthetic Pigments

Photosynthetic pigments are present in the chloroplasts of plants, in algae and in the membrane of photosynthetic bacteria, and they capture the light energy necessary for photosynthesis. Higher plants have two major types of pigments: carotenoids and chlorophylls.

  • a) Carotenoids — A group of yellow, orange, red or brown pigments that absorb blue, violet and green light. They are produced by plants, algae, several fungi and bacteria, and absorb different wavelengths than chlorophyll. Chlorophyll b and carotenoids together are called accessory pigments: they absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a, which starts the light reaction: Carotenoids → Chlorophyll b → Chlorophyll a. In flowers and fruits they attract insects, birds and other animals for pollination and seed dispersal, and they protect chlorophyll from oxidation by the oxygen produced in photosynthesis. There are two types: carotenes (red to orange hydrocarbons; the red colour of tomato and chilli is due to carotenes, and beta-carotene, the most common carotene, is converted to vitamin A by animals and human beings) and xanthophylls (yellow, oxygen-containing derivatives of carotenes; lutein and zeaxanthin are found in green leafy vegetables and eggs, and the yellow colour of leaves in autumn is due to lutein).
  • b) Chlorophylls — Green, main photosynthetic pigments which absorb violet, blue, orange and red wavelengths, while green and yellow are least absorbed and are reflected, so leaves look green. There are six types of chlorophyll (a, b, c, d, e and f); only two occur in the chloroplasts of higher plants, chlorophyll a and b. Chlorophyll c, d and e are found only in algae, while chlorophyll f is found in cyanobacteria.

Chlorophyll a and Chlorophyll b

Chlorophyll a occurs in all photosynthetic organisms except photosynthetic bacteria, so it is termed the universal photosynthetic pigment. It is also known as the primary photosynthetic pigment because it is involved in the primary reaction of photosynthesis, i.e. converting light energy into chemical energy. Its molecular formula is C₅₅H₇₂O₅N₄Mg. Chlorophyll b occurs in all photosynthetic organisms except brown, red and blue algae; its molecular formula is C₅₅H₇₀O₆N₄Mg.

Structure of Chlorophyll

Each chlorophyll molecule has two main parts: one flat, square part which absorbs light is the hydrophilic head; the other part is a long anchoring hydrophobic tail. The head is composed of four pyrrole rings (pyrrole is a five-sided, nitrogen-containing compound) having an Mg ion in the centre — an Mg-porphyrin with two side chains: an acid chain (a methyl ester) and a hydrocarbon chain, the long tail of the alcohol phytol, attached to one of the pyrrole rings by an ester linkage with propionic acid. Phytol is insoluble and serves to anchor the molecule in the membrane of the granum.

Chlorophyll aChlorophyll b
Blue-green in colourYellow-green in colour
Chemical formula C₅₅H₇₂O₅N₄MgChemical formula C₅₅H₇₀O₆N₄Mg
Possesses a methyl (–CH₃) groupPossesses an aldehyde (–CHO) group
Essential pigment: it can absorb and convert light energy into chemical energyAccessory pigment: absorbs energy of different wavelengths and transfers it by resonance to chlorophyll a

5.3 Role of Photosynthetic Pigments in Absorption and Conversion of Light Energy

The clusters of photosynthetic pigments are called a photosystem. When pigments absorb light they are said to be excited: light energy boosts the normally low-energy electrons of chlorophyll to a higher energy level. The high-energy electron is transferred to a primary electron acceptor and ultimately into chemical energy, so the chlorophyll becomes oxidized. The excited state is unstable; as molecules return to the unexcited state, the released energy can pass from one chlorophyll molecule to another. A spectrophotometer measures the relative abilities of pigments to absorb different wavelengths. Chlorophyll synthesis requires sunlight, N, Mg ions and warm temperature, so leaves synthesize more chlorophyll in summer.

5.4 Absorption Spectra of Chlorophyll a, b and Carotenoids

An absorption spectrum exhibits the absorbed amount of light of different wavelengths (different colours) from the visible spectrum. The main photoreceptors are chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, which absorb violet-blue (430 nm) and red light (670 nm); green light (550 nm) is least absorbed. Carotenoids absorb light between 430–470 nm and transfer it to chlorophyll b, then to chlorophyll a. Chlorophyll a and b show different absorption spectra: chlorophyll a shows absorption peaks at about 680 and 700 nm, while chlorophyll b absorption peaks range between 450–475 nm.

5.5 Arrangement of Pigments in Photosystem I and II

There are two photosystems in the light reaction, photosystem I (PS I) and photosystem II (PS II), named in the order of their discovery. Each photosystem contains several hundred pigment molecules and has two parts:

  • Antenna complex — Possesses many molecules of chlorophyll a, b and carotenoids. All these pigment molecules serve as an antenna for gathering solar energy, which is passed from one pigment to the other and finally transferred to the reaction centre.
  • Reaction centre — Contains one molecule of chlorophyll a along with the primary electron acceptor and electron carriers of the electron transport system, which plays a role in the generation of ATP by chemiosmosis.

PS I absorbs light of 700 nm and is called P700, while PS II absorbs light of 680 nm and is called P680. The primary electron acceptor traps the electrons from the reaction centre and then passes them to the series of electron carriers. Electrons have two pathways in the light reaction: the non-cyclic electron pathway, which is predominant and generates both ATP and NADPH, and the cyclic electron pathway, which is less common and generates only ATP.

Key Points

  • Higher plants have two pigment types: carotenoids (accessory, protective) and chlorophylls (main pigments); chlorophyll a is the universal, primary pigment.
  • Chlorophyll a (C₅₅H₇₂O₅N₄Mg, –CH₃ group) converts light into chemical energy; chlorophyll b (C₅₅H₇₀O₆N₄Mg, –CHO group) only transfers energy to a.
  • A chlorophyll molecule has a hydrophilic porphyrin head (four pyrrole rings, Mg at the centre) and a hydrophobic phytol tail that anchors it in the granum membrane.
  • Each photosystem has an antenna complex that gathers light and a reaction centre (P700 in PS I, P680 in PS II) with a primary electron acceptor.

lessons.title: Light Reactions: Non-cyclic and Cyclic Photophosphorylation
lessons.notes_html:
5.6 Mechanism of Photosynthesis — Light Dependent Reactions

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy using CO₂ and H₂O. It occurs in two main stages inside the chloroplast. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane of the chloroplast and require light energy. They convert light energy into chemical energy in the form of ATP and NADPH, releasing O₂ as a by-product. There are two pathways of light reactions.

1. Non-cyclic Photophosphorylation (Z-Scheme)

The purpose of the light reactions is the production of ATP, NADPH and O₂.

  • Step 1 — It starts with photon absorption by photosystem II (PS II): light excites electrons in chlorophyll a (680) in PS II.
  • Step 2 — Water is split to replace the lost electrons in PS II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The first electron acceptor of PS II is pheophytin.
  • Step 3 — Excited electrons pass from PS II → plastoquinone (PQ) → cytochrome complex (b₆f) → plastocyanin (PC). The energy released from the electrons pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid lumen, creating a proton gradient.
  • Step 4 — Protons flow back into the stroma via ATP synthase, forming ATP. The formation of ATP in this way is called photophosphorylation.
  • Step 5 — Photosystem I (PS I) also absorbs light, which excites electrons in P700 of PS I. These electrons come from the first electron transport chain. Electrons from PS I are transferred to ferredoxin (Fd), then to NADP reductase, which reduces NADP⁺ to NADPH. In PS I the electron acceptor chain passes electrons through iron-sulphur proteins to ferredoxin.

The end products of non-cyclic photophosphorylation are ATP, NADPH and O₂.

The Z-scheme: electrons rise at P680, fall through PQ, the cytochrome complex and PC, rise again at P700, and fall to NADP⁺ to form NADPH.

2. Cyclic Photophosphorylation

The purpose of cyclic photophosphorylation is to produce ATP only. It occurs when there is a low level of ATP or a high level of NADPH. Steps: (1) Photon absorption by PS I (P700) excites electrons, which pass to ferredoxin (Fd). (2) Electrons return to the cytochrome complex instead of going to NADP, then to plastocyanin and back to PS I — which is why it is called cyclic. (3) As electrons move through the cytochrome complex, protons are pumped, creating a proton gradient used to produce ATP. The end product is ATP only, and no NADPH and O₂.

Conditions leading to the cyclic pathway: (1) When production of ATP is low, the Calvin cycle does not begin. (2) Due to the slow rate of the Calvin cycle, NADPH is not oxidized into NADP. (3) Many other enzymatic reactions use ATP in the stroma, so the Calvin cycle becomes slow. (4) A limited supply of CO₂ also affects carbohydrate synthesis.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylationCyclic photophosphorylation
Electrons do not come back to the same moleculeElectrons come back to the same molecule
First electron donor is waterFirst electron donor is P700 (PS I)
Involves both PS I and PS IIInvolves PS I only
Last electron acceptor is NADPLast electron acceptor is P700
Net products are ATP, NADPH and O₂The product is ATP only

Key Points

  • Light reactions run in the thylakoid membrane and produce ATP, NADPH and O₂.
  • Non-cyclic flow (Z-scheme): water → PS II (P680) → PQ → cytochrome complex → PC → PS I (P700) → ferredoxin → NADP⁺, giving ATP, NADPH and O₂.
  • Protons pumped into the thylakoid lumen flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP — photophosphorylation.
  • Cyclic flow uses PS I only, returns electrons to P700, and makes ATP only — no NADPH and no O₂.

lessons.title: The Calvin Cycle and Cellular Respiration: Aerobic and Anaerobic
lessons.notes_html:
5.7 Light Independent Reaction or Dark Reaction (Calvin Cycle)

The reactions of the Calvin cycle occur in the stroma. The purpose of these reactions is to convert CO₂ into glucose or other carbohydrates, using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. These reactions do not require light directly, but depend on light-reaction products. Rubisco is the most abundant protein on Earth. The main phases of the Calvin cycle are:

  • a) Carbon fixation — Carbon dioxide is fixed into ribulose bisphosphate in the presence of the enzyme ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase (RuBisCO). Three molecules of CO₂ combine with three molecules of RuBP and form six molecules of 3-PGA, a 3-carbon compound.
  • b) Reduction — Each molecule of 3-PGA is phosphorylated by ATP and reduced by NADPH. This produces six molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). One molecule of G3P exits the cycle and is used to make glucose or other organic compounds.
  • c) Regeneration of RuBP — The remaining five G3P molecules (3-carbon each) are rearranged using ATP to regenerate three RuBP (5-carbon each). This allows the cycle to continue.

From the light reaction, 9 ATP and 6 NADPH are used in the Calvin cycle to produce one PGAL, which can be used to form glucose, fructose, etc.

The Calvin cycle in the stroma: fixation of CO₂ by Rubisco, reduction of PGA to G3P, and regeneration of RuBP.

5.8 Cellular Respiration

Respiration is a series of complex oxidation-reduction reactions in living organisms. In this process, cells get energy through the breakdown of various organic substances. There are two types of respiration: aerobic and anaerobic.

5.8.1 Anaerobic Respiration (Fermentation)

Anaerobic respiration takes place in the absence of molecular oxygen; it is also known as fermentation. It is an incomplete oxidation-reduction reaction and occurs in the cytoplasm. It has two types:

  • a) Alcoholic fermentation — It occurs in primitive cells and cells of some eukaryotic organisms, such as in yeast and plants. It consists of glycolysis followed by the decarboxylation of pyruvate; the pyruvate is further broken down by alcoholic fermentation into alcohol and CO₂. Overall: 2 Pyruvate + 2NADH + 2H⁺ → 2 Acetaldehyde + 2CO₂ → 2 Ethanol + 2NAD⁺. Net gain is 2 ATP.
  • b) Lactic acid fermentation — It takes place in many bacteria, animals and the muscles of humans. It consists of glycolysis followed by the reduction of pyruvate by NADH: each pyruvate molecule is converted into lactic acid in the absence of molecular oxygen. Overall: 2 Pyruvate + 2NADH + 2H⁺ → 2 Lactate + 2NAD⁺.

5.8.2 Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of molecular oxygen. Glucose is a high-energy molecule, and its breakdown products CO₂ and H₂O are low-energy molecules. This process releases stored energy: the electrons are removed from the substrate (e.g. glucose) and eventually received by an oxygen atom, which combines with H⁺ to form water. The overall equation for the breakdown of glucose is:

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 36ADP + 36Pi → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + 36ATP

Cellular respiration takes place in four steps: (1) Glycolysis, (2) Oxidation of pyruvic acid, (3) Krebs cycle, (4) Electron transport chain.

Key Points

  • Calvin cycle (stroma): fixation (3 CO₂ + 3 RuBP → 6 PGA by Rubisco), reduction (PGA → 6 G3P using ATP and NADPH), regeneration (5 G3P rebuild 3 RuBP).
  • One G3P in six leaves the cycle to make glucose and other sugars; 9 ATP and 6 NADPH are used per PGAL produced.
  • Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) runs in the cytoplasm without oxygen and nets 2 ATP: alcoholic (yeast, plants — ethanol + CO₂) and lactic acid (bacteria, muscles).
  • Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, fully breaks glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, and yields 36 ATP in the book's overall equation, through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain.

lessons.title: Glycolysis, Oxidation of Pyruvate and the Krebs Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
5.9 Glycolysis

Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm. It is the breakdown of glucose into two pyruvate molecules. It is found in all organisms and evolved before the Krebs cycle and ETC. It occurs in the cytosol and does not require molecular oxygen (thus probably the first life was anaerobic). Each step is catalysed by an enzyme. Glycolysis is divided into two phases: the preparatory phase and the oxidative phase. Overall it gives a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

a) Preparatory Phase (Energy Investment Phase)

  • 1. Phosphorylation of glucose takes place by ATP, producing an activated glucose 6-phosphate molecule, in the presence of the enzyme hexokinase.
  • 2. Glucose 6-phosphate is converted by the enzyme phosphohexose isomerase to its isomer fructose 6-phosphate.
  • 3. Another ATP molecule transfers a second phosphate group, forming fructose 1,6-biphosphate, by the enzyme phosphofructokinase.
  • 4. Fructose 1,6-biphosphate splits, with the help of the enzyme aldolase, into two 3-carbon isomers: phosphoglyceraldehyde (G3P or PGAL) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP).
  • 5. G3P and DHAP are isomers and readily interconvertible. DHAP is not directly utilized, so it changes into G3P with the help of phosphotriose isomerase. The preparatory phase is complete; glycolysis now proceeds with two molecules of G3P, so the remaining reactions occur twice.

b) Oxidative Phase (Energy Yielding or Pay-off Phase)

  • 1. Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized: two electrons (hydrogen atoms) are removed and transferred to NAD, which is reduced to NADH. Inorganic phosphate from the cytosol is added, forming 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG or DPG), by the enzyme G3P dehydrogenase.
  • 2. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (DPG) is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA). A phosphate bond is transferred from DPG to ADP, forming ATP — this is called substrate level phosphorylation. The reaction is catalysed by phosphoglycerate kinase.
  • 3. 3-PGA is converted to 2-phosphoglycerate (2-PGA); only the position of the phosphate group is changed, with the help of phosphoglycerate mutase.
  • 4. From 2-phosphoglycerate, a molecule of water is removed and phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) is formed, with the help of the enzyme enolase.
  • 5. PEP gives up its high-energy phosphate, which converts ADP to ATP by substrate level phosphorylation. The product is pyruvate or pyruvic acid (C₃H₄O₃).

5.10 The Oxidation of Pyruvic Acid

It takes place in two stages: (1) oxidation of pyruvic acid to form acetyl coenzyme A, and (2) oxidation of acetyl coenzyme A (through the Krebs cycle).

a) Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This is a transition (link) reaction — it connects glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, and CO₂ is released during it. Pyruvate enters the mitochondria via active transport with the help of pyruvate translocase. In the matrix it undergoes decarboxylation to acetaldehyde and CO₂; the acetaldehyde is oxidized (NAD is reduced to NADH) to an acetyl group, which joins coenzyme A to form the 2-carbon acetyl-CoA. It is both decarboxylation and oxidation (the dehydrogenase removes electrons from pyruvate, using NAD as coenzyme), and it occurs twice per glucose.

b) Oxidation of acetyl-CoA. It takes place through the Krebs cycle: a 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetate) binds with 2-carbon acetyl-CoA to become a 6-carbon compound. This passes through a series of electron-yielding oxidation reactions; two carbon dioxide molecules are given off, and finally the 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetate) is regenerated, free to bind another acetyl-CoA.

5.11 Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle)

The Krebs cycle is a cyclic metabolic pathway located in the matrix of the mitochondria. It was named after Sir Hans Krebs, the British scientist who discovered it in 1930. It is also called the citric acid cycle because the first substance produced is citric acid, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) because the first three compounds generated have carboxylic groups (COOH). Steps of the Krebs cycle:

  • 1. The 2-carbon acetyl group (from the transition reaction) joins with a 4-carbon oxaloacetate molecule, forming a 6-carbon citrate molecule, releasing CoA with the help of the enzyme citrate synthetase.
  • 2. Citrate is converted to an isomer, cis-aconitate, with the help of the enzyme aconitase, and then to isocitrate.
  • 3. Isocitrate is oxidized by NAD to 5-carbon alpha-ketoglutarate; NAD is reduced into NADH and CO₂ is released. This step is catalysed by isocitrate dehydrogenase.
  • 4. Alpha-ketoglutarate is converted into 4-carbon succinyl-CoA, NAD is reduced to NADH, and another molecule of carbon dioxide is removed, by alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
  • 5. Succinyl-CoA is oxidized to 4-carbon succinate by succinyl thiokinase. The reaction releases sufficient energy, which is used to form GTP, which then reacts with ADP to form ATP (substrate level phosphorylation).
  • 6. Succinate is converted to 4-carbon fumarate, and FAD is reduced into FADH₂, with the help of succinate dehydrogenase.
  • 7. Fumarate combines with water to produce 4-carbon malate, with the help of the enzyme fumarase.
  • 8. Malate, in the presence of malate dehydrogenase, is oxidized by NAD to oxaloacetate, and NADH is formed.
  • 9. Oxaloacetate is again ready to combine with acetyl-CoA to start a new citric acid cycle.

For two acetyl groups (one glucose), the cycle takes in 2 acetyl groups, 2ADP + 2Pi, 6NAD and 2FAD, and gives out 4CO₂, 2ATP, 6NADH and 2FADH₂.

Key Points

  • Glycolysis (cytoplasm, no oxygen needed) splits glucose into two pyruvates: the preparatory phase invests 2 ATP, the pay-off phase returns ATP by substrate level phosphorylation — net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
  • The transition reaction converts each pyruvate into acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO₂ and forming NADH; it links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
  • Krebs cycle (matrix): acetyl-CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C), which is oxidized step by step back to oxaloacetate, releasing CO₂.
  • Per glucose, the Krebs cycle outputs 4CO₂, 2ATP, 6NADH and 2FADH₂ — the NADH and FADH₂ carry electrons to the electron transport chain.

lessons.title: Electron Transport Chain, Chemiosmosis and Substrate Level Phosphorylation
lessons.notes_html:
5.12 Electron Transport Chain (ETC)

In the electron transport chain there is a series of protein complexes and electron carriers located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. They transfer electrons from NADH and FADH₂ to molecular oxygen (O₂) via a sequence of redox reactions. The flow of electrons is coupled with proton pumps, generating a proton pumping gradient across the membrane; the stored energy in this gradient drives the synthesis of ATP by ATP synthase. The electrons extracted in the Krebs cycle are temporarily housed within NADH and FADH₂ molecules; these enter the electron transport system, where H⁺ are removed, ATP and H₂O are formed. Each NADH + H⁺ gives 3 ATP in the electron transport chain, while each FADH₂ gives 2 ATP.

Steps of the Electron Transport Chain

  • 1. NADH transfers electrons to complex I in the presence of the enzyme NADH dehydrogenase. NADH donates 2 electrons to complex I, which passes them to ubiquinone, and 4 protons are pumped across the membrane.
  • 2. Electrons transfer from FADH₂ to complex II in the presence of the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, and no protons are pumped.
  • 3. Ubiquinone (Q) is reduced to ubiquinol (QH₂): electrons from both complex I and complex II reduce ubiquinone to ubiquinol.
  • 4. Electrons transfer from ubiquinol to complex III; 4 protons are pumped and electrons are passed to cytochrome C.
  • 5. Cytochrome C is a small mobile protein that transfers electrons from complex III to complex IV.
  • 6. Electrons transfer from cytochrome C to complex IV in the presence of the enzyme cytochrome c oxidase. Complex IV receives electrons and transfers them to oxygen, forming H₂O, and 2 protons are pumped.
  • 7. The proton gradient drives ATP synthesis, and the enzyme involved is ATP synthase.

The electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane: electrons from NADH and FADH₂ end at oxygen, and the proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

5.13 Chemiosmosis

Chemiosmosis is the movement of ions across a semipermeable membrane, down their electrochemical gradient — for example, the generation of ATP by the movement of H⁺ across a membrane during cellular respiration or photosynthesis. The chemiosmotic theory was proposed by Peter Mitchell, who got the Nobel Prize in 1978 for his chemiosmotic theory of ATP production in the inner membrane of mitochondria and chloroplasts. Chemiosmosis can also be defined as the coupling reaction in which synthesis of an ATP molecule occurs during the movement of H⁺ due to a proton gradient. Chemiosmosis generates more ATP as compared to substrate level phosphorylation.

Mechanism: (1) The mitochondrial membranes have transmembrane channels which can pump protons. The flow of electrons induces a change in the shape of the protein, so protons move out of the inner compartment of the mitochondria, and the proton (H⁺) concentration in the outer compartment (intermembrane space) becomes greater than that of the inner compartment. (2) A proton gradient is established between the outer and inner membrane. This gradient drives the protons back across the membrane; their movement induces the formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This process is controlled by the enzyme ATP synthase.

5.14 Substrate Level Phosphorylation

Substrate level phosphorylation occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. ATP formation from ADP and Pi needs an input of energy; the energy comes from the breakdown of organic molecules in the cells. This type of reaction, which releases energy, is called an exergonic reaction. An enzyme transfers a phosphate group to ADP from a substrate, so an ATP molecule is formed; the energy from the exergonic reaction is greater than the energy input necessary to drive ATP synthesis. It takes place in these steps: (1) during glycolysis, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is converted into 3-phosphoglycerate, and phosphoenol is converted into pyruvate; (2) during the Krebs cycle, succinyl-CoA is converted into succinate.

Adding all stages together, the energy yield is 36 or 38 ATP per glucose molecule: 4 ATP by substrate level phosphorylation, and 32 or 34 ATP through the electron transport chain.

Key Points

  • ETC (inner mitochondrial membrane): NADH → complex I → CoQ → complex III → cytochrome c → complex IV → oxygen, which forms water; FADH₂ enters at complex II.
  • Complexes I, III and IV pump protons (4, 4 and 2); each NADH gives 3 ATP and each FADH₂ gives 2 ATP.
  • Chemiosmosis (Peter Mitchell, Nobel Prize 1978): the proton gradient drives protons back through ATP synthase, joining ADP + Pi into ATP.
  • Substrate level phosphorylation makes ATP directly from a substrate in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle; total yield per glucose is 36 or 38 ATP.

lessons.title: G3P, Respiration of Fats and Proteins, Photorespiration and C4 Plants
lessons.notes_html:
5.15 Importance of G3P (PGAL)

PGAL is a 3-carbon compound which is an intermediate of both respiration and photosynthesis. In glycolysis, the preparatory phase completes with the splitting of fructose biphosphate into PGAL and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), and both are interconvertible. The oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate produces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and 2 NADH molecules, which lead to the formation of pyruvic acid.

PGAL is also formed during the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis: one PGAL molecule leaves the Calvin cycle and is converted into glucose phosphate within the chloroplast, which is converted into starch. Fixed carbons leave the chloroplast in the form of dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which is formed from PGAL. DHAP can be used to make the six-carbon sugars glucose and fructose, which become a disaccharide called sucrose; sucrose is then transported to other parts of the plants.

5.16 Formation of Acetyl-CoA from Fats

Acetyl coenzyme A is an organic molecule which takes part in many biochemical reactions. The main function of acetyl-CoA is to deliver the acetyl group to the Krebs cycle, so as to be oxidized for energy production. Fats are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol. Glycerol gets phosphate from ATP to become 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde, and fatty acids are changed by beta-oxidation into acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA then enters the Krebs cycle, where each acetyl group is oxidized into CO₂ and H₂O, and the energy released is used to form ATP.

5.17 Cellular Respiration of Proteins and Fats

Animals and humans, besides glucose, also consume fats and proteins to harvest energy. Fats are broken down into glycerol and three fatty acids: first the glycerol is phosphorylated, then it enters the glycolytic pathway at the level of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (PGAL), while fatty acids enter the mitochondrion, where their carbons are removed two at a time; they form acetyl-CoA (2C), which is the entry point for the Krebs cycle.

Animals digest proteins into amino acids. If amino acids are in excessive quantity, or the body is starved, they can be used as fuel. The size of the R-group determines whether the carbon chain is oxidized in glycolysis (pyruvate), in the Krebs cycle, or as acetyl-CoA. When amino acids are degraded, the amine group is removed to yield ammonia; this process is called the deamination reaction.

5.18 Photorespiration

Photorespiration is a light-dependent metabolic pathway in C₃ plants. In this process the enzyme Rubisco reacts with O₂ instead of CO₂ gas, converting ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate into one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of the 2-carbon compound phosphoglycolate. The phosphoglycerate is used in the Calvin cycle, but phosphoglycolate is not used in the Calvin cycle, so it must be recycled. This salvage process occurs in the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria. It consumes ATP and releases CO₂, thus effectively opposing net carbon fixation.

5.19 Events Occurring through Photorespiration

RuBP carboxylase, also known as Rubisco, also acts as an oxygenase (combining with O₂ instead of CO₂). As a carboxylase it adds CO₂ to RuBP to produce two PGA in the dark reaction; as an oxygenase it adds oxygen to RuBP, producing one PGA and one phosphoglycolate. Phosphoglycolate loses its phosphate to become glycolate, which is converted into glycine (an amino acid) by reactions in mitochondria, chloroplast and especially peroxisomes. Glycine diffuses into the mitochondria, where two glycine molecules are converted into serine and CO₂: 2 glycine → Serine + CO₂ + NH₃ + NADH. In the whole pathway RuBP is converted into serine and CO₂, using ATP and NADPH from the light reaction; serine is used to make other organic compounds.

5.20 Disadvantages of Photorespiration

Photorespiration occurs in C₃ plants during the daytime and has a number of disadvantages: it causes energy loss by using ATP and NADH without producing sugar; CO₂ is also lost, because instead of fixing CO₂ it is released; during hot, dry conditions, when stomata close to prevent water loss, the oxygen level inside the leaf rises and promotes photorespiration, which slows down the rate of photosynthesis; RuBP is also used up, reducing the availability of RuBP for carbon fixation; and it limits plant growth by reducing the production of sugars and other carbohydrates.

5.21 Effect of Temperature on the Activities of RuBisCO

The activity of RuBisCO depends on the relative concentration of CO₂ and oxygen in the leaf. When the CO₂ level inside a leaf becomes low, photorespiration initiates. This happens on hot, dry days, when the plant secretes abscisic acid, which closes the stomata and prevents excess water loss. If fixation continues while stomata are closed, CO₂ is used up and the oxygen released by photosynthesis cannot leave, so the oxygen-to-CO₂ ratio in the leaf increases.

5.22 Photosynthesis in C₄ Plants

In the normal process of photosynthesis, a 3-carbon compound called PGA is formed as the first detectable product of photosynthesis; therefore these plants are called C₃ plants. However, some plants growing in dry and hot conditions produce a four-carbon compound (C4) called oxaloacetate as the first product of photosynthesis in the dark reaction. These plants are called C₄ plants, and this type of photosynthesis is called C₄ photosynthesis. C₄ plants have an additional metabolic pathway in the light-independent phase, beside the Calvin cycle. This C₄ metabolic pathway is also called the Hatch-Slack cycle, and it is an adaptation to avoid photorespiration.

C₃ plants use Rubisco to react CO₂ with RuBP. C₄ plants use a different enzyme, phosphoenol pyruvate carboxylase (PEPCO), to fix CO₂ to a compound known as phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP). The PEP is reduced into another molecule called malate. The malate carries CO₂ to a special type of cells called bundle sheath cells, where the Calvin cycle proceeds.

C₃ PlantsC₄ Plants
Chloroplasts are located only in mesophyll cells of the leaf; all the mesophyll cells carry out the Calvin cycleChloroplasts are present both in mesophyll cells and in bundle sheath cells; only mesophyll cells fix CO₂ by PEPCO, while bundle sheath cells carry out the Calvin cycle
At high temperature, the rate of photosynthesis is lowAt high temperature, the rate of photosynthesis is high
Examples: most plants are C₃, such as pea, wheat, rice and all woody treesExamples: only some angiosperms, such as sugarcane, maize and most of the grasses

Key Points

  • G3P (PGAL) links respiration and photosynthesis: it is made in glycolysis and in the Calvin cycle, and it is the starting point for glucose, starch and sucrose.
  • Fats feed respiration through glycerol (entering at PGAL) and fatty acids (beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA); excess amino acids are deaminated, releasing ammonia, and their carbon chains enter at pyruvate, acetyl-CoA or the Krebs cycle.
  • Photorespiration: Rubisco acts as an oxygenase in C₃ plants, producing phosphoglycolate that is salvaged through chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria — wasting ATP and NADH and releasing CO₂, so it lowers photosynthesis, especially on hot, dry days.
  • C₄ plants avoid photorespiration: PEPCO fixes CO₂ into oxaloacetate (4C) in mesophyll cells, malate carries CO₂ to bundle sheath cells, and the Calvin cycle runs there (Hatch-Slack cycle), e.g. sugarcane and maize.

lessons.title: Acellular Life: History and Status of Viruses
lessons.notes_html:
A life form that exists without a cellular structure is called acellular or non-cellular life. Viruses show non-cellular life. The word virus was first used by the French biologist Louis Pasteur in 1884; it is derived from the Latin word venome, which means poison. Viruses are neither prokaryotic nor eukaryotic, because they have no cellular structure. They are tiny particles, seen only with an electron microscope, largely composed of proteins and a single type of nucleic acid (RNA or DNA). They are obligate (strict) intracellular parasites — they cannot live without a living host. The study of viruses is virology and its expert is a virologist. Viruses cause diseases such as AIDS, hepatitis, herpes simplex and polio in animals, and cotton leaf curl disease (CLCD) in plants. Other acellular forms are viroids (short circular single stranded RNA without a protein coat) and prions (infectious agents made entirely of protein).

6.1 History of Viruses

  • Charles Chamberland — French microbiologist. In 1884 he made special porcelain filters that separate bacteria from a diseased portion, because bacteria cannot pass through them; many infectious agents, e.g. of smallpox and tobacco mosaic disease, could pass through.
  • Iwanavsky — Russian biologist. In 1892, working on Tobacco Mosaic Disease (TMD), he found no bacteria on the porcelain filter and concluded the agents were not bacteria and were so small that they passed through the pores. He called them filterable viruses. Filtered juice rubbed on healthy leaves still produced the disease.
  • W. M. Stanley — American biologist. In 1935 he proved by experiments that TMD was caused by viruses, not bacteria. He isolated Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV); the TMV looked like rod-shaped silver crystals.
  • Twort and Herelle — Twort was British and Herelle was French. In 1917–1918 they independently discovered that viruses also infect bacteria; they called them bacteriophage.
  • Other biologists — After TMV, thousands of viral strains were discovered; according to microbiologists, millions of viruses are still undiscovered. Recently, corona virus was discovered in China, causing a dangerous respiratory disease.

6.2 Status of Virus

  • Living concept — Viruses have their own genetic material (DNA or RNA), are sensitive to the environment, undergo mutation, spread diseases, are intracellular parasites, reproduce inside a living cell, and are killed by ultraviolet radiations and strong chemicals.
  • Non-living concept — Viruses are acellular, do not respire, use the energy of the host, do not excrete, have no protoplasm, and can be stored in the form of crystals.
  • Borderline concept — Viruses are placed at the boundary between living and non-living things, because they show properties of both. Most biologists consider them non-living because they are not capable of autopoiesis (ability of reproduction) without a host.

Key Points

  • Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites made of protein and one type of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).
  • Chamberland (1884) made porcelain filters; Iwanavsky (1892) found filterable viruses; Stanley (1935) isolated TMV; Twort and Herelle (1917–1918) found bacteriophage.
  • Viruses sit on the borderline of living and non-living: they reproduce and mutate inside a host, but have no protoplasm and can be crystallised outside it.

lessons.title: Classification of Viruses and Structure of a Bacteriophage
lessons.notes_html:
Viruses cannot be classified by one method. There are four bases of classification (6.3): shape or capsid, host, nucleic acid or genome, and envelope.

Classification of Viruses

  • By shape or capsid — Rod-shaped viruses have a helical capsid, e.g. TMV. Some are rounded, e.g. polio virus. Some have a brick-shaped capsid, e.g. vaccinia virus and influenza virus. Some are tadpole-shaped, e.g. bacteriophage. Some have many-sided, polyhedral capsids, e.g. Adeno virus.
  • By host — Plant viruses (Phytophagineae) infect plants and have only RNA; more than 2000 plant viral diseases are known, e.g. tobacco mosaic disease. Animal viruses (Zoophagineae) infect animals including man, mostly have DNA but some have RNA; they cause foot and mouth disease in livestock, mumps and measles by paramyxo virus, and cancer in man by Rous sarcoma virus. Bacteriophage (Phagineae) infect bacteria and have only DNA, e.g. T₃ virus.
  • By nucleic acid or genome — Single stranded (ss) DNA virus, e.g. Paro virus (causes rashes in animals). Double stranded DNA virus, e.g. Adeno virus, Herpes virus, pox virus. Single stranded RNA reverse transcribing viruses (ss RNA RT), e.g. HIV (retro virus). Double stranded RNA virus (ds RNA), e.g. Reo virus, which causes diarrhoea.
  • By envelope — Some viruses have a lipid envelope derived from the host membrane. Non-enveloped or naked viruses have no envelope, e.g. bacteriophage. Enveloped or complex viruses have an envelope on their capsid, e.g. influenza virus. An enveloped virus gets its envelope as it buds through the host cell membrane, taking a piece of that membrane, with viral glycoprotein spikes, with it.

6.4 A. Bacteriophage: Structure of T₄ Phage

Viruses that reproduce inside a bacterium are bacteriophages (Greek: phage = eater). They vary from 24 to 200 nm in length (1 nm is a billionth of a metre). The body has two main parts, head and tail. The head is the upper swollen portion: its outer protein coat or capsid is icosahedral (20 equilateral triangular faces) and made of repeating protein units called capsomeres; the inner core contains only DNA, the genome of the phage, with from a few to over 100 genes. There is no cytoplasm. DNA and capsid together are called the nucleocapsid. The tail is a hollow tube through which nucleic acid enters the host, and has six parts:

  • Neck — Narrow area just under the head, not surrounded by protein sheath.
  • Sheath — Contractile protein layer around the tail; its contraction pushes the nucleic acid into the host.
  • Collar — Area under the neck from where the sheath starts.
  • Whiskers — Very thin filaments in the collar region; they control retraction and extension of the tail fibers.
  • Base plate (end plate) — Flat area at the lower end of the sheath, containing the enzyme lysozyme, which dissolves the bacterial cell wall. Base plate and tail fibers attach the phage to the bacterium.
  • Tail fibers and tail pins — Six thread-like fibers attached around the base plate; needle-shaped tail pins on its lower side recognise the part of the bacterial cell wall for entry of nucleic acid.

A T₄ bacteriophage: icosahedral head, contractile tail, base plate and six tail fibers.

Key Points

  • Viruses are classified by capsid shape, host, nucleic acid and envelope.
  • Plant viruses have only RNA, bacteriophages only DNA; animal viruses mostly DNA, some RNA.
  • T₄ phage: icosahedral capsid head with DNA, and a tail of neck, sheath, collar, whiskers, base plate and six tail fibers.

lessons.title: HIV Structure, Viruses and Their Hosts, and Survival Without a Host
lessons.notes_html:
6.4 B. HIV: Structure

HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is an RNA enveloped retrovirus — it can convert its RNA into DNA in a host cell. It causes AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome), belongs to the family Retroviridae, is spherical and about 120 nm in diameter. It is surrounded by a lipoprotein viral envelope derived from the host cell in which HIV multiplies. The envelope carries glycoprotein spikes: each spike has an upper knob of gp 120 and a lower rod, the transmembrane, made of gp 41; the spikes attach the virus to the host cell and let the viral RNA enter. Under the envelope is a layer of matrix protein, and in the centre a cone-shaped capsid. The inner core contains two identical single strands of RNA and three enzymes: reverse transcriptase (converts RNA to DNA), protease (breaks larger proteins into smaller proteins) and integrase (helps to integrate the viral DNA into host DNA). There are two varieties: HIV-I, the most common pathogenic strain, and HIV-II, not widely recognised outside Africa.

HIV: enveloped sphere with spikes, cone-shaped capsid, two RNA strands and three enzymes.

6.5 Viruses and the Hosts: The Parasitic Nature

Viruses cannot carry out their life processes on their own. They have no organelles such as mitochondria or ribosomes, cannot produce energy, grow or reproduce without a host, and depend completely on a host to survive and multiply. A virus cannot complete its life cycle without parasitising a host cell, because it cannot replicate its genetic material (DNA or RNA) by itself. The virus injects its genetic material into the host cell; this takes complete control of the cellular machinery, and the host cell is forced to produce viral components (proteins and nucleic acids). These are assembled into new viruses, which finally burst the host cell, come out and infect other cells. Viruses are host specific: their surface proteins fit only the receptors of particular cells — tobacco mosaic virus infects tobacco plants, polio virus infects humans and some primates, and each bacteriophage infects only specific bacteria.

6.6 Protection of Viruses Against the Immune System

  • i) Viruses infect and kill or inactivate the components of the immune system, e.g. HIV survives by infecting and destroying T₄ cells.
  • ii) Some viruses cover themselves with host proteins, so they are not recognised by the immune system.
  • iii) Many viruses change their shapes and antigens, so vaccines and the immune system become ineffective against them.
  • iv) Mutagenic variation occurs due to mutagens, which protects viruses from the host immune response.

6.7 Survival of Viruses Without a Host

Viruses have no necessary machinery (metabolic enzymes, ribosomes etc.), so isolated viruses are converted into crystals: they become inactive, look like dead bodies and show no metabolic activity, but their genome (RNA, DNA) remains alive for a long time. When viral crystals reach a living host, they become active again and multiply using the host machinery. This life inside host cells is also why viral diseases are harder to treat than bacterial diseases: a drug that kills the virus may harm the host cell too, and viruses mutate rapidly.

Key Points

  • HIV: spherical enveloped retrovirus, about 120 nm, gp 120 and gp 41 spikes, cone capsid, two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase.
  • Viruses are obligate parasites: the host cell provides all machinery for replication.
  • Viruses escape the immune system by destroying immune cells, wearing host proteins and changing antigens.
  • Outside a host, viruses form inactive crystals; the genome survives until a living host is reached.

lessons.title: Life Cycles of Bacteriophage and HIV, and Phage Use in Genetic Engineering
lessons.notes_html:
The life cycle of a bacteriophage is of two types (6.8): the lytic cycle and the lysogenic cycle.

A. Lytic Cycle (Master–Slave Relationship)

Phage DNA enters a bacterial cell, reproduces, bursts the cell and releases mature phages — master (virus) and slave (bacteria), because phage DNA gets complete hold over the host enzymatic system. The phage attaches by its tail fibers at a specific receptor site; lysozyme from the tail dissolves a portion of the bacterial cell wall, the tail sheath contracts and the tail pins form a hole, so phage DNA enters and the empty head and tail remain outside. The phage DNA destroys the bacterial DNA and replicates using the bacterial enzymes; it forces the bacterium to produce capsid and tail proteins — the cell becomes a factory for viral components. New viruses appear within 15 minutes, and after 25–30 minutes about 200 new bacteriophages are formed. The cell wall then bursts (lysis), due to the pressure of the new viruses and lysozyme attacking from the inner side, and the released phages attack new bacteria.

B. Lysogenic Cycle (Host–Guest Relationship)

Phage DNA enters the bacterial cell, associates with the bacterial DNA in a peaceful way and divides with the bacterium — host (bacterium) and guest (virus), because the viral DNA acts as a harmless guest and the cell reproduces normally; phage replication and bacterial growth start at exactly the same time. The integrated viral DNA is called a prophage and the process is lysogeny. The prophage replicates when the bacterial chromosome doubles, so each daughter bacterium inherits one copy. This may continue for many generations. Sometimes the viral DNA separates from the host chromosome and starts the lytic cycle; this is called induction.

Lytic cycleLysogenic cycle
Takes over at once; about 200 phages in 25–30 minutes; cell bursts. Master–slave.DNA joins the chromosome as a prophage and is copied quietly for many generations. Host–guest; induction can switch it to lytic.

6.9 Use of Bacteriophage in Genetic Engineering

  • Use as a vector — Phage DNA is used as a vector, called lambda; it is more efficient than a bacterial plasmid and can carry larger fragments of DNA.
  • To construct a genomic library — A genomic library is a collection of bacteriophage clones; the full set of genes of an individual is its genome. Viral DNA is removed and acts as a vector; a foreign gene is inserted to make recombinant DNA (rDNA); the virus infects a host bacterium and completes the lytic cycle, so many phages are formed, each with a copy of the foreign gene, which is then used to produce important compounds.
  • To stop bacterial growth — Viral enzymes like holins and lysins degrade the bacterial cell wall, so phages can control antibiotic-resistant bacteria, as an alternative to antibiotics.

6.10 Life Cycle of HIV

  • Recognition and entry — HIV recognises a T₄ cell: its gp 120 fits the CD₄ protein (cluster of differentiation) on the T₄ cell. HIV enters by endocytosis, its envelope is left outside, and the cone-shaped coat degenerates in the cytoplasm, freeing the two RNA strands and three enzymes.
  • Reverse transcription — Reverse transcriptase forms a complementary DNA strand (cDNA) on the viral RNA; ribonuclease degrades the viral RNA; a second DNA strand forms on the cDNA, giving double stranded DNA. This conversion of viral RNA to complete DNA is reverse transcription.
  • Integration — Integrase integrates this viral DNA into the host chromosome; the integrated DNA is called provirus, because it controls the formation of new viruses.
  • Formation and release — Proviral DNA forms genome RNA and mRNA (controlled by host RNA polymerase). Genome RNA is surrounded by capsid proteins; mRNA forms large proteins which protease breaks into virion structural proteins; the components form an immature virion, released by budding — it takes a portion of the cell membrane as its envelope and becomes a mature virion that affects other T₄ cells.

Key Points

  • Lytic cycle: attachment, lysozyme entry, takeover, about 200 phages in 25–30 minutes, then lysis.
  • Lysogenic cycle: prophage copied with the bacterium; induction switches it to the lytic cycle.
  • Lambda phage is a vector for genomic libraries and against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
  • HIV cycle: gp 120 binds CD₄, reverse transcription makes DNA, integrase forms a provirus, new virions bud off.

lessons.title: HIV and AIDS: Name, Specificity, Symptoms, Treatment and Prevention
lessons.notes_html:
6.11 Justification of the Name of HIV, Based on T-Helper Cells

A research team from the Pasteur Institute in France and the National Institute of Health in USA discovered the causal agent of AIDS in 1984; in 1986 it was named Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). The team also suggested the name Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS); a syndrome is a disease with many signs at the same time. T-helper cells are an important part of the immune system: they do not directly kill pathogens, but activate other immune cells to fight pathogens. HIV targets only T-helper cells, enters and replicates inside them; the cell stops its function and becomes a factory producing new HIV. As more T-helper cells are destroyed, the immune system becomes weak — this is immunodeficiency. When the immune system becomes severely weak from the loss of a very large number of T-helper cells, the person progresses to AIDS. CD₄ (Cluster of Differentiation 4) are glycoproteins.

6.12 Specificity of HIV on Host Cells

HIV targets only T-helper cells in human blood, a type of white blood cells (WBCs) crucial for the immune system. Its specificity is due to its requirement for a specific receptor: the CD₄ receptor is present on the surface of T-helper cells; HIV binds with this receptor and then enters the cell for replication.

6.13 Symptoms of AIDS: Three Stages of HIV Infection

  • A) Asymptomatic Carrier (AC) — First stage; no proper symptoms, although the person is highly infectious. Some report fever, chills, aches, swollen lymph glands and itchy rash; these disappear, with no other symptoms for nine months or longer. It can be identified by a standard HIV blood test. Screening is by ELISA, but the PCR test is recommended as more authentic.
  • B) AIDS Related Complex (ARC) — Second stage; swollen lymph glands in the neck, armpits or groin for months, night sweats, persistent cough, flu, persistent diarrhoea, loss of memory, depression and inability to think clearly.
  • C) Full Blown AIDS (FBA) — Final stage; severe weight loss, weakness, persistent diarrhoea and opportunistic infections due to a very weak immune system.

6.14 Opportunistic Diseases That Attack an AIDS Victim

Opportunistic infections are normally prevented by a strong immune system; they start when it becomes very weak:

  • Respiratory infections — Lungs and respiratory tract, e.g. pneumonia and tuberculosis.
  • Mouth and throat infections — By herpes simplex virus (HSV) and by yeast (a microscopic fungus).
  • Eye infections — Pink eyes and keratitis (infection of the cornea), by bacteria, viruses and fungi.
  • Cancer — Kaposi sarcoma (cancer of blood vessels) and lymphoma (cancer of the lymphatic system), caused by viruses.

6.15 Treatment of AIDS

There is no proper treatment or vaccine to cure AIDS. A) Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) — several antiretroviral drugs of different classes are used daily, minimising drug-resistant strains; they do not cure AIDS but help people with HIV live healthier and longer. Common drugs: azidothymidine (AZT) and didanosine (DDI). B) Stem cell based gene therapy — a genetically engineered hematopoietic stem cell is transplanted with anti-HIV genes, so new blood cells are formed that resist HIV. Hematopoietic stem cells give rise to new blood cells in the bone marrow (hematopoiesis). The red ribbon is a symbol of solidarity with AIDS patients; 1st December is World AIDS Day, observed since 1988.

6.16 Prevention Against the Transmission of HIV

  • Follow the Islamic teaching; refrain from immoral sexual activities, because AIDS is basically an STD (sexually transmitted disease).
  • Never reuse used syringes and needles; for transfusion, use blood only after proper screening for HIV.
  • Use all medical and dental appliances only after proper sterilisation.
  • An AIDS-affected mother should not feed her babies; have regular medical checkups; never reuse used razors, toothbrushes and blood bags.

Key Points

  • HIV (named 1986) destroys T-helper cells, which activate other immune cells — their loss causes immunodeficiency and then AIDS.
  • HIV is specific because only T-helper cells carry the CD₄ receptor that gp 120 binds.
  • Three stages: Asymptomatic Carrier, AIDS Related Complex, Full Blown AIDS.
  • No cure or vaccine; HAART (AZT, DDI) prolongs healthy life; prevention is screened blood, sterile instruments and no reuse of syringes, razors or toothbrushes.

lessons.title: Viral Diseases: Hepatitis C, Herpes, Polio and Cotton Leaf Curl Disease
lessons.notes_html:
Viruses cause many diseases in plants and animals including man (6.17); their sources of transmission are given in 6.18.

1. Hepatitis C

A fatal form of hepatitis; it may cause cirrhosis (degeneration) of the liver, or liver cancer and death, if not properly treated. It is caused by hepatitis C virus (HCV), an enveloped single stranded RNA virus; humans are the reservoir of HCV. Symptoms: jaundice, liver enlargement, abdominal pain, fatigue, sometimes fever, pale urine and faeces, nausea and anorexia. There is no vaccine and no hyper immuno globulins available for hepatitis C. Prevention: never use used syringes, blood bags, razors or toothbrushes, and transfuse blood only after proper screening of donor blood.

2. Herpes Simplex

A highly contagious, naturally occurring disease of mankind, caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), an enveloped double stranded DNA virus with a large genome. A) Oral herpes or cold sore herpes — caused by HSV type-1 (HSV1), transmitted by saliva, physical contact with an infected person, or sharing toothbrushes. Symptoms: cold sores around the lips and mouth, watery blisters around the neck and face, and vesicular lesions (painful changes of tissues). B) Genital herpes — caused by HSV type-2 (HSV2), transmitted through sexual contact (an STD). Symptoms: water blisters in the genital areas, burning sensation during urination, fever, vesicular lesions, muscle aches; sores are usually below the waist. Both types are prevented by avoiding physical contact with infected persons, and treated with antiviral medicines as ointments or pills; healthy food and rest speed recovery.

3. Polio

Poliomyelitis or polio is a highly infectious viral disease causing breathing problems, paralysis and even death. It occurs mostly in childhood, all over the world. The polio virus was first identified by Karl Landsteiner in 1908. Polio viruses are the smallest known viruses; they contain RNA in a spherical capsid and infect the cells of the central nervous system. The virus is usually spread by contaminated faecal matter entering the mouth, and by food and water contaminated by faeces or saliva. a) Non-paralytic symptoms: flu, weakness, fever, sore throat, headache, stiff neck, vomiting, fatigue, muscle tenderness. b) Paralytic symptoms: loss of muscle reflexes, severe muscle pain and spasm, damage to the motor nerves of the limbs, and paralysis of arms and legs. Polio is incurable once it occurs; relief measures are physical therapy, orthopedic surgery, moist heat for muscle pain, and braces or corrective shoes. Prevention is by hygienic measures and two vaccines: inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) and oral polio vaccine (OPV). Polio has been almost eradicated; the book notes Pakistan, Afghanistan and Nigeria as countries where polio cases are identified.

4. Cotton Leaf Curl Disease (CLCD)

A serious cotton disease causing heavy damage, caused by a complex of viruses called cotton leaf curl gemini virus (CLCuV); up to now 5 viruses of this complex have been identified. Plant disorders: curling of leaf margins, swelling and darkening of leaf veins, downward cupping of younger leaves and stunted growth; the infected leaf shows small and large vein thickening and leaf enation. CLCD is controlled by insecticides against the white fly (Bemisia tabaci), which spreads the viruses among plants. Prevention: remove affected plants, remove alternate hosts between cotton crops such as radish, tobacco and tomato, and grow resistant varieties.

6.18 Sources of Transmission

DiseaseSource of transmission
Hepatitis CMostly by blood, mainly through contaminated needles of syringes.
HerpesDirect contact with an affected person.
PolioPerson-to-person contact; water contaminated with infected faecal material; mucus of a patient who coughs or sneezes; touching the faeces of a patient.
Cotton leaf curl diseaseSpread to plants by the white fly (Bemisia tabaci).

Key Points

  • Hepatitis C (HCV, enveloped ssRNA) can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer, and has no vaccine.
  • Herpes (HSV, enveloped dsDNA): oral HSV1 by saliva and contact; genital HSV2 is an STD.
  • Polio (smallest virus, RNA in a spherical capsid) attacks the central nervous system, is incurable, and is prevented by IPV and OPV.
  • CLCD is caused by the CLCuV complex, spread by the white fly Bemisia tabaci.

lessons.title: Prions and Viroids, Global Economic Loss and Flu Vaccine Limitations
lessons.notes_html:
6.19 Prions and Viroids

Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles that accumulate within nerve cells and destroy them. They were discovered in 1982 by the American biologist W. M. Stainly (name as printed in the book). They are composed of only proteins, with no nucleic acids or genetic material: all organisms carry genetic information in nucleic acid, but prions contain information in their proteins. They are a modified form of normal proteins synthesised in the brain and bone marrow, have a different structure from normal body protein, are resistant to the protease enzyme, and are more resistant to heat and UV radiations than viruses. Viroids are the smallest known infectious agents, made of a single molecule of circular RNA, first discovered by T. O. Diener in 1971. A viroid contains 246–270 nucleotides and has no protein coat or envelope, so viroids are called simple RNA. The mechanism of viroid replication is unclear so far, and viroids are smaller than viruses.

6.20 Diseases Caused by Prions and Viroids

Prions affect the nervous system of humans and other mammals. Human diseases: Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (CJD), kuru and Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI), caused by eating beef and products from cattle with prion diseases. Mad cow disease is a common prion disease of bovine (cattle); the book also calls it scrapie. Prion diseases are incurable; the illness is progressive and may lead to death. Viroid diseases occur in plants, e.g. potato spindle tuber disease and cucumber pale fruit; the only known human disease caused by viroids, according to the book, is Hepatitis D.

PrionsViroids
Composed of only protein; larger than viroids; filamentous shape.Composed of only RNA; smallest known pathogens; circular shape.
Cause animal diseases that affect nervous tissues.Affect plants (only known human disease is Hepatitis D, per the book).
More resistant to heat and UV radiations.Less resistant to heat and UV radiations.

6.21 Viral Infections and Global Economic Loss
