Viral infections cause a great loss in the global economy. Affected persons must remain at home and cannot travel, which badly affects transportation, hotels, restaurants and tourism. Many people fall ill, healthcare expenditures increase, factory schedules are disturbed and production decreases, so the chain of demand and supply is disturbed worldwide — a heavy loss to industrial sectors. Fear and uncertainty make consumers avoid spending. a) COVID-19 has caused extreme bad effects since early 2020: stock markets crashed, poverty increased, oil prices fell to record lows, unemployment rose sharply, many businesses shut down temporarily, small businesses closed permanently, and global trade slowed down. b) Bird flu (avian influenza) infects birds, especially chickens, is deadly, and can affect humans in contact with infected birds. In an outbreak, millions of birds are killed to stop the spread: poultry farmers lose heavily, food prices rise from shortages of eggs and meat, poultry workers lose jobs, and human infection adds healthcare costs — billions of dollars of global losses across agriculture, trade, health and employment. A vaccine is a substance used to stimulate the immune system against a specific disease or pathogen; development of immunity without infection is called immunisation.

6.22 Limitations of the Vaccine for the Common Cold / Flu Virus

Vaccines are available for many diseases, e.g. polio, T.B. and measles, and a vaccine is also prepared for flu, but with many limitations. There is no single flu virus: flu is caused by many strains, so one vaccine is not enough for all of them. Flu viruses quickly change their genetic make-up by mutation and exchange their genetic material, so new varieties are formed which the previously prepared vaccine cannot control, and new varieties develop resistance against the old vaccine. Flu-like symptoms also appear due to allergy and bacterial infection, which a flu vaccine cannot control. Every year the flu vaccine is modified to deal with the new strains.

Key Points

  • Prions are infectious proteins causing CJD, kuru, FFI and mad cow disease; they resist heat, UV and protease.
  • Viroids are naked circular RNA of 246–270 nucleotides causing potato spindle tuber and cucumber pale fruit diseases.
  • COVID-19 and bird flu show how viral infections cause billions in global economic losses.
  • Flu vaccines are limited because flu viruses mutate and exchange genes; the vaccine is remade every year.

lessons.title: Prokaryotes: Taxonomic and Phylogenetic Position, and Occurrence of Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
A prokaryote (Greek: Pro = before, Karyons = nucleus) is a unicellular organism with a simple structure that lacks a membrane bound nucleus and other membrane bound organelles like mitochondria and Golgi complex. Prokaryotes have great economic and environmental importance, greatly affect human health, and are largely used in research and biotechnology. Archaea, eubacteria and cyanobacteria are examples of prokaryotes. Archaea and bacteria evolved independently from one ancient common ancestor that lived about 2.5 to 3.2 billion years ago.

7.1 Taxonomic Position of Prokaryotes

Earlier, the term bacteria was used for all single celled microscopic prokaryotes, and biologists placed them in a separate kingdom, Monera. Characteristics of Monera: all organisms are unicellular, generally non-motile, though some show simple movement by gliding or by flagella; mostly heterotrophs, some photosynthetic or chemosynthetic; nucleus and cell organelles are absent; all contain naked coiled DNA; the most common example is bacteria. Later, molecular systematic studies showed that prokaryotic life is composed of two separate domains:

  • 1) Archaea — Archaios is a Greek word meaning ancient. A smaller group of primitive forms of bacteria: single celled microorganisms distinct from bacteria and eukaryotes, with a basic difference in the mRNA and tRNA of archaea and bacteria. They have no peptidoglycan in their cell walls; their plasma membrane contains special types of lipids that allow them to live in extreme conditions; their RNA polymerase enzymes are more complex than those of bacteria. They are often found in extreme environments and are called extremophiles. By habitat they are of three types: Methanogens (methane producers) in swamps and marshes, e.g. Methanobacterium formicom; Halophiles (salt lovers) in extremely salty conditions, e.g. Halobacterium halobium; Thermoacidophiles (heat and acid lovers) in hot and acidic volcanic areas, hot springs and geysers, e.g. Thermus aquaticus.
  • 2) Eubacteria — Eu is a Greek word meaning true: a larger group of true bacteria. Bacterium (plural bacteria) is a Greek word meaning small stick or rod. Their cell walls contain peptidoglycan. Mostly they are parasites or saprobes, but some are autotrophs. They show asexual reproduction by binary fission and sexual reproduction by genetic recombination. They spread many diseases in plants, animals and human beings, while certain kinds are beneficial, e.g. in making yogurt, cheese and vinegar.

7.2 Phylogenetic Position of Prokaryotes

  • A. rRNA as a molecular clock — Carl Woese in 1977 proposed that archaea have a separate line of evolutionary descent from bacteria. His phylogenetic taxonomy is based on genes encoding ribosomal RNA (rRNA): rRNA is ancient and there is no change in rRNA generation after generation, so ribosomal RNA is commonly recommended as a molecular clock for reconstructing phylogenies. Prokaryotes are now divided into two evolutionary domains, Archaea and Eubacteria.
  • B. Gene sequencing — Gene sequencing studies explain that bacteria diverged first, either from archaea or eukaryotes. Research indicates that the common ancestor of archaea and bacteria was probably a hyperthermophile that lived about 2.5 to 3.2 billion years ago.

7.3 Occurrence of Bacteria

Bacteria show a wide range of habitat and distribution. They are found in soil and air, in fresh water and under the depth of the sea, even in glaciers and highly polluted water. They can live in drought conditions in which other plants would die. They are abundant in the bodies of living and non-living animals and plants, in hot springs, alkaline and acidic soils, humid forests, milk, the roots, leaves and fruits of plants, and in the digestive tract, throat, large intestine and on the skin surface. Briefly, bacteria are found in any environment in which life can exist. The book notes about 5 x 10^30 bacteria on Earth.

Key Points

  • Prokaryotes lack a membrane bound nucleus and organelles; the old kingdom Monera is now split into the domains Archaea and Eubacteria.
  • Archaea have no peptidoglycan and include methanogens, halophiles and thermoacidophiles; eubacteria are the true bacteria with peptidoglycan walls.
  • Carl Woese (1977) used rRNA as a molecular clock; the common ancestor lived about 2.5 to 3.2 billion years ago.
  • Bacteria occur everywhere life can exist: soil, air, water, glaciers, hot springs and inside other organisms.

lessons.title: Structure of a Typical Bacterium and Cyanobacteria
lessons.notes_html:
The bacterium is presented as a model prokaryote, as it shows all the properties of prokaryotic cells (7.4). Its body is divided into cell wall, capsule, slime layer, cell membrane, flagella, pili, fimbriae, cytoplasm and nuclear region. The bacterial cell membrane lacks cholesterol.

Parts of a Bacterial Cell

  • Cell wall — The outer covering, without cellulose or chitin, made of a special compound called peptidoglycan (murein), composed of protein and sugar. It is a dead structure, because the bacterial cell can survive if it is removed. It gives shape to the cell, acts as a barrier, protects from external damage, and materials are exchanged through it.
  • Capsule — A thick, rigid extracellular layer outside the cell wall in some bacteria, tightly attached and not easily washed away, made of simple sugar or polysaccharide and rarely proteins. It is an additional protective layer: it prevents loss of water and protects from phagocytosis. Encapsulated bacteria cause disease while the same bacteria without a capsule do not, e.g. Diplococcus pneumoniae, which causes pneumonia.
  • Slime layer — A sticky, wet extracellular layer loosely attached to the cell wall, easily washed off, an unorganised layer with irregular boundaries made of polysaccharide, glycoprotein and glycolipid. It protects from drying, helps the cell adhere to host tissues and may trap nutrients.
  • Cell (plasma) membrane — A thin membrane under the cell wall surrounding the cytoplasm. It contains respiratory enzymes. The mesosome is a unique structure in it: an invagination of the plasma membrane. The membrane moves substances in and out; mesosomes help in respiration, in forming new cross walls during cell division, and increase surface area for enzymatic reactions.
  • Flagella — Thread-like structures for movement in most bacteria, made of non-contractile protein called flagellin, arising from a basal body in the cytoplasm under the cell membrane.
  • Pili (singular pilus) — Thicker, hollow, long hair-like tubular extensions, made of the protein pilin, about 1–10 on a bacterial cell, found only in Gram negative bacteria. They help in conjugation and transfer of genetic material, and attach the cell to a surface.
  • Fimbriae — Thin, bristle-like short fibers made of the protein fimbrilin, about 200–400 on a cell, found in both Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria; they help the cell attach to host tissues.
  • Cytoplasm — A dense fluid under the cell membrane, composed of 90% water, oil droplets, dissolved salts and granules of proteins, fats and glycogen called inclusion bodies. It has many small 70S ribosomes; membrane bound organelles (mitochondria, Golgi bodies, E.R.) are not found. It is the place of many metabolic activities, a storehouse of nutrients and enzymes, the area for DNA replication and protein synthesis, and home of ribosomes, plasmids and the nucleoid.
  • Nuclear region (nucleoid) — A lighter region in the cytoplasm, not covered by a nuclear membrane, with a single chromosome in the form of a double helical circular DNA; because of this single chromosome the bacterium is a haploid organism. Plasmids are small rounded broken rings of DNA in this region; they contain genes for drug resistance, heavy metal and insect resistance, replicate independently of the chromosome, and are used as vectors in genetic engineering.

A generalised bacterium: cell wall, cytoplasm with 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmid, fimbriae and flagellum.

7.5 Cyanobacteria

Cyanobacteria play a vital role in supporting life on Earth. They are the first oxygen producing photosynthetic organisms and produce about 21% oxygen, which is used by other organisms for respiration. They slowly added oxygen to the oceans and atmosphere; this oxygenation started about two billion years ago and helped aerobic organisms to appear on Earth. They also improve soil fertility, because one third of them can fix nitrogen from the air and convert it into nitrates in the soil: Nostoc and Anabaena are grown in soil to increase nitrogen content and help better plant growth. The oxygen produced by cyanobacteria helps to form the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere, which protects living things from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations of the sun, which destroy the proteins and nucleic acids of organisms.

Key Points

  • A bacterium has a peptidoglycan wall, capsule or slime layer, membrane with mesosomes, flagella, pili, fimbriae, 90% water cytoplasm with 70S ribosomes, and a nucleoid with one circular DNA plus plasmids.
  • Pili (1–10, Gram negative only) serve in conjugation; fimbriae (200–400) serve in attachment.
  • Cyanobacteria were the first oxygen producers (about 21% oxygen), started oxygenation about two billion years ago, and many fix nitrogen (Nostoc, Anabaena).

lessons.title: Bacterial Cell Wall, Gram Staining Groups, Shapes, Size and Endospores
lessons.notes_html:
7.6 Bacterial Cell Wall and Peptidoglycan

The cell wall is absent in Mycoplasma; all other bacteria have a cell wall. It does not contain cellulose, but is made of a rigid special sugar-protein complex called peptidoglycan (peptide = amino acid, glycan = sugar), also called murein, found in the form of a large molecule. The sugar forms long parallel chains, and short side chains of 4–5 amino acids are attached to the chains of sugars. Some bacteria have a slimy capsule of polysaccharides outside the wall; bacteria may survive when the capsule is removed. The wall gives shape to the cell and protects the inner components from external effects.

Chemical Composition: Gram Positive and Gram Negative

  • Gram positive — A thicker peptidoglycan layer; the peptidoglycan forms a thick complex network in the outer layer of the cell wall.
  • Gram negative — A thin layer of peptidoglycan is present between two plasma membranes. The outer membrane contains three compounds: lipopolysaccharides, phospholipid and lipoproteins. Gram negative bacteria are more resistant than Gram positive bacteria due to the outer thick membrane, which makes them resistant to many antibiotics like penicillins.

7.7 Comparison of Gram Positive and Gram Negative Cell Walls

CharacteristicGram positiveGram negative
Number of major layersOneTwo
Chemical compositionPeptidoglycan, teichoic acid, lipoteichoic acid, lipidsLipoproteins and peptidoglycan
Overall thickness20–80 nm8–11 nm
Outer membraneAbsentPresent
Periplasmic spacePresent in somePresent in all
Permeability of moleculesMore permeableLess permeable
LipidLess (1–4%)More (11–12%)
PeptidoglycanMore (50%)Less (10%)

7.8 Shapes and Size of Bacteria

  • A. Coccus (plural cocci) — Spherical, single or colonial, non-motile due to the absence of flagella. Simple coccus: solitary, no colony. Diplococcus: pairs, e.g. Diplococcus pneumoniae. Streptococcus: long chains, e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tetrad: four cocci in a square, e.g. Micrococcus. Sarcinae (octet): eight cocci in a cube, e.g. Peptostreptococcus magnus. Staphylococcus: irregular grape-like clusters, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus.
  • B. Bacillus (plural bacilli) — Straight or rod-shaped, single or colonial, motile because they have flagella. Simple bacillus: solitary, e.g. Escherichia coli (E. coli). Diplobacillus: pairs arranged longitudinally, e.g. Neisseria meningitidis (as given in the book). Streptobacillus: chains, e.g. Pseudomonas. Coccobacillus: very short and ovoid. Palisade: like a stack of coins, e.g. Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • C. Spirillum (plural spirilla) — Spiral shaped, generally solitary and motile. Spirilla: thick and rigid spirals with terminal flagella, e.g. Helicobacter pylori. Spirochetes: thin and flexible spirals, e.g. Treponema pallidum. Vibrio: curved form like a comma, e.g. Vibrio cholerae.
  • Size — On average bacteria range from 0.5–5 micrometer (micrometres). Mycoplasma are the smallest bacteria, 100–200 nm in diameter. E. coli is 1–3 micrometres in length and about 0.5 micrometres in width. The length of spirochetes ranges from 3–500 micrometres.

7.9 Sporulation and the Endospore

Sporulation is the process by which a single spore is formed by a bacterium, produced at a late stage of growth. An endospore is a dormant, tough and non-reproductive structure formed inside some Gram positive bacteria to sustain an unfavourable period. When conditions are not favourable (lack of nutrients or water, high temperature etc.), the bacterium forms a copy of its chromosome; the cell membrane encloses the chromosome and other cytoplasmic material, and a thick, impermeable cell wall forms around it — this thick-walled rounded body inside the cell is the endospore, and in it metabolism stops due to the removal of water. Its parts (book figure) include small acid-soluble proteins (SAPs), dipicolinic acid complexed with calcium (Ca-DPA), core, inner membrane, cortex, outer membrane and spore coat. The endospore is very resistant to heat, radiation, pH and desiccation, can live in boiling water for many hours, and can remain dormant but viable for centuries. It is formed to pass the unfavourable period, not to reproduce. When conditions become favourable, the cell takes up water and enlarges, the cell wall ruptures, the endospore comes out and becomes a bacterium.

Key Points

  • Peptidoglycan (murein): sugar chains cross-linked by short chains of 4–5 amino acids; absent only in Mycoplasma, which has no wall.
  • Gram positive walls are thick (20–80 nm, 50% peptidoglycan, no outer membrane); Gram negative walls are thin (8–11 nm) with an outer membrane that resists antibiotics.
  • Shapes: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods) and spirilla (spirals, including vibrio and spirochetes); sizes average 0.5–5 micrometres.
  • The endospore is a dormant survival structure, resistant to boiling, radiation and drying for centuries — it is not reproduction.

lessons.title: Flagellum and Motility, Genomic Organisation and Nutrition in Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
7.10 A. Structure of the Bacterial Flagellum

The flagellum is a thin, hair-like structure for movement, about 20 nm in diameter and 5–20 micrometres in length, made of a non-contractile protein called flagellin. It comes out through the cell membrane and cell wall and consists of three parts: Basal body — a proteinaceous structure in the cytoplasm just beneath the cell membrane; it anchors the flagellum with the cell membrane and cell wall, produces rotatory motion, and consists of two pairs of rings or discs connected by a short central rod. Hook — a short curved structure projecting from the cell surface, connecting the basal body to the filament. Filament — a helical and hollow structure arising from the hook, made of many twisted chains of flagellum protein forming a helix around a hollow core. The mechanism differs from the eukaryotic flagellum: when energy is used to rotate the basal body, the flagellum rotates up to 360°, and the bacterial cell spins and moves forward.

7.10 B. Motility in Bacteria

  • Non-motile (atrichous) — No flagella, e.g. most cocci. Motile bacteria have flagella, e.g. bacilli and spirilla.
  • Movement without flagella — 1. Gliding: movement of atrichous bacteria over solid surfaces, e.g. Neisseria and Pseudomonas. 2. Twitching: bacteria extend pili to anchor a surface and then retract them, moving forward. 3. Twisting: spirochetes have a thin, flexible spiral body that helps them twist as they move.
  • Movement with flagella (swimming) — By arrangement of flagella: Peritrichous — flagella all over the body, e.g. Salmonella typhi. Polar or terminal — flagella at the end of the bacterium: Monotrichous, a single flagellum at one pole, e.g. Vibrio cholerae; Lophotrichous, a tuft of flagella at one pole, e.g. Helicobacter pylori; Amphitrichous, a single flagellum at each end, e.g. Rhodospirillum rubrum; Amphilophotrichous, a tuft of flagella at both poles, e.g. Azotobacter vinelandii.

7.11 Genomic Organisation of Bacteria

The genome of bacteria is located in the nuclear region or nucleoid, a distinct region in the cytoplasm with no nuclear membrane around it. Bacteria are haploid organisms. In most bacteria the genome is present as a single circular chromosome: a circular double helical DNA molecule of 0.16 to 12.2 million base pairs, an extremely long molecule tightly folded to fit inside the cell. Some extra-chromosomal circular rings of DNA may also be present, called plasmids. Plasmids replicate independently of the chromosome, often contain antibiotic, disease and insect resistant genes, and are important vectors in modern genetic engineering.

7.12 Nutrition in Bacteria

  • A. Heterotrophic bacteria — Cannot prepare their organic food from simple inorganic substances; they get ready-made food from autotrophs, each other and organic wastes (heterotrophy). a) Parasitic bacteria: live in or on a living host for food and energy, have no enzyme system of their own and depend on the host enzymes; they may be harmless or cause serious diseases and even death, e.g. the TB bacterium causes tuberculosis in humans and Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia. b) Saprotrophic bacteria (saprobes): get food from dead organic matter (humus in the soil); they have an active enzyme system and secrete enzymes that break complex compounds into simpler soluble compounds, which are then absorbed, e.g. hay bacillus and many soil bacteria.
  • B. Autotrophic bacteria — Prepare their food from simple inorganic substances (autotrophy). a) Photosynthetic bacteria: have special chlorophylls (bacterial chlorophyll, i.e. chlorophyll e and f) in the cell membrane or dispersed in the cytoplasm; they use sunlight energy to form carbohydrates from CO₂, using H₂S instead of H₂O as a source of hydrogen and releasing sulphur instead of oxygen: 2H₂S + CO₂ → (CH₂O)n + H₂O + S. Examples: green sulphur bacteria, purple sulphur bacteria and purple non-sulphur bacteria. b) Chemosynthetic (chemoautotrophic) bacteria: colourless bacteria that oxidise inorganic substances like iron (Fe), sulphur (S), ammonia (NH₃) and nitrates (NO₃) to get energy: 2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + H₂O + energy, and the energy is used to make carbohydrate. Examples: sulphur bacteria, iron bacteria and nitrifying bacteria.

7.13 Photosynthesis in Cyanobacteria versus Other Photosynthetic Bacteria

CyanobacteriaPhotosynthetic bacteria
Contain chlorophyll a.Contain bacterial chlorophyll, i.e. e and f.
Photosynthetic system closely resembles eukaryotes (chlorophyll a and photosystem-II present).Have only photosystem-I.
Apparatus in an extensive intracellular system of membranous sacks called thylakoids.Bacterial chlorophyll in the cell membrane or dispersed in the cytoplasm.
Use water as a source of hydrogen and electron donor.Use H₂S.
Release oxygen during photosynthesis.Release sulphur during photosynthesis.
Use phycobilins as an accessory pigment.No accessory pigments are found.

Key Points

  • The flagellum (flagellin) has a basal body, hook and hollow helical filament; the basal body rotates it up to 360°.
  • Motility without flagella: gliding, twitching (pili) and twisting (spirochetes); flagellar arrangements run from monotrichous to peritrichous.
  • The bacterial genome is one circular chromosome of 0.16 to 12.2 million base pairs, plus independent plasmids.
  • Nutrition: heterotrophs (parasitic and saprotrophic) and autotrophs (photosynthetic, using H₂S and releasing sulphur, and chemosynthetic); cyanobacteria differ by using water and releasing oxygen.

lessons.title: Growth Phases and Reproduction in Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
7.14 Phases of Growth

Growth in bacteria is defined as an increase in the number of bacteria in a population rather than in the size of a bacterium. Bacterial growth mostly occurs by the asexual method of binary fission: there is no mitosis, and a bacterial cell simply splits into two daughter bacteria. Growth needs favourable conditions: suitable temperature, availability of nutrients and a suitable medium. The time taken by a bacterial population to become double is called generation time; it can range from a few minutes to several days depending on the species and conditions — in Escherichia coli (E. coli) it is 20 minutes under favourable conditions. The four phases of bacterial growth are:

  • A. Lag phase — A phase of no growth. The cells are metabolically active, attain their maximum size and prepare themselves for division under the new environmental conditions.
  • B. Log phase — A phase of rapid growth in a geometric manner: after each division the bacterial number doubles, and if conditions are favourable a large number of bacteria are formed.
  • C. Stationary phase — The size of the population becomes constant because the rate of death is equal to the rate of reproduction; it happens due to shortage of nutrients.
  • D. Death phase — The death of cells in the population increases more than the formation of new cells, due to extreme shortage of nutrients and accumulation of poisonous compounds.

The bacterial growth curve: lag, log (exponential), stationary and death phases.

7.15 Reproduction in Bacteria

There are two types: asexual, and sexual (genetic recombination). Bacterial reproduction is mostly asexual, by binary fission; sexual reproduction is genetic recombination by conjugation, transduction and transformation.

Asexual Reproduction: Binary Fission

The parent cell enlarges and the chromosome divides into two chromosomes, which attach to the cell membrane and move away from each other to opposite poles of the cell. The plasma membrane pinches inward at the centre to form a partition wall called the transverse septum; the cell wall grows inward within the septum and divides the cell into two daughter cells, which separate from each other.

Sexual Reproduction: Genetic Recombination

In a strict sense bacteria do not show sexual reproduction, because there is no gamete formation and fertilisation. In genetic recombination, the DNA of two bacteria combines to form a new type of bacterium, called a recombinant. There are three types:

  • A. Conjugation — Discovered by Joshua Lederberg and E. L. Tatum in 1946; they were awarded the Nobel Prize for this discovery. One bacterium unites with another through a tube for the exchange of genetic material: DNA is transferred by direct cell-to-cell contact through a tube formed by pili, called the conjugating tube or conjugation bridge. The bacterium containing DNA or the F plasmid (F = fertility) is the donor, regarded as F⁺ (male); the bacterium lacking the F plasmid is the recipient, F⁻ (female). The donor produces a conjugation pilus; an enzyme separates one strand of the donor plasmid, this single strand is transferred to the recipient, and the single circular plasmid in both F⁺ and F⁻ cells replicates and becomes double stranded — the F⁻ cell, after gaining the F-plasmid, becomes F⁺.
  • B. Transduction — Discovered by Joshua Lederberg and Norton Zinder in 1952 during research on genetic recombination in Salmonella. A piece of DNA is transferred from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage (a third party). In general transduction any of the genes of the donor are transferred; in special transduction only a few specific genes are involved. Phage DNA enters a donor cell and the bacterial chromosome is degraded; phage DNA multiplies, and sometimes pieces of bacterial DNA become integrated with phage DNA, so some new phages contain a piece of donor DNA (transducing phages). The donor bacterium bursts, and a transducing phage infects a new recipient bacterium and injects both DNAs; the donor DNA is incorporated into the recipient chromosome, making a transduced bacterium.
  • C. Transformation — Discovered by Frederick Griffith in 1928 during research on pneumococcus bacteria, which cause pneumonia. The genotype of a bacterial cell is changed by the absorption of DNA from the medium: it is the simplest form of bacterial DNA transfer. When bacteria die or reproduce, they release fragments of their DNA into the environment (donor bacteria); the fragments may be absorbed by recipient bacteria, and if the recipient is capable of transformation, the donor fragment combines with its DNA and its genotype is transformed. Transformation may occur by DNA fragments or by plasmids.

Key Points

  • Growth means increase in number; generation time of E. coli is 20 minutes; phases are lag, log, stationary and death.
  • Binary fission: chromosome copies move to opposite poles, a transverse septum forms, and two daughter cells separate.
  • Genetic recombination: conjugation (Lederberg and Tatum, 1946, via the F plasmid), transduction (Lederberg and Zinder, 1952, via phage) and transformation (Griffith, 1928, DNA absorbed from the medium).

lessons.title: Bacteria as Recyclers, Their Economic Importance, Research Use and Human Flora
lessons.notes_html:
7.16 Bacteria as Recyclers

Bacteria play an important role in the recycling of nutrients. They decompose the dead remains of plants and animals in the soil and break down complex organic compounds into simpler substances, so nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and sulphur are released into the atmosphere and become available again for new organisms. The nitrogen cycle is controlled by bacteria: nitrogen fixing bacteria (Rhizobium), living in the root nodules of leguminous plants, convert nitrogen gas into ammonium, which is then converted into nitrates by other bacteria, and these nitrates are converted back into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria.

A. Ecological Importance

Bacteria clean the environment by breaking down waste and dead plants and animals into simpler substances used by other organisms; this prevents the accumulation of dead bodies on Earth, so decomposing bacteria are called nature cleaners. A lot of carbon dioxide (CO₂) is produced by bacterial decomposition; this CO₂ is used by green plants for photosynthesis — without bacteria there would be no CO₂, plants could not make food, and all life on Earth would be affected. Decomposed dead organisms form a nutrient-rich material called humus, which increases the fertility of soil and helps the soil hold more water, making it better for plant growth. In sewage treatment plants, bacteria break down waste, help to clean the water and produce useful byproducts like biogas.

B. Economic Importance

  • In agriculture — Saprobes decompose dead animals and plants; bacterial enzymes convert complex compounds into simpler forms used by other organisms, especially green plants. Decomposition increases humus, soil fertility and water retention. Bacteria also kill plant pests.
  • In industries — Many industrial substances cannot be prepared chemically without bacteria: i) dairy products (yogurt, cheese, butter etc.); ii) flavouring of tobacco, coffee and tea; iii) preparation of ethyl alcohol, acetone, acetic acid (vinegar), vitamin K and B₁₂, enzymes and antibiotics; iv) in the leather industry, hair and fats are removed from skin by bacteria; v) antibiotics such as Terramycin, Neomycin and Auromycin are produced by various species of Actinomycetes.

7.17 Role of Bacteria in Research and Technology

Bacteria are largely used in research and biotechnology. A. D. Hershey and M. Chase in 1952 discovered that DNA is hereditary material, using T-bacteriophage and bacteria. Many growth hormones, enzymes, antibiotics and vitamins are prepared on a commercial scale using bacteria, e.g. phenylalanine (an amino acid) is prepared by genetically engineered bacteria. To prevent pollution, special biodegradable plastic (Poly Beta hydroxybutyrate) is produced by transgenic bacteria. Bacteria are used to form a genomic library, a collection of bacteria and bacteriophage clones. Many bacteria degrade synthetic poisonous chemicals and pollutants. Insulin is produced by combining bacterial DNA with the DNA (gene) for insulin. Bacteria are used in the leaching process to extract metal from low grade to high grade in the mining industry: Thiobacillus ferrooxidans is used in leaching of rock metal sulphides, and T. ferrooxidans and Leptospirillum ferrooxidans are used to extract gold and uranium. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is not complete without the enzyme Taq-polymerase, extracted from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which lives in hot springs.

7.20 Bacterial Flora of Human Beings

There are different types and large numbers of bacteria in a human body — there are more bacteria in the mouth of one person than there are people in the world. This presence of bacteria in the human body is called the bacterial flora of humans. Its types are: 1. Normal flora — the large number of various microorganisms (especially bacteria) routinely found growing in the body of healthy persons. 2. Resident flora — microbes that live in the body for an extended period. 3. Transient flora — bacteria that live for a short time in a body.

Residing siteBacterial flora
Oral cavityStreptococcus species, Viridans streptococci, Lactobacillus species
Respiratory tractStaphylococcus and Corynebacterium, Viridans streptococci
Urinogenital tractLactobacillus species, Escherichia coli
IntestineEscherichia coli, Enterobacteria, Clostridium species (book spelling: Clostrium)
SkinStaphylococcus epidermidis (book spelling: epidermits)

7.21 Benefits of Bacterial Flora to Humans

Intestinal bacteria help in digestion, breaking down complex large biomolecules (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) into simpler substances, and help in the absorption of nutrients. Many normal flora in the gut prepare useful vitamins like vitamin B and K, thiamine and folic acid, and produce essential nutrients like biotin and folate; these vitamins are important when the diet of a person is inadequate. Some gut resident bacteria detoxify compounds that are harmful for the human body. Normal flora protect the human body from pathogens by preventing the multiplication of harmful bacteria in the gut, help to keep homeostasis, and develop the immune responses, so the immune system becomes strong against pathogens. Some gut bacteria produce beneficial compounds like butyrate and short chain fatty acids, which have anti-inflammatory and metabolic benefits.

Key Points

  • Bacteria recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and sulphur; Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.
  • Economic uses: humus and soil fertility, dairy products, alcohol, vinegar, vitamins, enzymes and antibiotics, and leather processing.
  • In research, bacteria produce insulin and phenylalanine, give Taq-polymerase for PCR, leach metals and form genomic libraries.
  • Human flora (normal, resident, transient) aid digestion, make vitamins B and K, detoxify harmful compounds and protect against pathogens.

lessons.title: Bacterial Diseases in Humans and Plants, and Control of Harmful Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
7.18 Bacterial Diseases in Human Beings

  • A. Cholera — Caused by the Gram negative bacterium Vibrio cholerae, which enters the body through sewerage-contaminated food and water. Symptoms: severe diarrhoea, vomiting, muscular pain due to loss of fluids and electrolytes, and anuria. Treatment: proper antibiotics, and ORS to compensate the loss of water and electrolytes. Prevention: vaccination, drinking clean water, and using vegetables and fruits after proper washing.
  • B. Typhoid fever — Caused by the Gram negative bacterium Salmonella typhi. Symptoms: fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and severe headache. Treatment: proper antibiotics. Prevention: avoiding undercooked food, especially barbecue; a vaccine is available but is only 50–70% effective.
  • C. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) — Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In pulmonary TB the alveoli burst and are replaced by inelastic connective tissues. Symptoms: chest pain, cough with blood in sputum, fever and sweating at night, difficulty in breathing and weakness. Treatment: anti-TB medicines taken every day without missing any dose for up to 8 months; it can be controlled using the DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short Course) method. Prevention: TB vaccine, clean water, well-cooked food and a neat, clean environment; TB is highly contagious, so the patient should stay in isolation.
  • D. Pneumonia — Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram positive diplococcus bacterium. Symptoms: difficulty in breathing, chest pain, red brown or rusty colour sputum, cough and high fever. Treatment: antibiotics like penicillin or erythromycin. Prevention: clean environment, clean water, well cooked food and pasturised boiled milk; a vaccine can prevent about 90% of pneumonia cases.

7.19 Bacterial Diseases in Plants

  • i) Leaf spots — Infected leaves develop small, dark, round or irregular spots, which turn brown and dry; circular spots with yellow holes are formed between the veins, and spots may merge and damage large areas. Caused by Xanthomonas or Pseudomonas; spread through wind, rain, tools or insects. Control: proper spray of bactericides; prevention by removing and destroying infected plants, growing resistant varieties, using disease free seeds and disinfecting agricultural tools.
  • ii) Blights — Rapid and heavy damage to leaves, stems, flowers or fruits: water soaked spots that later turn brown or black, irregular yellowish-brown patches with ring-like lines, and leaves and stems that look burned. E.g. Xanthomonas oryzae infects rice and Erwinia amylovora causes blight in apple. Spread by wind, rain, insects and contaminated tools. Control: bactericide spray, removing and destroying infected plants, resistant varieties, healthy disease free seeds, and avoiding movement of workers and machinery between diseased and disease free areas, particularly in wet weather.
  • iii) Soft rots — A very common disease of vegetables and fruits, especially potatoes, tomatoes, carrots and onions, in the field and more commonly during transport or storage. Brownish metallic spots appear; the infected parts become watery and soft, with a foul smell due to tissue decay. Caused by many species of the Erwinia group; spread through water, contaminated tools and insects. There is no proper treatment; control is by removing and destroying affected plants, resistant varieties, healthy seeds, clean and good aeration to dry storage houses, and disinfecting agricultural machinery.
  • iv) Wilting — Loss of rigidity in nonwoody parts of plants: young trees rapidly wilt and decline, many leaves drop, and leaves become dull green and bent downward. Caused by different bacteria in different plants, e.g. Xanthomonas, solanacearum and Ralstonia (as listed in the book). No proper treatment is available; prevention by removing and destroying affected plants, sowing healthy disease free seeds, avoiding poorly drained sites and keeping proper spacing among plants.
  • v) Crown galls or galls — Tumor-like growths or galls on roots, stems and branches, usually at the crown where roots and stem meet; galls are round, rough or spongy when young, and become hard, woody and dark in colour as they mature. E.g. Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes galls in many shrubs and Agrobacterium rubi causes crown galls in grapes. Prevention: remove affected plants, select healthy seeds, select disease resistant species for propagation, and spray the soil with proper drugs before sowing.

7.22 Control of Harmful Bacteria

Harmful bacteria are controlled by two methods, physical and chemical. A. Physical methods — using physical agents is called the sterilising process; sterilisation is the destruction of all life forms, using dry heat, steam, gas, filtration and radiation:

  • 1. High temperature — Dry heat causes oxidation of the chemical compounds of microbes and kills them, at 120–126°C for 12–90 minutes under high pressure; moist heat causes coagulation of proteins and kills the bacteria.
  • 2. Radiation — Certain electromagnetic radiation below 300 nm is effective in killing microorganisms; gamma rays are generally used for sterilisation.
  • 3. Membrane filters — Bacteria are separated from heat sensitive compounds (antibiotics, hormones, seras) by membranes with extremely minute pores; in hospitals, filtered air is provided to operation theatres and burn wards.
  • 4. Pasteurisation — Liquid food is heated to kill non-spore forming bacteria: milk is pasteurised at 71°C for 15 seconds or at 62°C for 32 minutes, and its taste remains unchanged.
  • 5. Low temperature — Meat, egg, milk, vegetables and fruit are kept in refrigerators or ice boxes at 10°C to 15°C for several days. 6. Freezing — Vegetables, meat, fish and fruit are saved from spoilage for several months at -10°C to -18°C. 7. Drying — Water content of food is reduced to a point at which bacteria cannot grow, e.g. dried milk, dried meat and biscuits.

B. Chemical methods:

  • 1. Preservatives — a) Addition of acids lowers the pH of food to stop microbial growth. b) Addition of salt or sugar reduces the water content, making conditions unfit for bacterial growth. c) Addition of chemicals: pickles, candies, jams and breads are preserved with chemicals like sodium benzoate salts and potassium metabisulphite.
  • 2. Antiseptics — Chemical compounds used on living tissues to stop the growth of bacteria, e.g. chloroxylenol.
  • 3. Disinfectants — Chemical compounds used on non-living surfaces to stop the growth of vegetative cells; oxidising and reducing agents such as halogens and phenols, hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate, alcohol and formaldehyde.
  • 4. Chemotherapeutic agents — Chemotherapeutic chemicals and antibiotics work with the natural defence and destroy or inhibit the growth of microorganisms in living tissues, e.g. sulphonamide, tetracycline and penicillin.

Key Points

  • Human diseases: cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella typhi), pulmonary TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae).
  • Plant diseases: leaf spots, blights, soft rots, wilting and crown galls; control rests on bactericides, destroying infected plants, resistant varieties and disease free seed.
  • Physical control: heat, radiation below 300 nm, membrane filtration, pasteurisation (71°C for 15 seconds), refrigeration, freezing and drying.
  • Chemical control: preservatives, antiseptics on living tissue, disinfectants on surfaces, and chemotherapeutic agents such as penicillin.

lessons.title: Protists: A Diverse Group of Eukaryotes
lessons.notes_html:
Protists are unicellular or simple multicellular eukaryotic organisms. They are the very first eukaryotes, and they include organisms that resemble early plants, e.g. algae, early animals, e.g. Amoeba, and fungus-like organisms, e.g. slime molds. Because of their varied morphology, modes of nutrition and types of reproduction, they are very difficult to place with the other eukaryotes.

The chapter also introduces fungi (singular: fungus): a large, diverse group of spore-producing thallophytes that look like plants but have no chlorophyll. They are heterotrophs, living as saprotrophs or parasites, and their cell walls contain chitin while plants have cellulose. The main body of a fungus is the mycelium, made of thin thread-like hyphae (singular: hypha). The study of fungi is called mycology and the specialist is a mycologist.

8.1 Protists as a Diverse Group of Eukaryotes

The word protist is derived from the Greek word protistos, which means "very first". Protists are the first eukaryotes, evolved from prokaryotes (Monera), while fungi, plants and animals have evolved from protists. They are unicellular or simple multicellular eukaryotes that cannot be classified with fungi, plants or animals because of their diversified morphology, mode of nutrition and methods of reproduction.

Diversity of Protists

  • Protists are a polyphyletic group, i.e. they do not arise from a common ancestor. Any eukaryotic organism that does not fit with fungi, plants or animals is placed in this kingdom — it is defined only by exclusion from the other groups.
  • Some protists, like Euglena and slime molds, show characters of plants, animals and fungi together.
  • Most protists are aquatic. Some form underwater forests, e.g. kelp in the ocean.
  • Some are free living, e.g. Amoeba. Some show mutualistic symbiosis, e.g. Trichonympha and Colonympha. Some live as parasites, e.g. Plasmodium.
  • There is great variation in body form: mostly simple and unicellular; some are coenocytic (multinucleate) but not multicellular; some are multicellular without specialized tissues.
  • Few protists are sessile, while most are motile at some stage of their lives. They move by pseudopodia, cilia or flagella, and some use two or more means together, e.g. both flagella and pseudopodia.
  • Modes of nutrition also vary widely in protists.

Key Points

  • Protists are unicellular or simple multicellular eukaryotes — the first eukaryotes, from which fungi, plants and animals evolved.
  • They are a polyphyletic group, defined only by exclusion: any eukaryote that is not a fungus, plant or animal is a protist.
  • Protists may be free living, mutualistic or parasitic, and move by pseudopodia, cilia or flagella.
  • Fungi are heterotrophic, spore-producing thallophytes with chitin in their walls; their body is a mycelium of hyphae.

lessons.title: Animal-like Protists: Protozoans
lessons.notes_html:
There are three major groups of protists: animal-like protists (protozoans), plant-like protists (algae) and fungus-like protists (water molds, oomycetes, etc.). This lesson covers the protozoans.

General Characters of Protozoans

The term protozoa was first used by the German zoologist George August Goldfuss in 1818, from two Latin words: "proto" (first) and "zoan" (animal). Protozoans are also polyphyletic — they lack a common ancestor.

  • Most are aquatic: fresh water (Amoeba, Paramecium), marine (actinopods, foraminifera) or parasitic (Plasmodium, Entamoeba).
  • They are unicellular and microscopic, yet the single cell carries out all life activities: nutrition, respiration, locomotion, homeostasis and reproduction.
  • Food vacuoles ingest, digest and egest food; in fresh water forms, contractile vacuoles remove water and nitrogenous wastes.
  • Locomotory organs may be pseudopodia (Amoeba), cilia (Paramecium) or flagella (Trypanosoma), or absent (Plasmodium). Some produce shells and are found as fossils, e.g. foraminifera. They show regeneration of lost parts, form a cyst in unfavourable conditions, and reproduce by asexual and sexual methods.

Common Groups of Protozoans

  • Amoebas — Mostly free living, e.g. Amoeba proteus. Entamoeba histolytica lives in the human intestine and causes amoebic dysentery; Naegleria fowleri (in fresh warm water) damages the human brain. They move and capture food with pseudopodia (false feet), have food and contractile vacuoles, reproduce only asexually, and keep changing their body shape.
  • Zooflagellates — They move by flagella and have a proteinaceous pellicle. Trypanosoma causes African sleeping sickness, transmitted by the bite of an infected tse-tse fly. Trichonympha lives in the gut of termites: its bacteria produce cellulase to digest cellulose, so both partners get nutrients — an excellent example of mutualism. Choanoflagellates are sessile flagellates attached by a stalk, the flagellum surrounded by a collar like the collar cells (choanocytes) of sponges.
  • Ciliates — Named from a Latin word meaning "eye lash": the cell is covered with hair-like cilia and a proteinaceous pellicle. Uniquely, they have two types of nuclei: the macronucleus controls normal metabolism, while the micronuclei are concerned with reproduction. They reproduce sexually by conjugation and asexually by binary fission, e.g. Paramecium.
  • Foraminifera and Actinopods — Marine protozoans with porous shells of beautiful geometric pattern, through whose pores ray-like cytoplasmic projections extend. Foraminifera shells are made of calcium (calcareous); actinopod shells of silica (siliceous). Fossil foraminifera shells created vast limestone in the ocean.
  • Apicomplexans — Parasites named for the apical complex and the specific arrangement of organelles at one end of the cell. They are non-motile (moving by flexing), form a spore at some life-cycle stage for transmission to a new host, and have complex life cycles needing two hosts: Plasmodium (malaria) completes its cycle in the female mosquito and in human beings.

Key Points

  • Protozoans are unicellular, microscopic animal-like protists; food vacuoles digest food and contractile vacuoles remove water and wastes.
  • Amoebas move by pseudopodia, zooflagellates by flagella, and ciliates by cilia; apicomplexans are non-motile parasites.
  • Ciliates have two kinds of nuclei: a macronucleus for metabolism and micronuclei for reproduction.
  • Foraminifera have calcareous shells and actinopods siliceous shells; apicomplexans such as Plasmodium form spores and need two hosts.

lessons.title: Plant-like Protists: Algae
lessons.notes_html:
Algae (Latin word meaning sea weeds; singular: alga) form an important group of the thallophyta. The thallus is a plant body with no differentiation into true roots, stem or leaves as found in higher plants.

General Characters of Algae

  • They are the typical plants of moist and aquatic habitats, common in fresh water and relatively abundant as seaweeds in seawater.
  • Size ranges from unicellular and microscopic, to filamentous, to multicellular and several feet long; filaments may be coenocytic (without cross-walls) or made of distinct cells.
  • Algae are photosynthetic and carry out probably 50 to 60 percent of all photosynthesis on earth. All have chlorophyll a, but the green colour is often masked by other pigments: yellow and orange carotenoids, xanthophylls and phycoerythrin.
  • Reserve food is starch, oil and various other substances. Some show only asexual reproduction; most show both sexual and asexual reproduction, and many show isomorphic alternation of generations, e.g. Ulva.
  • All algae except Rhodophyta (red algae) form flagellated motile cells at some life stage; red algae form none at any stage.

Major Groups of Algae

  • 1. Euglenoids — Small freshwater organisms, mostly unicellular flagellates with usually two flagella and a proteinous pellicle. They show both animal and plant characters and reproduce asexually by longitudinal cell division. Euglena is the famous member.
  • 2. Dinoflagellates — Unicellular marine algae with a hard, stiff covering of cellulose and silica and two flagella: one encircles the cell like a belt, the other is perpendicular to it. Colour may be yellow, green, brown, blue or red depending on pigments. They are one of the most important producer groups in marine ecosystems, e.g. Ceratium.
  • 3. Diatoms — Common in fresh water, especially abundant in cool ocean water; mostly unicellular. The wall has two halves like a box and its lid, with silica deposited in beautiful symmetrical patterns. They are major aquatic producers and are called the pastures of the sea, e.g. Pinnularia.
FeatureBrown AlgaeRed AlgaeGreen Algae
HabitatColder marine waterMainly warm ocean; a few in fresh water and on soilMostly oceans; some fresh water and terrestrial
Colour / pigmentBrown: fucoxanthin masks chlorophyllRed; body often of feathery filamentsGreen due to chlorophyll; some orange, red or rust
BodyMulticellular, largest algae, a few cm to about 75 m; kelps have blade, stipe and holdfast; some have air bladdersSome unicellular, most multicellular, attached by a basal holdfast; up to one meter longUnicellular (Chlorella), colonial (Volvox), filamentous (Spirogyra) or leaf-like (Ulva)

ExampleFucus; kelps form kelp beds (underwater forests)PolysiphoniaChlamydomonas, Chlorella, Volvox, Spirogyra, Ulva

Key Points

  • Algae are photosynthetic protists with a thallus body; they carry out about 50–60 percent of all photosynthesis on earth.
  • Euglenoids show both plant and animal characters; dinoflagellates have two flagella and a cellulose and silica covering.
  • Diatoms have a two-halved silica wall and are the pastures of the sea.
  • Brown algae (kelps) are the largest algae; green algae are closest to plants, with cellulose walls and starch as stored food.

lessons.title: Fungus-like Protists, and the Importance of Protists
lessons.notes_html:
Some protists are closely related to the fungi: they are not photosynthetic and, like fungi, their body is generally made of thread-like hyphae. Yet they are not true fungi, because they have centrioles (absent in fungi), their cell walls contain cellulose (fungal walls are chitin), and they form motile sex cells, which fungi do not form. The major phyla are the slime molds (Myxomycota) and the water molds (Oomycota).

a) Slime Molds (Myxomycota)

Slime molds are fungus-like in one phase of the life cycle and amoeba-like in the other. Physarum is a common example. They are non-photosynthetic and differ from fungi by the motile stage in their life cycle and by cellulose walls. The life cycle has two forms:

  • Mobile plasmodium — The feeding stage: a diploid, multinucleated mass of cytoplasm covered by a slime sheath, up to 30 cm in diameter. It streams over damp decaying logs and leaf litter, ingesting bacteria, yeast and decaying organic matter.
  • Stationary filamentous form — In unfavourable conditions the plasmodium forms haploid spores by meiosis inside sporangia. In favourable conditions the spores germinate, releasing a haploid biflagellated or amoeboid cell; two such cells fuse into a diploid zygote, which feeds, grows and again forms a multinucleated plasmodium by mitosis.

b) Water Molds (Oomycota)

Oomycota consists of water molds, white rusts and downy mildews. All members are parasites or saprotrophs; most are aquatic and some live in soil. Their hyphae are aseptate and their walls contain cellulose, not chitin.

  • Asexual reproduction — Biflagellated zoospores are formed in a sporangium and, after release, give rise to a new body.
  • Sexual reproduction — The female gametangium is the oogonium and the male the antheridium; gametes are produced by meiosis. Antheridia contain several male nuclei; oogonia contain 2–8 eggs. Male gametes enter the oogonium and fuse with the eggs, forming zygotes that develop a thick wall — the oospore, which later gives rise to a new body.

8.3 Importance of Protists

  • Useful — protozoans and fungus-like protists: zooplanktons feed on phytoplankton and are important primary consumers in the food chain; fungus-like protists are used in genetics and other physiological research.
  • Useful — algae: euglenoids are used in research; dinoflagellates are food for small ocean animals; diatoms are an important source of food and oxygen for heterotrophs. Algin from brown algae is used in ice creams, toothpastes and shaving creams; brown algae also give vitamins A, C, D and E, serve as fertilizer, and kelps are human food in many countries. Agar from red algae is a culture medium for bacterial growth, used for capsules of vitamins and medicines and as a base of cosmetics. Green algae are important producers; Chlorella is used for photosynthesis research, in the synthesis of antibiotics, and as single cell protein (SCP) "health food", especially in Taiwan and Japan.
  • Harmful — protozoans: malaria (Plasmodium) is one of the most common infectious diseases — according to a WHO survey, 1 to 2 million people die from it every year. Acanthamoeba causes eye infections in contact lens users, Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery, and Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness.
  • Harmful — plant-like and fungus-like: dinoflagellates sometimes produce a neurotoxin that kills fish and causes paralytic shellfish poisoning, and they sometimes block water pipes. Phytophthora infestans causes late blight of potato, responsible for the Irish potato famines of 1845 and 1847 (deaths from 250,000 to more than one million); white rusts and downy mildews are also important plant diseases.

Key Points

  • Fungus-like protists have hyphae but are not true fungi: they have centrioles, cellulose walls and motile sex cells.
  • Slime molds alternate between a mobile, multinucleated plasmodium and a stationary, spore-forming filamentous form.
  • Oomycota reproduce asexually by biflagellated zoospores and sexually by oogamy, forming thick-walled oospores.
  • Useful protists give food, oxygen, algin, agar and single cell protein; harmful ones cause malaria, dysentery, sleeping sickness and late blight of potato.

lessons.title: Fungi: Zygomycota and Ascomycota
lessons.notes_html:
Fungi are a very large, diverse group of spore-producing thallophytes. They look like plants but do not have chlorophyll. They are heterotrophs, living as saprotrophs or parasites, contain chitin in their cell walls instead of cellulose, and store food as glycogen. The main body of a fungus is the mycelium, made of thin thread-like hyphae. Fungi are classified into four main groups: Zygomycota, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota and Deuteromycota.

1. Zygomycota (Zygomycetes)

This phylum has about 2000 species, called zygospore-producing fungi or conjugating fungi because of conjugation and zygospore formation. They are mainly saprophytes on dead, decomposing matter: moist stale bread, jelly, horse dung, decaying fruits, cheese, moist leather and soil humus. The hyphae are non-septate and the mycelium is well developed and branched. Examples: Rhizopus (black bread mold) and Pilobolus (spitting fungus).

  • Asexual reproduction — By conidia and spores. Spores form in a sporangium; it bursts, spores are dispersed by wind, and on a suitable place form a new mycelium.
  • Sexual reproduction (conjugation) — Between hyphae (stolons) of two strains, plus (+) and minus (-). Nuclei accumulate at each tip; the tip swells and a septum cuts it off as a gametangium. The (+) and (-) gametangia meet by hormonal action, their walls dissolve by enzymes, and the nuclei fuse into a diploid zygote. A thick wall forms around it: the zygospore, resistant to unfavourable conditions. After rest it germinates by meiosis: its wall splits, a vertical hypha (promycelium) emerges, and its tip forms a sporangium full of spores, which give new mycelia.

2. Ascomycota (Ascomycetes)

Ascomycota are called sac fungi because their sexual spores form in little sacs called asci (singular: ascus). They occur in many habitats all year, mostly terrestrial, some marine or fresh water. It is the largest group of fungi, about 32,000 species, unicellular (yeast) or multicellular (truffles). The mycelium has septate hyphae with porous septa, so cytoplasm moves between compartments, and the walls contain a large amount of chitin. Examples: morels, truffles, yeast and Neurospora.

  • Asexual reproduction — There are no sporangia in sac fungi. In budding (yeast), a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent, grows and separates as a new independent yeast. Conidia (naked spores) form at the tips of specialized hyphae called conidiophores, are dispersed by wind, and each forms a new mycelium on a suitable place.
  • Sexual reproduction — Two monokaryotic hyphae (n) grow together and their cytoplasm mingles (plasmogamy); the nuclei migrate but do not fuse, forming dikaryotic hyphae (n+n), which form a fruiting body, the ascocarp. In the ascus the two nuclei fuse (karyogamy) into a diploid zygote (2n); meiosis gives four haploid nuclei and mitosis in each gives eight haploid ascospores. The mature ascus swells and bursts, and air currents carry the ascospores to germinate into new mycelia.

Key Points

  • Fungi are heterotrophic thallophytes with chitin walls; they store glycogen and are classified into Zygomycota, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota and Deuteromycota.
  • Zygomycetes (about 2000 species) have non-septate hyphae and reproduce sexually by conjugation, forming a thick-walled zygospore. Example: Rhizopus.
  • Ascomycetes (about 32,000 species, the largest group) have septate hyphae and form eight ascospores inside each ascus.
  • Sac fungi reproduce asexually by budding (yeast) and by conidia formed on conidiophores.

lessons.title: Basidiomycota, Deuteromycota and Yeast
lessons.notes_html:
3. Basidiomycota (Basidiomycetes)

Basidiomycetes are also called club fungi, because they develop club-shaped reproductive structures called basidia; at the tip of each basidium, four basidiospores develop. Nearly 22,300 species have been discovered, e.g. mushrooms and bracket fungi. The hyphae are septate, with perforated septa, so cytoplasm moves among the cells.

  • Sexual reproduction — The +ve and -ve primary monokaryotic hyphae grow towards each other; their cytoplasm fuses (plasmogamy) through a bridge and nuclei migrate into the other hypha, forming a secondary, dikaryotic mycelium (n+n) whose cells each contain two haploid nuclei that do not fuse. This mycelium forms a fruiting body, the basidiocarp: a stalk and a cap, the lower surface of the cap bearing many thin plates called gills, radiating from the stalk to the edges.
  • In the gills, the two nuclei in each basidium fuse into a diploid zygote (2n), which immediately undergoes meiosis to produce four (+) and (-) haploid basidiospores. Released spores are carried by wind and animals to a moist habitat and germinate into +ve and -ve mycelia.

A mushroom (basidiocarp): basidia on the gills under the cap produce four basidiospores each.

4. Deuteromycota (Deuteromycetes)

This phylum includes about 25,000 species, e.g. Aspergillus and Penicillium. They are called imperfect fungi because no sexual stage has been observed in their life cycle. They live saprophytically or parasitically on plants, and their morphology and biochemistry show they are sac fungi that have lost the ability to reproduce sexually. Hyphae may be non-septate or septate. Asexual reproduction is by conidiospores formed on special hyphae called conidiophores; the non-motile conidia are dispersed by wind, water or animals, and each gives rise to a new mycelium.

8.5 Yeast — a Single-Celled Fungus

Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is a unicellular fungus, round or oval and a few micrometers in diameter, heterotrophic, and naturally found on fruits and leaves. Its importance:

  • Food industry — Used commercially to prepare bread: mixed with flour, it ferments and the CO₂ formed is trapped as bubbles, so the dough rises with a light texture; alcohol and CO₂ evaporate during baking, making the bread porous. Different strains give different flavoured breads.
  • Beverages — Ethyl alcohol is prepared by fermentation of grapes, cereals, potatoes, fruits and sugar cane: C₆H₁₂O₆ + yeast —(enzymes)→ 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
  • Vaccines and medicines — Yeast is the only organism used for the formation of the hepatitis B vaccine, and is used in medicines such as ergotine (for migraine) and lovastatin (for lowering blood cholesterol).
  • Research and gene vector — Used to study the effects of chemicals and medicines, in genetic recombination experiments and to study mutation; its plasmids can carry genes from one body to another (gene vector).

Key Points

  • Basidiomycetes (club fungi, about 22,300 species) form four basidiospores on each basidium; the basidiocarp has a stalk, cap and gills.
  • Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi, about 25,000 species) have no observed sexual stage and reproduce by conidiospores. Examples: Aspergillus, Penicillium.
  • Yeast is a unicellular fungus used in bread making and alcohol production by fermentation, and for the hepatitis B vaccine, medicines, research and as a gene vector.

lessons.title: Antibiotics, Mutualism, Edible Fungi and the Roles of Fungi
lessons.notes_html:
8.6 Fungi from which Antibiotics are Obtained

Many antibiotics are prepared from fungi:

Name of AntibioticSpecies of Fungus
CyclosporinsTolypocladium inflatum
CephalosporinCephalosporin acremonum
PenicillinPenicillium notatum and P. crysogenum
GriseofulvinP. nigricans, P. griseofulvum
CitrininP. citrinum
PalutinP. palutum
Fusidic acidFusidium coccineum

8.7 Mutualism in Fungi

Mutualism is the association between two different organisms in which both partners get benefits. Fungi form two mutualistic associations:

  • Lichens — Made up of a fungus (mostly ascomycetes), a cyanobacterium (blue green algae) and a green alga (Chlorophyta). The fungus receives nutrients from the algal cells, and the algal cells get protection from desiccation. Lichens survive where there is low moisture, low temperature and even no soil at all. The body has three layers: an upper layer, thin and tough, of fungal hyphae; a middle layer of fungal hyphae interwoven with photosynthetic cells; and a bottom layer of loosely packed fungal hyphae.
  • Mycorrhizae — From Greek words meaning "fungal roots": a mutualistic relationship between soil fungi and the roots of most higher vascular plants, occurring in about 90–95% of all land plants; such plants show better growth. The fungus gets sugar, amino acids and other substances from the roots, and benefits the plant by decomposing organic matter in the soil and by increasing the absorptive surface for water and inorganic salts like K, Zn, Cu, P, etc. In endomycorrhizae the hyphae penetrate only the cell wall of the outer root cells, form coils, swellings and minute branches, and extend several centimeters into the soil; common with angiosperms. In ectomycorrhizae the hyphae form a dense net around the root, remain between the cells without penetrating them, and form no coils or swellings; mostly with pines and firs, and less beneficial than endomycorrhizae.

8.8 Edible Fungi

  • Yeast — A good source of vitamin B and protein; yeast is composed of 50% protein.
  • Morels and truffles — Morel (Morchella esculenata) and truffle (Tuber melanosporum) are used as proteinaceous food.
  • Mushrooms — More than 200 species are edible, e.g. Agaricus spp.; used in soups, to flavor cheeses and in pizzas. Warning: certain mushrooms are poisonous and can even cause death, e.g. Amanita phalloides (Death cap).

8.9 Ecological Importance of Fungi

  • Decomposers — Fungi decompose dead leaves, stems and animals; their potent enzymes break tough materials like lignin and cellulose that other organisms cannot digest, which is especially important in woodlands. They prevent the accumulation of dead organic matter on earth, so they are called scavengers.
  • Recyclers — Nutrients blocked in dead bodies are brought back into the soil for other organisms, and a large amount of CO₂ is released into the air, which photosynthetic organisms use to prepare food. Thus fungi maintain the ecological balance of the environment.

8.10 Pathogenic Role of Fungi

  • Plant diseases — Rusts of cereals by Puccinia and smuts of cereals by Ustilago (both Basidiomycota); sac fungi cause Dutch elm disease, chestnut blight, red rot of sugarcane, powdery mildews, potato wilt, cotton root wilt, apple scab and brown rot of stone fruits.
  • Animal diseases — Aspergillus spp. cause reproductive disorders (e.g. abortion); ringworm in dogs and horses by Trichophyton rubrum and Microsporum audovinii; carp and salmon are affected by Saprolegnia parasitica; Aspergillus causes lung infection of chickens.
  • Human diseases — Ringworm and athlete's foot; ergotism from purple ergot of rye (nervous spasm, convulsions, psychotic delusions, gangrene); candidiasis of mouth, throat and vagina by Candida spp.; Rhizopus and Mucor cause histoplasmosis (lung infection) and infections of the digestive tract and brain; Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxin, a cancer-causing chemical in improperly stored grains; dandruff is caused by Microsporum furfur; Neurospora and Fusarium infect the cornea of the eye.

Key Points

  • Important antibiotics from fungi include penicillin (Penicillium), cephalosporin, griseofulvin, cyclosporins and fusidic acid.
  • Lichens are a mutualism of a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium; mycorrhizae are a mutualism of fungi with plant roots, found in 90–95% of land plants.
  • Edible fungi include yeast, morels, truffles and more than 200 mushrooms; Amanita phalloides (Death cap) is poisonous.
  • Fungi are decomposers and recyclers maintaining ecological balance, but also cause diseases of plants, animals and humans.

lessons.title: Bryophytes and the Life Cycle of Polytrichum
lessons.notes_html:
Plants are multicellular, predominantly photosynthetic and eukaryotic organisms. They have well-defined body parts, cell walls of cellulose, develop from an embryo, store carbohydrate as starch, and are non-motile. It is the second largest kingdom, comprising over 3,60,000 species. The major groups are bryophytes (seedless, non-vascular), pteridophytes (seedless vascular plants) and the seeded plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms). Plants live in almost all habitats: deserts, mountains, tundra, tropical and subtropical regions, and water.

9.1 Bryophytes

Bryophytes are the first land plants, evolved from green algae; up to now 15,000 species have been discovered. They are homosporous, i.e. they produce one type of spores.

  • They grow mostly in damp, shady places near water. They have no vascular tissues, so transport of minerals and food takes place by diffusion.
  • They need water for fertilization, so they are called amphibious plants (the amphibians of the plant kingdom).
  • The gametophyte generation is dominant, green and photosynthetic, while the sporophyte is non-photosynthetic and dependent on the gametophyte. They are seedless and non-flowering.
  • The male sex organ is the antheridium (many sperms are formed in it); the female sex organ is the archegonium (a single egg is formed in it). They show alternation of generations: dominant gametophyte with reduced sporophyte.
  • Three major groups: Liverworts (Hepaticeae), e.g. Marchantia, Riccia, Pellia; Mosses (Musci), e.g. Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum; Hornworts (Anthocerotae), e.g. Anthoceros, Notothylos, Megaceros. Liverworts are closely related to mosses.

9.2 Life Cycle of Polytrichum

Polytrichum (a moss) shows heteromorphic alternation of generations, because its gametophyte and sporophyte generations have different morphology.

  • Gametophyte generation — Dominant, autotrophic, independent and haploid: a leafy shoot bearing antheridia and archegonia intermixed with multicellular hair-like paraphyses. Many motile sperms form in the antheridium and a single non-motile egg in the archegonium. Water (rain or dew) is necessary: sperms swim in water by their cilia to the archegonium, and only one fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote (2n), retained inside the archegonium.
  • Sporophyte generation — The zygote is the first cell of the sporophyte (2n); it develops into an embryo and then a sporophyte plant, which is dependent on the gametophyte for nutrition. It has three parts: the foot, embedded in the gametophyte and absorbing nutrients from it; the long stalk or seta, which elevates the capsule and provides it food and water; and the capsule (sporangium), inside which spores are formed by meiosis. The haploid spores are unicellular with thick walls, are dispersed by wind, and germinate into a filamentous protonema with buds and branches, which gives rise to a leafy gametophyte again. (The book's exercise notes the ciliated sperms as the only positive evidence of the aquatic ancestry of bryophytes.)

The moss sporophyte: a capsule (sporangium) raised on a seta, with its foot embedded in the leafy gametophyte on which it depends.

Key Points

  • Plants are multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose walls; they store starch and number over 3,60,000 species.
  • Bryophytes are seedless, non-vascular first land plants — the amphibians of the plant kingdom — with a dominant gametophyte.
  • Bryophytes have three groups: liverworts, mosses and hornworts.
  • In Polytrichum, the dependent sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) grows on the gametophyte, and its spores germinate into a protonema.

lessons.title: Vascular Plants, Their Division and Pteridophytes
lessons.notes_html:
9.3 General Features of Vascular Plants (Tracheophytes)

Vascular plants are the largest and most successful group of land plants. They have vascular tissues: xylem, which gives support and conducts water and dissolved salts from roots to leaves, and phloem, which transports organic food from leaves to other parts. Their xylem has special conducting cells called tracheids, so they are called tracheophyta. They have a diploid (2n) dominant sporophyte and a haploid (n) reduced gametophyte, stomata, well-protected sporangia, true roots, stem and leaves, and heteromorphic alternation of generations. They fall into two major groups:

  • Seedless vascular plants — No seeds are produced, e.g. ferns. Four subgroups: i) Psilopsida, e.g. Psilotum; ii) Lycopsida, e.g. Lycopodium; iii) Sphenopsida, e.g. Horse tail; iv) Pteropsida, e.g. Ferns.
  • Seeded vascular plants — Seeds are produced: i) Gymnosperms, e.g. Pines; ii) Angiosperms, e.g. Rose.

9.4 Division among Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms

FeaturePteridophytesGymnospermsAngiosperms
Seeds and flowersSeedless, flowerlessSeeded, flowerlessSeeds and flowers present
Vessels in xylemAbsentAbsentPresent
Companion cells in phloemAbsentPresentPresent
Dominant generationSporophyteSporophyteSporophyte
ReproductionBy sporesBy seedsBy seeds
Spores / seedsSpores in sporangiaSeeds on surface of scale leavesSeeds in fruits
Sperms reach eggThrough waterBy pollen tubeBy pollen tube
OriginFirst vascular plants on landEvolved from pteridophytesEvolved from gymnosperms
SporophyllsPresentPresentAbsent
Sporophylls formCone or strobilusCone or strobilusCones absent
ExamplesFernsPine, CycadsRose, Grasses

9.5 General Characters of Pteridophytes

Pteridophytes (Greek: Pteron = feather, Phyton = plant) are seedless, flowerless and fruitless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves. The xylem is without vessels and the phloem without companion cells. They show heteromorphic alternation of generations, with a dominant diploid (2n) sporophyte (the main plant body) and a reduced haploid (n) gametophyte.

  • Sporangia burst and spores are dispersed by wind; the spores germinate into gametophytes that are independent from the sporophyte. (A fern differs from a moss in having an independent sporophyte.)
  • The sex organs are multicellular: sperms form in antheridia and eggs in archegonia. Sperms swim in a film of water (rain, dew) to the archegonia, so pteridophytes are water-dependent for fertilization.
  • Examples in the book: Psilotum, Lycopodium, Equisetum and Nephrolepis.

Key Points

  • Vascular plants (tracheophytes) have xylem with tracheids and phloem, true roots, stem and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.
  • Seedless vascular plants have four subgroups: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida and Pteropsida; seeded plants are gymnosperms and angiosperms.
  • Pteridophytes are seedless, flowerless and fruitless, with no vessels in xylem and no companion cells in phloem.
  • Pteridophyte gametophytes are independent, but fertilization still needs water for the sperms to swim.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Fern
lessons.notes_html:
Adiantum (an example of a fern) shows heteromorphic alternation of generations, in which the dominant sporophyte alternates with a reduced gametophyte.

A. Sporophyte Generation

  • The main plant body, in the form of a herb: the dominant, diploid (2n) generation. Its stem is a rhizome — short and underground — from which roots arise, and special large leaves or fronds arise from its upper side.
  • On the underside of the leaflets of fronds, groups of sporangia or sori (singular: sorus) are formed, first green, then dark brown or black when mature. The sporangia-bearing leaves are called sporophylls.
  • Each sporangium is a flattened biconvex capsule with a multicellular stalk, in which many haploid spores are formed by meiosis. Each spore is a simple cell of cytoplasm and a nucleus, with an outer wall called exine and an inner wall called intine.
  • The mature sporangium bursts; spores are dispersed by wind, and a spore falling on moist soil germinates into a small haploid gametophyte, the prothallus.

A fern sporophyte: fronds bear sori (groups of sporangia) on the underside of their leaflets; the short underground stem is the rhizome.

B. Gametophyte Generation

  • The gametophyte or prothallus is heart-shaped and autotrophic, about 1/3 of an inch in size, with many rhizoids on its lower side that anchor it in the soil and absorb water and minerals.
  • It is monoecious (bisexual), containing both sex organs. The antheridium produces a large number of flagellated sperms (antherozoids). The archegonium is flask-shaped: the upper, enlarged part is the neck and the broad lower part is the venter, which contains an egg or oosphere.
  • Water is necessary for fertilization. The antheridium bursts, sperms swim by their flagella towards the archegonium (archegonia secrete a sweet substance that attracts them), and one sperm enters the venter through the neck and unites with the egg to form a zygote or oospore. After many divisions the zygote forms an embryo inside the archegonium, which develops into a sporophyte — at first attached to the gametophyte, later independent.

Key Points

  • The fern sporophyte is dominant and diploid, with a rhizome, roots and fronds bearing sori on the underside of leaflets.
  • Spores formed by meiosis in the sporangia germinate into a small, heart-shaped, independent gametophyte — the prothallus.
  • The prothallus is monoecious, bearing antheridia and flask-shaped archegonia, and its rhizoids anchor it and absorb water and minerals.
  • Flagellated sperms swim in water to the egg; the young sporophyte starts attached to the prothallus and later becomes independent.

lessons.title: Gymnosperms and the Life Cycle of Pinus
lessons.notes_html:
9.7 Gymnosperms

The word gymnosperm is derived from two Greek words: Gymnos = naked and sperma = seed. They are commonly called evergreen plants, are found worldwide, and make up one third of the world's forest. They are woody plants — shrubs, trees or rarely vines (in some Gnetophytes) — with about 700 living species.

  • The main plant body is the sporophyte; the gametophyte is reduced. They are flowerless and fruitless and usually bear cones; the seeds are born on the exposed surface of fertile leaves, mostly combined to form a cone.
  • Leaves are of two types, foliage and scale. Foliage leaves are evergreen with xerophytic features like a thick, tough cuticle and sunken stomata (needle-shaped foliage leaves are found in gymnosperms).
  • The xylem consists of tracheids and xylem parenchyma. Two spore types form: microspores (male) on microsporophylls and megaspores (female) on megasporophylls; the female gametophyte is retained in the ovule permanently. Alternation is heteromorphic, with an independent dominant sporophyte and a dependent reduced gametophyte. Polyembryony is common, but usually a single embryo matures.
  • Important genera: cycads (Cycas spp.), pines (Pinus spp.), hemlock (Conium maculatum), deodar (Cedrus deodara), maidenhair tree (Ginkgo biloba), joint pine (Ephedra sinica) and Himalayan spruce (Picea smithiane).

9.8 Classification of Gymnosperms

There are four main groups of gymnosperms: i) Conifers, ii) Ginkgos, iii) Cycads, iv) Gnetophytes. Cycads belong to the non-flowering seed plants.

9.9 Life Cycle of Pinus

Pinus is a conifer. Its dominant, diploid sporophyte alternates with a small, dependent haploid gametophyte, and there is no vegetative reproduction in Pinus.

  • Sporophyte — A tall evergreen tree, up to 36 meters, with roots, a woody stem, branches, needle-like green leaves and brown scale-like leaves. It bears cones or strobili of two types, male and female, on separate branches of the same plant, so Pinus is monoecious.
  • Male cone — Smaller, in clusters, with many microsporophylls spirally arranged on a central axis; each has a stalk (filament) and a terminal leafy expansion (anther), and two pouch-like microsporangia (pollen sacs) on its underside. Each microspore mother cell produces four haploid microspores (pollen grains) by meiosis. Each pollen grain has an outer coat (exine), an inner coat (intine) and two air-filled, balloon-like wings, so it can float in air and travel long distances.
  • Female cone — Larger, formed from one to three at a point, with many megasporophylls spirally arranged on a central axis. Each megasporophyll has two scales: a small, thin, dry bract scale below, and a larger, thicker, woody ovuliferous scale above it, bearing two sessile ovules (megasporangia) on its upper surface.
