Each ovule has a mass of tissue called the nucellus, a single integument with an opening, the micropyle. The megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores by meiosis; three degenerate and one becomes functional.
  • Male gametophyte — The microspore nucleus forms a small prothelial cell (which degenerates) and a sister cell, which gives a second prothelial cell and an antheridial cell; the antheridial cell divides into a generative nucleus and a tube nucleus. Released microspores reach the female cone by wind (pollination); the exine bursts and the intine forms a pollen tube carrying both nuclei. The tube nucleus degenerates; the generative nucleus divides into a stalk cell (which degenerates) and a body cell, which forms two sperms. The pollen tube with two gametes is the male gametophyte.
  • Female gametophyte and seed — It develops during the year following pollination. The functional megaspore (n) divides by mitosis inside the megasporangium and is never set free; many free nuclei form, then walls form between them, making gametophytic tissue called endosperm. At the micropyle end, two archegonia form, each flask-shaped with a neck of eight cells, a ventral canal cell and the egg. The pollen tube enters an archegonium and bursts near the egg, releasing the sperms; one sperm unites with the egg to form a zygote, which divides repeatedly into an embryo. The integument becomes the seed coat and the ovule is now a seed with a wing. Seeds are dispersed when the ovuliferous scales open apart, and germinate into a new young sporophyte. The life cycle of Pinus is completed in about three years.

Key Points

  • Gymnosperms are naked-seeded, evergreen, woody plants with cones, no flowers and no fruits; about 700 living species in four groups: conifers, ginkgos, cycads and gnetophytes.
  • Pinus is monoecious: smaller male cones in clusters and larger female cones with bract and ovuliferous scales, each bearing two ovules.
  • Pinus pollen grains have two air-filled wings, so they float in air and travel long distances to the female cone.
  • The female gametophyte (endosperm) stays inside the ovule and forms archegonia; the fertilized ovule becomes a winged seed, and the whole life cycle takes about three years.

lessons.title: Angiosperms and Their Classification
lessons.notes_html:
9.10 Angiosperms

The word angiosperm is derived from two Greek words: Angion = enclosed and sperma = seed. Rose (Rosa spp.), apple (Malus domestica), mango (Mangifera indica) and sheesham (Dalbergia sissoo) are examples of angiosperms — the group of flowering and seeded plants.

  • It is believed that angiosperms diverged from gymnosperms about 300–350 million years ago (Triassic period). It is the most diverse group of plants, with approximately 416 families, 13,164 genera and 295,383 species.
  • Angiosperms are flowering plants and contain their seeds in fruits. The main plant body is the dominant sporophyte, while the gametophyte generation is reduced.
  • The sporophyte is heterosporous (it produces microspores and megaspores) and varies greatly in size: duckweed is about one mm long, while Eucalyptus is about 100 m high.
  • They have well-developed xylem and phloem, and form pollen tubes to transport sperms towards the egg in the ovules. They show heteromorphic alternation of a dominant sporophyte with a reduced gametophyte, and resemble gymnosperms in the presence of ovules.

9.11 Classification of Angiosperms

According to the number of cotyledons in the embryo, angiosperms are divided into two classes: Liliopsida (monocot) and Magnoliopsida (dicot).

  • Monocotyledons (Liliopsida) — A single cotyledon in the seed; mostly herbaceous plants; leaves usually long and narrow with parallel veins; flowers usually with three or a multiple of three petals and six stamens; mature seeds usually contain endosperm (nutritive tissue). Examples: wheat, sugarcane, orchids, rice, bamboo, grasses, maize, lilies, palm.
  • Dicotyledons (Magnoliopsida) — Two cotyledons in the seed; herbaceous (tomato) or woody (apple tree); leaves broader than monocot leaves, with veins in a network; sepals and petals usually in fours or fives, or multiples of these; the mature seed usually lacks endosperm, which is absorbed by the two cotyledons before germination. Examples: apples, guava, roses, sunflower, sheesham, oak, cacti.
FeatureMonocotDicot
Pollen grainsOne pore or furrowThree pores or furrows
SeedsOne cotyledonTwo cotyledons
FlowersThree floral parts (or multiples)Four or five floral parts (or multiples)
LeavesNarrow, parallel veinsOval or palmate, net-like veins
Vascular bundlesSmall, spread throughout the stemArranged in a ring around the stem
RootsFibrous rootsTap roots

Difference between monocot and dicot, as shown in the book (Fig. 9.7).

Key Points

  • Angiosperms are flowering plants with enclosed seeds in fruits — the most diverse plant group, with about 416 families and 295,383 species.
  • The sporophyte is dominant and heterosporous; the gametophyte is much reduced, and sperms reach the egg by a pollen tube.
  • Monocots (Liliopsida) have one cotyledon, parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots and floral parts in threes.
  • Dicots (Magnoliopsida) have two cotyledons, net-like leaf veins, tap roots and floral parts in fours or fives.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant: Double Fertilization, Seed and Fruit
lessons.notes_html:
Like all other vascular plants, angiosperms show heteromorphic alternation of generations, in which a diploid, dominant sporophyte alternates with a reduced gametophyte.

A. Sporophyte Generation

The main plant body is the diploid, dominant sporophyte. Flowers are the reproductive parts: a flower contains the male reproductive part, the anther, and the female reproductive part, the carpel. Angiosperms are heterosporous, producing two types of haploid spores in the flowers. (Gametes differ from spores: gametes fuse in fertilization to form a zygote, while spores germinate directly into a new gametophyte.)

  • Microspores (male spores) — Formed in the anther (microsporangium) of the stamen, which usually has four elongated pollen sacs. Mitotic divisions produce diploid microspore mother cells; each divides by meiosis into four haploid microspores. The microspore nucleus then divides by mitosis into a vegetative or tube nucleus and a generative nucleus, and the thick-walled microspore becomes a pollen grain with a double folded wall.
  • Megaspores (female spores) — Produced by meiosis in the ovule (megasporangium), an integumented, oval female sporangium attached to the inner wall of the ovary by a short stalk; an ovary may contain one, two, or several thousand ovules. A megaspore mother cell (megasporocyte) undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid cells; only one survives and the other three degenerate — the survivor is the megaspore.
  • Pollination — Binucleate pollen grains are carried by wind, insects or other means to the stigma of carpels.

Parts of a flower: the carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovule) and the stamen (anther and filament), with petals and sepals on the thalamus.

B. Gametophyte Generation

The gametophyte generation is much reduced: the male gametophyte is just a three-celled structure and the female gametophyte a seven-celled structure.

  • Male gametophyte — The pollen grain is held on the stigma by a sticky secretion and germinates to form a pollen tube, which grows down the style into the ovary. The two nuclei move down into the tube; the generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two sperms, while the tube nucleus stays near the tip. The pollen tube with its two sperms is the male gametophyte.
  • Female gametophyte — Inside the ovule, the megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis three times to produce eight haploid nuclei in the embryo sac, the microscopic structure at the centre of the ovule, surrounded by integuments that leave a small opening, the micropyle. Walls form around the nuclei, giving a seven-celled structure: the egg apparatus near the micropyle (two synergids, which guide the pollen tube and then degenerate, plus the egg); three antipodal cells at the opposite side (functionless, later disorganized); and the fusion nucleus, formed when the two central polar nuclei fuse into a diploid endosperm mother cell.
  • Double fertilization — The pollen tube enters the embryo sac through the micropyle; the tube nucleus degenerates, the tube tip ruptures and releases the two sperms. One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus (2n) to form the triploid (3n) endospermic nucleus. This is double fertilization, found only in angiosperms.
  • Seed and fruit — The zygote develops into an embryonic plant (embryo: one or more cotyledons, an epicotyl and a hypocotyl on a rod-like axis), and the endospermic nucleus develops into triploid (3n) endosperm tissue, rich in starch that is broken down to glucose when the seed germinates. As the ovule matures into a seed, the micropyle closes and the integuments become the seed coat or testa, protecting the embryo. Most flower parts die, but the ovary enlarges into the fruit; the ripe fruit releases seeds, which are dispersed and germinate into new sporophyte plants.

Key Points

  • In flowering plants the flower is the reproductive part: microspores (pollen) form in the anther and the megaspore forms in the ovule.
  • The male gametophyte is the pollen tube with a tube nucleus and two sperms; the female gametophyte is the seven-celled embryo sac.
  • The embryo sac contains the egg apparatus (egg and two synergids), three antipodal cells and a fusion nucleus formed from two polar nuclei.
  • Double fertilization — one sperm fuses with the egg (zygote) and the other with the fusion nucleus (triploid endosperm) — occurs only in angiosperms.
  • After fertilization the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

lessons.title: Families of Angiosperms: Brassicaceae, Solanaceae and Poaceae
lessons.notes_html:
Angiosperms are divided into many families; three families are discussed in the book.

A. Brassicaceae — the Mustard Family

Also called Cruciferae; Brassica (Sarson) is its famous genus. Worldwide in distribution, with 350 genera and 3000 species (in Pakistan 92 genera and about 250 species). Plants are mostly herbs, usually with a watery sap and a smell like sulphur.

  • Vegetative characters — Tap roots; stems erect and hairy; leaves petiolate or sessile and simple.
  • Floral characters — Inflorescence raceme or corymb. Flowers tetramerous, bisexual and actinomorphic: calyx of four free sepals (polysepalous); corolla of four petals spreading in a cross (cruciform); androecium of six stamens — the outer two shorter, the inner four longer; gynoecium of two united carpels (syncarpous). Fruit capsular, dry and dehiscent; seeds dicotyledonous, non-endospermic, with a large embryo.
  • Economic importance — Vegetables: roots of Brassica rapa (turnip) and Raphanus sativus (radish), leaves of Brassica campestris (mustard, sarson), flowers of Brassica oleracea (cabbage). Ornamentals: Cheiranthus cheiri (wall flower), Iberis amara (candy-tuft). Condiments: Brassica nigra, Brassica alba. Oil for cooking and hair: Brassica campestris. Medicinal: Brassica juncea, Raphanus sativus, Sisymbrium irio (Khoob Kalan). Oil cakes (Khal) are used as cattle fodder and manure. Capsella bursa-pastoris (shepherd's purse) is a common weed.

B. Solanaceae — the Potato Family

Named after its famous plant, the potato. Distributed in tropical and temperate regions; a large family with about 90 genera and 2000 species (in Pakistan 14 genera and about 52 species). Plants are herbs, shrubs or small trees.

  • Vegetative characters — Tap root; stem erect and branched, underground in potato; leaves simple and usually alternate.
  • Floral characters — Inflorescence usually cymose. Flowers pentamerous, bisexual and actinomorphic: calyx of five fused green sepals (gamosepalous); corolla of five fused petals (gamopetalous), tubular, bell-shaped or funnel-shaped; androecium of five stamens united with the petals (epipetalous); gynoecium of two united carpels (syncarpous). Fruit a berry or capsule; seeds dicotyledonous and endospermic.
  • Economic importance — Vegetables: Solanum tuberosum (potato), Solanum lycopersicum (tomato), Solanum melongena (brinjal). Condiment: Capsicum annuum (chilly). Ornamental: Petunia alba. Medicinal: Solanum nigrum (mako). Stems and leaves of Nicotiana tabacum (tobacco) are used in smoking.

C. Poaceae — the Grass Family

Also called Graminae; one of the largest families of angiosperms, found all over the world, with 600 genera and 10,000 species (in Pakistan 158 genera and 492 species). Most plants are annual or perennial herbs; bamboos are its woody members.

  • Vegetative characters — Fibrous adventitious roots; stem erect and jointed, hollow (bamboos) or filled with stored food (sugarcane); leaves narrow and long, forming a long sheath at the base around the stem.
  • Floral characters — Small flowers on a dense spike or open clusters, made of units called spikelets, each with two glumes (empty bracts) at the base. Each flower is enclosed in two bracts, the lemma and palea. Calyx and corolla are not distinguishable: the perianth is represented by two reduced scales below the ovary, called lodicules. Stamens usually three, long and delicate, with free anthers. Carpels 2–3, syncarpous, with feather-like stigmas. Fruit a simple, dry caryopsis (grain); seeds endospermic and monocotyledonous.
  • Economic importance — The major source of food for man and animals: Triticum aestivum (wheat), Oryza sativa (rice), Zea mays (corn), Saccharum officinarum (sugarcane — the major source of sugar throughout the world); bamboo shoots and grass stems and leaves are animal food. Grasses are used for paper and cardboards; bamboos for construction, baskets, huts and light furniture; grasses for lawns, gardens and playgrounds (Cynodon, Poa); fibers for ropes, mats and cordage (Saccharum munja); barley water (Hordeum vulgare) is used medicinally to remove kidney stones, and barley is also used for wines and alcohols; some grasses are cultivated for aromatic oils (Rusa oil).

Key Points

  • Brassicaceae (mustard family): tetramerous flowers, four petals in a cross, six stamens (2 outer short, 4 inner long), capsular fruit.
  • Solanaceae (potato family): pentamerous flowers, five fused petals, five epipetalous stamens, fruit a berry or capsule.
  • Poaceae (grass family): flowers in spikelets with glumes, lemma and palea; perianth reduced to two lodicules; fruit a caryopsis.
  • Poaceae is the major food family of man and animals: wheat, rice, maize and sugarcane all belong to it.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Form and Functions in Plants

lessons.title: Plant Nutrition: Macro and Micronutrients and Carnivorous Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Form and functions in plants means that the physical structures of plants are designed to perform specific functions. Nutrients are the components used by organisms to get energy for the maintenance of their lives. Plant nutrition is the study of the chemical elements and compounds necessary for plant growth and metabolism.

10.1 Nutrition in Plants

Plants are autotrophs: they prepare their own organic food by using inorganic nutrients. The plant nutrients are 23 in number, out of which 16 are important. Mineral nutrients are present in the soil as salts; the salts ionize in water and are absorbed in the form of ions.

  • Macronutrients — Required in large amounts; nine in number. Non-minerals (3), from water and air: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen. Minerals (6), from soil: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulphur, calcium, magnesium.
  • Micronutrients — Required in trace amounts, from soil. Seven are mostly required: boron, chlorine, copper, iron, manganese, molybdenum and zinc. Others named in the book: aluminium, cobalt, sodium, nickel, selenium and vanadium.

Functions of the Nutrients

NutrientMain functions in the book
Carbon, Oxygen, HydrogenC is the backbone of biomolecules; O is a component of H₂O, CO₂ and organic compounds; H is necessary for building sugars, proteins and lipids.
Nitrogen (N)Part of chlorophyll, all proteins and nucleic acids (DNA, RNA); helps rapid growth; needed for coenzymes.
Phosphorus (P)Component of nucleic acids, ATP and phospholipids; helps sugar and starch formation.
Potassium (K)Helps opening and closing of stomata; enzyme activator; improves fruit and seed quantity.
Sulphur (S)Improves root growth and seed formation; part of enzymes, vitamins and amino acids like cysteine and methionine; promotes nodule formation in legumes.
Calcium (Ca)Essential part of the plant cell wall; helps normal transportation of water; activator of many enzymes.
Magnesium (Mg)Part of chlorophyll; helps flower and fruit formation; activator of enzymes for carbohydrate metabolism.
Boron (B), Chlorine (Cl)B: seed and flower development, pollen tube growth, use of calcium. Cl: photosynthesis, movement of water by osmosis, ionic balance.
Copper (Cu), Iron (Fe)Cu: nitrogen metabolism, photosynthetic enzymes, fruit flavour. Fe: cell division and growth; enzymes for respiration, photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation.
Manganese (Mn), Molybdenum (Mo), Zinc (Zn)Mn: chlorophyll formation, nitrogen metabolism. Mo: enzymes in nitrogen metabolism, conversion of nitrates (NO₃) to ammonia (NH₃). Zn: starch formation, early growth, photosynthetic enzymes.

10.2 Nutrition in Carnivorous Plants

Carnivorous (insectivorous) plants are autotrophic but get some nutrients, especially nitrogen, by trapping and digesting insects and small organisms. They usually grow where the soil has less nitrogenous material. They have special adaptations such as modified leaves, bright colours and sticky materials. Trapped insects are digested by enzymes secreted by the leaves, and the nitrogenous compounds are then absorbed.

  • Sun dew (Drosera capensis) — Radiating leaves bear hair-like tentacles with glands at their tips; insects adhere to the glands.
  • Bladderwort (Utricularia macrorhiza) — Some leaflets are modified into a bladder-like trap.
  • Pitcher Plant (Nepenthes rafflesiana) — A modified leaf forms a pitcher shape with a lid at the top.
  • Venus Fly Trap (Dionaea muscipula) — The lamina has two halves with a midrib in the centre; each half has teeth that interlock with the other half to capture insects.

Key Points

  • Macronutrients (9): C, H, O from air and water, and N, P, K, S, Ca, Mg from soil.
  • Micronutrients are needed in trace amounts; the seven mostly required are B, Cl, Cu, Fe, Mn, Mo and Zn.
  • Nitrogen is part of chlorophyll, proteins and nucleic acids; magnesium is part of chlorophyll.
  • Carnivorous plants trap insects mainly for nitrogen, because their soil is nitrogen-deficient.

lessons.title: Gaseous Exchange, Transpiration and Conducting Tissues: Xylem and Phloem
lessons.notes_html:
The stomata and mesophyll tissues of leaves play an important role in the exchange of gases, i.e. CO₂ and O₂. Transpiration and gaseous exchange both mostly occur through the leaves, and the conducting tissues xylem and phloem move water, minerals and food through the plant body.

10.3 Role of Stomata and Mesophyll in Exchange of Gases

Stomata are small openings in leaves for gaseous exchange and transpiration, and the major sites of gaseous exchange between plants and the environment. They lead to the intercellular spaces between the mesophyll cells, where exchange of gases takes place from the moist surface of the mesophyll. Oxygen from air enters through the stomata, travels towards the cells by diffusion, dissolves in the surface moisture of their walls and passes into the cells; release of CO₂ follows the same pathway in the opposite direction. Stomata open and close due to the movement of guard cells: exchange occurs when stomata are open and stops when they are closed. Mesophyll cells are thin-walled living parenchymatous or chlorenchymatous cells between the upper and lower epidermis; they have chloroplasts and are metabolically active due to photosynthesis.

  • Palisade mesophyll — Cells have more chloroplasts, so they are responsible for most of the photosynthesis in the leaf.
  • Spongy mesophyll — Cells are loosely packed, with air spaces among them, under the palisade and above the lower epidermis; through these spaces, exchange of gases easily takes place through the stomata.

Internal structure of a leaf: palisade above, spongy mesophyll with air spaces below, and a stoma in the lower epidermis.

10.4 Transpiration and Gaseous Exchange

Loss of water from the aerial parts of a plant in the form of vapours is called transpiration; the inward and outward movement of gases is gaseous exchange. The two are interconnected: when stomata are open, CO₂ enters and O₂ formed in photosynthesis is removed, and extra water is also removed, helping transpiration. Though stomata occupy only 1-2% of the total leaf area, about 90% of total transpiration occurs through stomata. In dry conditions the stomata close to reduce water loss; this limits gaseous exchange, so photosynthesis stops. Transpiration helps in cooling the plant and in pulling water and minerals from roots to leaves, so it indirectly supports photosynthesis.

10.5 Xylem and Phloem

Xylem (Greek Xylon - wood) is a complex permanent tissue that conducts water and dissolved mineral salts upward from roots to leaves. Its elongated cells are joined end to end, forming a tube-like structure. Mature tracheids, vessels and fibres are non-living; xylem parenchyma is living.

  • Tracheids — Found in all vascular plants (so they are called tracheophytes). Elongated, dead cells with tapering ends, lignified secondary walls and pits; they have lost their protoplast, so passages form for water flow. They conduct water and give mechanical support.
  • Vessels — Found only in flowering plants (Angiosperms). Vessel members are arranged one over the other like a water pipeline; dead, shorter, much wider and less tapered than tracheids, with pits and perforated end walls. More conductive than tracheids due to the wider lumen.
  • Xylem fibres — Thick-walled dead elongated cells, pointed at both ends; supporting in nature. Xylem parenchyma — Living, thin-walled storage cells.

Phloem (Greek phloios - bark) is a complex permanent tissue for the translocation of organic food from the leaves to the various plant organs. Phloem fibres are dead; the other three members are living.

  • Sieve tube — Thin-walled sieve tube elements placed end to end; their oblique, perforated transverse walls are called sieve plates. They lack a nucleus and are associated with the nucleus of companion cells; they are the main route for translocation of organic food.
  • Companion cells — Thin-walled, living, elongated cells linked with the sieve tube through plasmodesmata, found only in angiosperms, with a large nucleus and very many mitochondria; they provide energy to other phloem cells.
  • Phloem fibres — Non-living, thick-walled elongated cells with tapering ends; mechanical support. Phloem parenchyma — Living, thin-walled storage cells; radial conduction of organic food is also carried out by these cells.

Key Points

  • Stomata are the major sites of gaseous exchange; palisade does most photosynthesis, spongy air spaces allow gas movement.
  • Transpiration and gaseous exchange are interconnected through the same stomata.
  • Xylem conducts water and minerals upward: tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma.
  • Phloem translocates organic food: sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma.

lessons.title: Water Potential, Uptake of Water by Roots and Ascent of Sap (TACT Theory)
lessons.notes_html:
Water moves between plant cells and their environment by osmosis, is absorbed by root hairs, crosses the root by three pathways, and then rises from roots to leaves as the ascent of sap.

10.6 Osmosis and Water Potential

Osmosis is a special type of diffusion in which water flows from the region of higher water concentration towards the region of lower water concentration through a semipermeable membrane, until both regions attain equal concentration. Water moving into the cell is endosmosis; water moving out is exosmosis.

  • Water potential — The total kinetic energy of water molecules in a system due to which they move from one point to another; directly proportional to the concentration of water molecules. Pure water has maximum water potential, value zero; all solutions have lower, negative values. It is represented by Greek Psi and measured in Kilopascal (kPa). Water potential = solute potential + pressure potential. Water always moves from higher to lower water potential.
  • Solute potential (osmotic potential) — The measure of the change in water potential due to the presence of solute molecules. Its value is always negative: dissolved solutes lower the water potential.
  • Pressure potential (turgor pressure) — The pressure of the protoplast on the cell walls from inside. When water enters by endosmosis, the protoplast increases in volume and presses on the wall; the cell becomes turgid, and the wall pressure forces water from one cell to another.

10.7 Uptake of Water by Root Hairs

Water and minerals are absorbed from the soil by root hairs, tiny hair-like structures; a root system has millions of them. The cell sap of a root hair is more concentrated than the soil solution, so water enters by osmosis. Root hair walls are freely permeable, their membranes partially permeable. Water passes through epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, finally to the xylem, by three pathways:

  • Apoplast pathway — The apoplast is the continuous system of adjacent cell walls; water moves between the spaces of cell walls of adjacent cells. It is discontinuous in the endodermis due to Casparian strips of suberin, a waterproof waxy material on the endodermis walls. Ions then enter by diffusion or active transport, and water and ions pass through the pericycle into the xylem.
  • Symplast pathway — Water moves from one cell to the other through plasmodesmata, the cytoplasmic microscopic channels between adjacent cells. It occurs due to a concentration gradient of cell sap down the cortex, endodermis, pericycle and xylem, and due to the streaming movement of cytoplasm.
  • Vacuolar pathway — Water and dissolved salts move from vacuole to vacuole of neighbouring cells by osmosis. Water faces high resistance, so there is little flow; it is less efficient than the apoplast and symplast pathways.

10.8 Ascent of Sap: TACT Theory

The upward movement of sap (water and dissolved minerals) from roots to leaves through xylem, against gravity and without any mechanical pump, is the ascent of sap. The most accepted explanation is the TACT theory, proposed by two Irish plant physiologists, Dixon and Jolly in 1894 and elaborated by Dixon in 1914; it is also called the cohesion-tension theory. TACT = T - Transpiration, A - Adhesion, C - Cohesion, T - Tension.

  • Transpiration — Loss of water vapour from aerial parts generates a pull shifted downward, the transpirational pull. It pulls water at about 8 metres per hour, and more than 300 atm pressure is created by transpirational pull.
  • Adhesion — Sticking together of molecules of different kinds, between water and cellulose fibres in xylem vessel walls (both polar). It keeps the water column from breaking and helps water adhere to the walls.
  • Cohesion — Clinging together of molecules of the same kind; water molecules cohere due to hydrogen bonds.
  • Tension — The pulling force creates tension in the xylem water, which forms a solid chain-like column; xylem tension can pull water up to 200 m (more than 600 feet).

Mechanism: water evaporates from mesophyll tissues and out through the stomata, so the water potential of mesophyll cells drops and they draw water from the leaf xylem by osmosis. By cohesion, this creates a tension transmitted downwards to the roots, and water moves in the xylem as a continuous column; the vessels do not collapse because of their strong walls. Pathway: Soil → Epidermis (root hair) → Cortex → Endodermis → Pericycle → Root xylem → Stem xylem → Leaf xylem → Mesophyll cells → Air.

Key Points

  • Water potential = solute potential + pressure potential; pure water = 0, solutions are negative.
  • Root hairs absorb water by osmosis; water crosses the root by apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways.
  • Casparian strips of suberin make the apoplast discontinuous at the endodermis.
  • TACT theory (Dixon and Jolly, 1894): transpiration pull, adhesion, cohesion and tension raise the sap.

lessons.title: Opening and Closing of Stomata, Translocation and Osmoregulation
lessons.notes_html:
Stomata open when guard cells are turgid and close when they are flaccid. Food moves in the phloem by pressure flow, and the plant keeps its water and solute balance by osmotic adjustment and osmoregulation.

10.9 Opening and Closing of Stomata

A. Starch-Sugar Interconversion Hypothesis (German botanist H. Van Mohl): opening and closing is due to interconversion of starch and sugar because of a change in pH of guard cells, the only cells of the leaf epidermis that carry out photosynthesis. Opening (day): photosynthesis consumes CO₂, so acidity falls and pH increases; at high pH the enzyme phosphorylase converts starch into glucose. Glucose dissolves, water potential decreases, the guard cell solution becomes hypertonic, water enters by endosmosis from surrounding epidermal cells, the guard cells become turgid, their outer thin walls expand and force the inner thick walls outward, and a stoma is formed. Closing (night): no photosynthesis, CO₂ concentration increases, acidity increases and pH decreases; phosphorylase converts glucose into insoluble starch, water potential becomes high, water moves out, the guard cells become flaccid, the inner thick walls move inward and the stoma closes.

B. K⁺ Ions Influx-Efflux Hypothesis (presented by Levitt): opening and closing depends upon the movement of K⁺ ions into or out of the guard cells, controlled by the blue wavelength in sunlight and the level of CO₂ inside the leaves. Opening: glucose is converted to pyruvic acid, which reacts with CO₂ to form malic acid; in blue light, malic acid is ionized to malate⁻ and H⁺. The H⁺ ions are pumped out to epidermal cells, and K⁺ ions enter to balance the charge and combine with malate⁻ to form potassium malate. Solute potential increases, water enters, the guard cells become turgid and the stoma opens. Closing: at night CO₂ increases and pH decreases; potassium malate is ionized, K⁺ ions move out (efflux) into epidermal cells, malate⁻ recombines with H⁺ to form malic acid and then glucose and starch, water leaves the guard cells, they become flaccid and the stoma closes.

10.10 Translocation of Organic Solutes

The transportation of sucrose and amino acids in phloem, from the region of production to the region of storage or utilization, is called translocation. The translocating fluid consists of 70% water and 10-25% dry matter; the dry matter contains 90% sucrose and 10% other organic molecules like proteins and lipids. Phloem sap always moves from source (where food is manufactured or stored, or its concentration is high, e.g. green leaves, stem) to sink (where food is utilized, or its concentration is low, e.g. roots, yellow leaves).

The most acceptable mechanism is the pressure flow (mass flow) mechanism, proposed by Ernst Munch in 1927. Glucose formed in leaves is mostly converted into sucrose, which is pumped into sieve tubes using ATP, so its concentration increases there. Water enters the sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis, hydrostatic pressure increases, and the pressure moves the sucrose towards the sink (e.g. root, fruit), where sucrose is unloaded. Water then moves out into nearby xylem vessels, pressure decreases, and a pressure gradient is set up by entry of sucrose at the source and its removal at the sink.

10.11 Osmotic Adjustment

Osmotic adjustment is a physiological process in which plants regulate the solute concentration within the cells to maintain osmotic potential and water balance. It helps the plant to live in different habitats and to retain water; osmotic potential is necessary for cellular functions and structural support.

10.12 Osmoregulation in Plants

To keep the level of water and solute in the body at a normal constant state is called osmoregulation. Each cell has a definite amount of water in relation to salts, and movement of water depends upon whether the environment is isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic.

  • Isotonic (iso - same) — Water potential and solute concentration are similar inside and outside the cell; balanced movement of water, and the cell remains in its actual shape.
  • Hypotonic (hypo - under) — Outside has low solute concentration and higher water potential, so water moves into the cell by endosmosis and the plant cell becomes turgid.
  • Hypertonic (hyper - over) — Outside has higher solute concentration and lower water potential, so water moves out by exosmosis and the cell shrinks (plasmolysis).

Key Points

  • Starch-sugar hypothesis: day - high pH, starch to glucose, water in, stoma opens; night - low pH, glucose to starch, water out, stoma closes.
  • Levitt hypothesis: opening is due to influx of K⁺ ions (potassium malate forms); closing is due to K⁺ efflux.
  • Translocation moves sucrose and amino acids from source to sink by pressure flow (Munch, 1927).
  • Isotonic: no net change; hypotonic: water enters, cell turgid; hypertonic: water leaves, plasmolysis.

lessons.title: Osmoregulation in Different Habitats, Thermoregulation, Turgor and Support
lessons.notes_html:
Water availability divides plants into four habitat groups. Plants also regulate their temperature, and turgor pressure and supporting tissues keep them upright against gravity.

10.13 Osmoregulation in Plants of Different Environments

  • Hydrophytes (hydro - water) — Grow where there is plenty of water in soil, e.g. Hydrilla and Vallisneria. Adaptations: no cuticle around their cell walls, to get rid of excess water; large leaves with a large number of stomata for rapid transpiration; short roots with no or fewer root hairs.
  • Xerophytes (xeros - dry) — Grow where there is a shortage of water, in deserts, ice or snow-covered Arctic regions, e.g. Cactus, Acacia and Opuntia. Adaptations: very deep roots; leaves modified into spines in some plants; thick cuticle; water stored in the body (succulents, e.g. Opuntia); fewer, sunken stomata, generally closed in the day and open at night; short life cycles from seed to seed, and seeds with long dormancy.
  • Mesophytes (meso - middle) — Grow in average conditions of water; the largest group of plants on land, and most angiosperms are mesophytes. Adaptations: cuticle on leaves; automatically regulated stomata; water stored in leaves (e.g. garlic) and underground stem (e.g. ginger); well developed fibrous root system; leaves dropped in the dry period (e.g. in autumn); bifacial leaves.
  • Halophytes (halos - salt) — Grow in salt-rich saline soils, e.g. Date Palm and Atriplex. They face a hypertonic environment: excess of solute and shortage of water, so water continuously comes out of the plants (exosmosis). Adaptations: thick cuticle on leaves; water stored in stems to dilute solute concentration; long roots with a very large number of root hairs; extra salt excreted by hydathodes; many have small leaves.

10.14 Thermoregulation in Plants

The ability of an organism to keep its body temperature at a constant normal level, even when the surrounding temperature is continuously fluctuating, is called thermoregulation.

  • Low temperature — Affects enzyme action and protein structure; movement of water and organic food slows down; membrane permeability changes as phospholipids become crystallized, so solutes may come out of the cell; ice crystals form in the cytoplasm. Adaptations: hard stems with thick bark; tough and needle-like leaves with thick cuticle; leaves shed in autumn; special antifreeze proteins prevent crystal formation in the cytoplasm; cold-resistant seeds; life cycle finished quickly in the warm season; more unsaturated fatty acids added to membrane fats so cells work in cold.
  • High temperature — Enzymes and proteins are denatured, so metabolic activities slow down or stop; plants become dehydrated due to the high rate of transpiration; wilting and death occur. Adaptations: well developed root system absorbs maximum water, stored in the body to keep the plant cool; thick waxy cuticle and sunken stomata; special heat shock proteins prevent enzymes and proteins from denaturing; shiny cuticle reflects sun radiations; leaves modified into spines in some plants.

10.15 Turgor Pressure

The force exerted by the water within the cell against its cell wall is called turgor pressure. Herbaceous plants have no specialized supporting tissues; their strength and upright growth are supported by this water (hydrostatic) pressure, which causes rigidity — if they lose turgidity due to water shortage, they wilt and cannot stand upright. Turgor is created by the large vacuole in mature parenchyma cells: the vacuole contains cell sap (a concentrated solution of mineral salts, sugars, organic acids, oxygen, CO₂, etc.), surrounded by a thin layer called the tonoplast. Because of the higher ionic concentration in the vacuole, water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid. Significance: herbaceous plants stand upright and maintain their shape; turgor is important in cell expansion and growth; opening and closing of stomata depends upon turgor in guard cells.

10.16 Support in Plants

Support is provided by four types of tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma and vascular tissues.

  • Parenchyma (para - beside, enkhuma - infusion) — The chief supporting tissue of non-woody (herbaceous) plants. Living, most abundant cells, spherical or oval, with thin flexible walls and a large central vacuole filled with water; their turgidity provides strength and support to soft parts like leaves, flowers and fruits.
  • Collenchyma (kolla - glue) — Living elongated cells found in cortex, petioles, midribs, beneath the epidermis of dicot stems and pedicels of flowers. Thick primary walls of cellulose and pectin, not uniform, with extra deposition of cellulose at the corners.
  • Sclerenchyma (scleros - hard) — Mature dead cells, the chief supporting cells of hard parts like wood and seed coats, with extremely thick secondary walls making up 90% of cell volume. Fibres: non-living, long and cylindrical, often associated with xylem, phloem and pericycle. Sclereids: variable in shape, shorter than fibres, found in cortex, pith, seed coats and nuts. Both make the plant hard and stiff.
  • Vascular tissues — Vascular bundles having xylem are tough; in dicot plants they are arranged in a ring, which provides effective support.

Key Points

  • Hydrophytes live in water, xerophytes in dry places, mesophytes in moderate conditions, halophytes in salty soil.
  • Low temperature crystallizes membrane phospholipids and forms ice crystals; high temperature denatures enzymes and proteins.
  • Turgor pressure from the vacuole and cell sap keeps herbaceous plants upright; loss of turgor causes wilting.
  • Support: parenchyma in herbaceous plants; collenchyma, sclerenchyma (fibres and sclereids) and vascular tissues in woody plants.

lessons.title: Plant Growth, Annual Rings, Meristems and Growth Hormones
lessons.notes_html:
Growth is produced by dividing meristems, recorded in woody stems as annual rings, and controlled by plant growth regulators.

10.17 Plant Growth

Growth is the permanent increase in size, weight, form and volume in the body of a plant, through cell division and enlargement.

  • Primary growth — Increase in length due to division of meristematic cells of the apical meristem; it produces elongation in root and stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and primary xylem and phloem.
  • Secondary growth — Increase in thickness or diameter due to cell division of the lateral meristem or cambium; it produces secondary xylem and phloem, and cork is formed, so root, branches and stem become thick.

10.18 Annual Rings (Growth Rings)

The ring mark in a woody stem which shows one year of growth is called an annual ring. The rings appear as concentric layers, formed due to new growth in the vascular cambium, and show the amount of wood produced during one growing season. Spring wood (early wood) is formed in spring and early summer by quick division of cambium: soft, light-coloured, a broad strip. Autumn wood (late wood) is formed in late summer or autumn when growth slows down: dense, dark-coloured, a narrow strip. Both together are collectively called an annual ring, so counting the rings gives the age of the tree, and biologists study them to know the past climate of the area. Dendrochronology is the scientific method of dating tree rings to the exact year they were formed.

10.19 Meristems

A meristem is a group of specialized cells which retain the ability to divide by mitosis; when it divides, some cells remain meristematic while others form specialized cells. The term was first used in 1858 by Karl Wilhelm Von Nageli, from the Greek word Merizein, meaning to divide. Three types: apical meristem at the tips of growing root and shoot; intercalary meristem located between regions of permanent tissue (shown in the book in bamboo, a monocot); lateral meristem located towards the outer part of the stem. The apical meristem is responsible for primary growth (increase in length) and for production of lateral branches, leaves and flowers. It also produces the hormone auxin, which controls plant shape by regulating lateral shoot growth (apical dominance).

10.20 Plant Growth Hormones

Plant hormones or plant growth regulators (PGRs) are naturally occurring organic compounds which control growth and many other physiological functions. They are produced in very small quantities in one part of the plant and transported to another part, where they promote, inhibit or modify growth. There are five main types:

  • Auxins (Indole acetic acid, IAA) — Formula C₁₀H₉NO₂, naturally formed in apical meristems. Synthetic auxins include 2, 4-D, NAA and IBA; substances that inhibit auxins are called antiauxins. Auxins maintain apical dominance; low concentration promotes root growth while higher concentration inhibits it; they increase shoot length by promoting elongation of cells, affect phototropism and geotropism, delay flower production when applied on leaves, and help healing of injury.
  • Gibberellins — More than 75 types discovered (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃, etc.); GA₃ is the most active and best known, obtained from a rice fungus, called gibberellic acid, formula C₁₉H₂₂O₆. They promote flowering, help germination (e.g. grasses), break dormancy of seeds and buds, promote cell division in the stem, increase the number and size of fruits (e.g. grapes), and promote bud initiation and leaf growth.
  • Cytokinins — Derivatives of adenine, like kinetin and zeatin (C₁₀H₁₃N₅O), mostly found in meristematic regions. Their main function is to promote cell division (cytokinesis); they break dormancy of seeds and buds, promote leaf and fruit growth, and inhibit primary root growth.
  • Abscisic Acid (ABA) — A terpenoid, formula C₁₅H₂₀O₄, formed in leaves, fruits and seeds and moving in the vascular system. Under stress it checks growth of roots and stems, induces bud dormancy, is responsible for leaf and fruit drop (abscission), and helps seed development and maturation.
  • Ethylene — A gaseous hormone, formula C₂H₄, produced in trace amounts in most organs of higher plants. Its main function is promotion of fruit ripening; it inhibits root growth and axillary bud development at higher concentration, breaks dormancy of buds, and promotes dropping of leaves and fruit (abscission).

Key Points

  • Primary growth increases length (apical meristem); secondary growth increases thickness (lateral meristem or cambium).
  • One annual ring = spring wood (broad, light) + autumn wood (narrow, dark) of one year.
  • Meristems divide by mitosis: apical, intercalary and lateral; apical meristem auxin regulates lateral shoots.
  • Five PGRs: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene.

lessons.title: Growth Movements, Photoperiodism, Phytochrome and Vernalization
lessons.notes_html:
Plant parts move in response to stimuli, and flowering is controlled by the relative length of day and night, the pigment phytochrome, and, in many plants, a period of cold.

10.21 Growth Movements

Movements in plants are very slow; we cannot see them happening directly but can see their effects, e.g. growth in size and opening of flowers. They happen due to changes in the environment called stimuli.

  • Tactic movement — The whole organism shows movement due to the effect of an external stimulus.
  • Nastic movement — The organs of plants show movements due to a non-directional stimulus.
  • Tropic movement (tropose - turn) — Growth by turning of the plant in response to a stimulus acting from one side. Bending towards the stimulus is positive; bending away is negative.

Types of tropic movements: Phototropism — due to light: stem towards light (positive), root away (negative). Geotropism or gravitropism — due to gravity: root positive, stem negative. Hydrotropism — in response to water: root positive, stem negative. Chemotropism — due to the influence of chemicals. Thigmotropism — in response to touch or contact, e.g. stem tendrils help the plant to climb up a support.

10.22 Photoperiodism

Photoperiodism shows how plants respond to the relative length of day and night. A plant will only bloom if the day length is right for it; this specific day length is called the critical photoperiod.

  • Short day plants — Flower when day length is below some critical photoperiod, otherwise they continue to grow vegetatively; they usually develop flowers in late summer, e.g. soyabean, sugar cane, cocklebur, tobacco, Maryland mammoth and chrysanthemum.
  • Long day plants — Flower when day length exceeds some critical photoperiod; they usually flower in summer, e.g. hibiscus, cabbage, sugar beet, spring wheat and spinach.
  • Day neutral plants — No response to photoperiod for flowering; they flower after attaining a certain stage or age, usually throughout the year, e.g. cucumber, sweet pea, beans, tomato, rose and maize.

Research has shown that flowering depends not on the light period but on a critical period of continuous, uninterrupted darkness: short day plants are actually long night plants (a flash of light interrupting the dark period prevents flowering), and long day plants are actually short night plants (a brief flash of light interrupting a long dark period induces flowering).

10.23 Flowering in Plants: Phytochrome

Flowering in short day and long day plants is due to the interconversion of phytochrome red (Pr) and phytochrome far-red (Pfr). Phytochrome is a coloured photoreceptor that plants use to detect light, present in very small quantity; it is a blue-green pigment, a protein to which a non-protein part is attached.

  • Pr — Absorbs red light (660 nm); the inactive form, and more stable than Pfr.
  • Pfr — Absorbs far-red light (730 nm); the active form.

During daytime, Pr is converted into Pfr by red light (quick conversion). At night, Pfr is slowly converted back into Pr (dark reversion; far-red light also converts it back), so the plant can sense whether it is night or day. In short day plants, Pr causes flowering (Pr ratio higher due to long darkness); in long day plants, Pfr is needed (Pfr ratio higher due to long light). When the optimum ratio is attained, the hormone florigen is produced in leaves, travels to the shoot apical meristem and initiates flowering.

Interconversion of phytochrome: red light converts Pr to Pfr in the day; darkness and far-red light convert Pfr back to Pr at night.

10.24 Vernalization

The word is derived from the Latin word vernus, meaning the spring; the term was first used by the Russian biologist Lysenko in 1920. Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by treating the plant with low temperature, by which a winter variety can be grown in spring. A temperature of 0-10°C is provided, but the best is 4°C; the whole plant, or only stem or roots, or the seeds, may be chilled. In some plants it is extremely important, otherwise they will not flower, e.g. carrot and winter wheat. Lysenko thought that during chilling a hormone called vernalin is produced, which transforms vegetative buds into floral buds; later studies explain that vernalin is actually gibberellins. Importance: winter plants can be grown in spring (the farmers of Siberia grow winter wheat in the short summer season), and the vegetative period is reduced, promoting early flowering.

10.25 Low Temperature Treatment in Biennial and Perennial Plants

Low temperature treatment ensures flowering during favourable conditions in spring, uniform flowering in a crop (which helps in pollination), and timely flowering for seed production and ornamental value. Biennial plants (e.g. carrot, cabbage, beets) require it to progress from the vegetative to the reproductive stage: in the first year they show only vegetative growth (roots and leaves), and cold treatment in winter is necessary to start flowering in the second growing season. Perennial plants: many herbaceous perennials (e.g. tulips, daffodils) require a specific number of chilling hours to break dormancy of flower buds; cold also affects vegetative buds and underground storage organs like bulbs or rhizomes, and prepares perennials to renew reproductive growth each year. If proper cold periods are not available, it may result in poor or delayed flowering, reduced flower size, or complete failure to flower.

Key Points

  • Tropic movements are directional: phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, chemotropism and thigmotropism.
  • Photoperiodism: short day (long night), long day (short night) and day neutral plants; the critical factor is uninterrupted darkness.
  • Phytochrome: Pr (660 nm, inactive) and Pfr (730 nm, active) interconvert; the right ratio produces florigen.
  • Vernalization (Lysenko, 1920): chilling at 0-10°C, best 4°C, promotes flowering; essential for many biennials and perennials.

lessons.title: Criteria for Animal Classification
lessons.notes_html:
The kingdom Animalia includes all animals. The word animal is derived from the Latin word anima, which means breath or soul. Animals are multicellular, ingestive, heterotrophic organisms, and they originated from animal-like protists. The branch of biology that deals with the study of animals is called Zoology.

11.1 Two Subkingdoms: Parazoa and Eumetazoa

Kingdom Animalia is divided into two subkingdoms, Parazoa and Eumetazoa, on the basis of the presence or absence of cellular organization.

  • Parazoa (para = beside, zoon = animal) — The simplest multicellular animals, believed to have evolved from protozoans. The body is just a collection of cells not differentiated into tissues or organs; there is some division of labour among the cells, but they are not strongly associated to perform a specific collective function. The only surviving Parazoans are the sponges, phylum Porifera (cellular level of organization).
  • Eumetazoa — Animals in which body cells are arranged into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems. Their cells are arranged into germinal layers: diploblastic (two germ layers) or triploblastic (three germ layers), present during the development of the embryo.

Symmetry: Grade Radiata and Grade Bilatera

The geometrical view of an organism is called symmetry; asymmetrical animals do not exhibit symmetry. On the basis of body symmetry, Eumetazoa is classified into grade Radiata and grade Bilatera.

Grade RadiataGrade Bilatera
Body organs arranged around a central axis; the body can be cut into two identical halves from any plane passing through the central axis.The body can be cut into two identical halves from a single longitudinal plane running down the middle line.
No right and left side.Right and left sides, anterior and posterior ends, dorsal and ventral surfaces.
Mostly sessile animals; an adaptation for a sessile life.Mostly motile animals; an adaptation to motility.
Radially symmetrical animals, e.g. coelenterates and adult echinoderms.Bilaterally symmetrical animals, from phylum Platyhelminthes to Chordata.

Diploblastic and Triploblastic Animals

  • Diploblastic — Two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with a non-cellular jelly-like mesoglea between them. Mostly without specialized organs; no specialized nervous system, only a network of neurons with few ganglia. A gastrovascular cavity with a single opening acts as both mouth and anus, e.g. Coelenterata (Cnidaria).
  • Triploblastic — Three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, visible only during embryonic development and later transformed into organs. Specialized organs, organ systems and a nervous system with ganglia or a brain are present. Bilaterally symmetrical, with a tubular digestive system having an anterior mouth and a posterior anus or cloaca, e.g. from Platyhelminthes to Chordata.

Classification According to Coelom (Body Cavity)

The coelom is a fluid-filled cavity between the outer body wall and the alimentary canal, lined by mesodermal membranes. Grade Bilatera is divided into three groups on the basis of the kind of coelom:

AcoelomatesPseudocoelomatesCoelomates
No body cavity; found only in Platyhelminthes. Between the digestive tract and the body wall, the mesoderm forms a loose cellular tissue called parenchyma or mesenchyma.A false coelom (pseudocoelom); found only in nematodes (Aschelminthes). It lies between mesoderm and endoderm, is not covered by coelomic epithelium, and is the remnant of the blastocoel.A true coelom; found from annelids to chordates. The mesoderm splits into outer parietal and inner visceral layers, and the cavity is filled with coelomic fluid.

The three kinds of body cavity: acoelomate, pseudocoelomate and coelomate (centre circle = gut).

Protostomes and Deuterostomes

Coelomates are classified into two groups on the basis of early development. In Protostomes (mollusks, annelids, arthropods) the mouth develops from the blastopore. In Deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates) the anus develops from the blastopore and the mouth forms later. (Cleavage is the division of the zygote in which the number of cells increases but the size of cells hardly increases; cleavage is either radial or spiral.)

Key Points

  • Animalia is divided into Parazoa (cellular level, sponges only) and Eumetazoa (tissue, organ and organ-system levels).
  • Radiata are radially symmetrical and mostly sessile; Bilatera are bilaterally symmetrical and mostly motile.
  • Diploblastic animals have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic animals also have mesoderm.
  • On the basis of coelom, Bilatera are acoelomates, pseudocoelomates or coelomates; coelomates are protostomes or deuterostomes.

lessons.title: Invertebrates and Vertebrates, and Phylum Porifera (Sponges)
lessons.notes_html:
Most biologists have divided animals into two major groups on the basis of the presence or absence of a vertebral column (backbone): invertebrates, which lack a vertebral column, and vertebrates, which possess one. Invertebrates account for more than 95% of known animal species and are divided into eight major phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematodes, Annelids, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata.

11.3 Differences Between Invertebrates and Vertebrates

InvertebratesVertebrates
Vertebral column (backbone) is absent.Vertebral column is present.
Mostly small in size, slowly moving or sessile.Large in size and mostly fast moving.
About 95% of all animal species.Only 5% of all animal species.
No pharyngeal gill cleft.Pharyngeal gill cleft increases the efficiency of breathing.
Ventral, solid tube of nervous system.Hollow, fluid-filled dorsal central nervous system.
Endoskeleton absent; if present, non-living.All possess a living endoskeleton (skull and vertebral column).
Heart, if present, is dorsal or lateral; mostly an open blood vascular system.Heart is ventrally located; closed blood vascular system.
May have more than two pairs of limbs; compound eyes present; tail usually absent.Not more than two pairs of limbs; no compound eyes; tail usually present.

11.4 Phylum Porifera — the Sponges

Porifera (Greek: poros = channels; Latin: ferre = to bear). The name Porifera was given by Robert E. Grant in 1836. Sponges are the simplest multicellular animals.

  • Habit and habitat — The larval stage is motile while the adult is sessile; about 10,000 species have been recorded. Their size ranges from a few millimetres wide to more than a metre long (e.g. Scolymastra joubini from Antarctica).
  • Body — No tissues and no organ organization; either asymmetrical or radially symmetrical. The body wall has an outer dermal layer, the pinacoderm, made of pinacocytes, and an inner layer, the choanoderm, containing flagellated collar cells called choanocytes. Between the two layers is a gelatinous matrix, the mesenchyma, containing many kinds of wandering amoeboid cells; amoeboid cells store food and give colour, while scleroblasts are the spicule and spongin fibre forming cells.
  • Canal system — The body has a single body cavity, the spongocoel, divided into canals. Water enters through numerous incoming pores, the ostia, and leaves through a single large outgoing pore, the osculum.
  • Nutrition — Heterotrophic: food comes in with the water current through the ostia, moved by the flagella of choanocytes, and intracellular digestion takes place. Digested food is transported by mesenchymal cells. Waste diffuses out through the body wall or the osculum; the nitrogenous product is ammonia, removed from each body cell by diffusion.
  • Nervous system and skeleton — The nervous system is absent, but neuron and neurosensory cells help to coordinate the water flow. The skeleton is mostly formed of needle-like spicules (calcareous or siliceous), while some sponges, like the bath sponge, possess spongin fibres.
  • Reproduction — Both asexual and sexual. Asexual reproduction is by external budding or internal budding (gemmule formation); regeneration is also common. Sponges are mostly hermaphrodite (bisexual) and protandrous (male gametes develop before the female). Fertilization is internal and occurs in the mesenchyma.
  • Examples — Sycon (marine sponge), Leucosolenia (erect, tube-shaped), Euplectella (glassy frame work) and Spongilla (fresh water sponge).

Anatomy of a sponge: water enters through the ostia into the spongocoel and leaves through the osculum.

Importance of Sponges

  • Bath sponges are used for washing and bathing by humans.
  • Sponges greatly absorb water, so they are used in surgical operations for absorbing fluid and blood.
  • In large buildings, sponges are used for sound absorption, to prevent echo.
  • They are also used for decorative purposes and in shoe or vehicle polishing.

Key Points

  • Invertebrates lack a backbone and make up more than 95% of animal species; vertebrates have a backbone and a closed blood vascular system.
  • Sponges (Porifera) are the simplest animals: cellular organization, no tissues, no nervous system.
  • Water enters a sponge through ostia and leaves through the osculum; choanocytes move the water and capture food.
  • The sponge skeleton is made of spicules or spongin fibres; gemmules are internal buds.

lessons.title: Phylum Cnidaria and Phylum Platyhelminthes
lessons.notes_html:
After the sponges, the next two phyla are the cnidarians, the first animals with true tissues and a gastrovascular cavity, and the flatworms, the first triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical animals.

11.5 Phylum Cnidaria (Coelenterata)

The name Cnidaria is given to this phylum because of the specialized stinging cells called cnidocytes, present all over the body, which give rise to nematocysts. The nematocyst is a capsule with paralyzing venom which acts as an offensive and defensive organ.

  • Habit and habitat — Either sessile (e.g. Hydra) or free-living and motile (e.g. jellyfish); many are colonial (e.g. Obelia). Most are carnivores. All cnidarians are aquatic, both marine and fresh water. Size ranges from microscopic (Hydra) to very large (e.g. Brachioceranthus, up to two metres in length).
  • Body — Radially symmetrical and mostly diploblastic: an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm, with a gelatinous substance, mesoglea, between the two layers. A single hollow internal cavity, the enteron or gastrovascular cavity, has a single opening, the mouth, which acts both as mouth and anus. The mouth is surrounded by tentacles.
  • Nervous system — An irregularly placed network of neurons with few ganglia. Some colonial cnidarians exhibit polymorphism: a species has two or more very different structural forms, with division of labour among units called zooids — polyps or hydrozooids (cylindrical feeding zooids) and medusae (umbrella-shaped reproductive zooids).
  • Reproduction — Both asexual and sexual. Asexual reproduction is by budding and regeneration (as in Hydra). In sexual reproduction gametes are formed. Alternation of generation is shown by some cnidarians (like Obelia): the polyp asexually produces male or female medusae, which undergo sexual reproduction to produce larvae that develop into new polyps.
  • Importance — Coral reefs protect the shores from erosion by tidal waves; many jewellery items are made from corals; cnidarians are used as decoration in aquariums and rock gardens; but some cnidarians sting humans (jellyfish and sea anemone). In Pakistan they are common at the sea shores of Mekran and Karachi. A coral reef is made up of a colony of coral polyps held together by calcium carbonate and is found in the warm shallow water of tropical oceans; the Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Queensland, Australia, is the largest coral reef system in the world, stretching over 2,300 km.

11.6 Phylum Platyhelminthes — the Flatworms

Platyhelminthes (Greek: platy = flat, helminth = worm) are also called flatworms or acoelomate worms.

  • Habit and habitat — Either free-living (e.g. Planaria) or parasitic (e.g. tapeworm). They are found in both fresh water and marine water, while parasitic worms are also found in the liver and gut of human beings.
  • Body — Triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and soft-bodied; the body is dorsoventrally flattened and acoelomate. They possess an incomplete digestive system, with a single opening, the mouth, which is less developed or absent in parasitic forms. The excretory system is a well developed protonephridial system containing flame cells.
  • Nervous system and locomotion — The nervous system consists of a network of nerves, with two longitudinal nerves and an anterior cerebral ganglion. Locomotion occurs by means of cilia located on the underside of the body.
  • Reproduction — Asexual reproduction by fission (regeneration) and sexual reproduction are both present. These worms are bisexual (hermaphrodite) with well developed gonads, ducts and accessory organs; fertilization is internal and development may be direct or indirect. Parasitic forms show special parasitic features: suckers and hooks for attachment, no digestive system of their own in tapeworms, and enormous egg production.
  • Examples — Planaria (Dugesia), liver fluke (Fasciola) and tapeworm (Taenia).

Key Points

  • Cnidarians are diploblastic and radially symmetrical, with stinging cnidocytes and nematocysts for offence and defence.
  • The gastrovascular cavity of cnidarians has one opening that serves as both mouth and anus; Obelia shows alternation of generation between polyp and medusa.
  • Flatworms are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and acoelomate, with flame cells for excretion.
  • Planaria is free-living; liver fluke and tapeworm are parasitic flatworms with suckers and hooks.

lessons.title: Phylum Aschelminthes and Phylum Mollusca
lessons.notes_html:
The roundworms are the first animals with a false body cavity and a complete digestive tube, while the mollusks are soft-bodied coelomates with a mantle, a muscular foot and, in most, a shell.

11.7 Phylum Aschelminthes — Nematodes or Roundworms

Aschelminthes (Greek: askos = cavity, helminthes = worms) are the nematodes or roundworms.

  • Habit and habitat — Parasitic or free-living. Some are intestinal parasites of humans and other animals, but most are free-living in soil and in the roots of plants. Size varies from microscopic to large, such as Ascaris, more than one foot in length. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 24% of the world population is infected with soil-transmitted helminths (worms).
  • Body — Triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical; segmentation is absent; the body is cylindrical and pointed at both ends. The body cavity is a pseudocoel.
  • Digestive system — Complete: a single tube with a mouth at the anterior end and an anus at the posterior end. The muscular layer is not continuous; it is divided into four longitudinal quadrants (two dorsolateral and two ventrolateral).
  • Nervous system — A nerve ring from which the nerve cord and fibres extend in various directions. Sensory papillae are present on the front part of the body, especially on the lips.
  • Reproduction — Sexual; sexes are mostly separate, some are hermaphrodite; fertilization is internal. Circulatory and respiratory systems are absent.
  • Importance — Nematodes cause many serious parasitic diseases: Ascaris lumbricoides, a human intestinal parasite, causes anaemia, abdominal pain and fever, and also migrates to the lungs. Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) lives in the caecum, appendix and colon of man and causes itching of the anus, inflammation of the colon and appendix, insomnia and loss of appetite. Hookworms are also parasites of the human intestine and cause bleeding. Free roundworms in soil cause disease to potato, onion, cotton and apple. Beneficial nematodes are used in biological pest control against insect pests in their larval and pupal stages.

11.8 Phylum Mollusca — Soft-Bodied Animals

Mollusca (Latin: mollis = soft). The term mollusk was introduced in 1650; about 50,000 species are recorded. The squid is the largest invertebrate, 15 metres long including tentacles.

  • Habit and habitat — Mostly free-living; some are attached (sessile). Found in fresh water, marine water, moist soil and on mountain rocks, all over the world.
  • Body — Soft-bodied and triploblastic. They are mostly haemocoelomate: the coelom is divided into blood spaces. The body contains a head, a visceral region and a muscular foot.
  • Mantle and shell — The whole body is covered by an envelope of glandular epithelial tissue called the mantle. The mantle in many cases secretes a calcareous shell, which may be internal (cuttlefish), external (snail), or absent (octopus).
  • Systems — Most body systems are well developed (digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous and reproductive). Respiration is through gills or the mantle. The blood circulatory system is of the open type, except in class Cephalopoda. They have a tongue-like structure provided with horny teeth called the radula (the rasping tongue). Nephridia are the excretory organs (one, two or six). The nervous system consists of a collection of ganglia in the head region forming a ganglionic mass, connected with the ganglia of the foot and visceral mass.
  • Reproduction — Mostly unisexual, a few bisexual; development is indirect through the trochophore larva.
  • Economic importance — Useful: some oysters make precious pearls (pearl oyster); shells of fresh water mussels are used in the button industry; oyster shells are mixed with tar in road building; mollusks are used for making ornaments and are a source of food in many countries (oyster, mussel, clam). Pearl culture (pearl farming) induces pearl formation in oysters by surgically implanting a nucleus and mantle tissue; the oyster secretes nacre, layer by layer, around the nucleus, forming a pearl over several years. Harmful: Teredo, a shipworm, destroys the wood of ships; some mollusks destroy plants by cutting up their roots and stems.
  • Examples — Snail, mussel (Unio), octopus and chiton.

Key Points

  • Roundworms (nematodes) are pseudocoelomates with a complete digestive tube — separate mouth and anus.
  • Ascaris lives in the human small intestine; pinworm lives in the caecum, appendix and colon.
  • Mollusks are soft-bodied animals with a head, visceral mass and muscular foot, covered by a mantle that secretes the shell.
  • The radula is the rasping, tongue-like feeding organ of mollusks; nephridia are their excretory organs.

lessons.title: Phylum Annelida and Phylum Arthropoda
lessons.notes_html:
Annelids are the first truly segmented coelomate worms, and arthropods — with jointed legs and a chitinous exoskeleton — form the biggest phylum of the animal kingdom.

11.9 Phylum Annelida — Segmented Worms

Annelida (Latin: annulus = a little ring; Greek: eidos = form).

  • Habit and habitat — Free-living, found in soil (earthworm), fresh water and marine water (Nereis); some are ectoparasites (leech).
  • Body and metamerism — Triploblastic and metamerically segmented: in metamerism the body is divided into segments both internally and externally, by a transverse partition called a septum between segments. Annelids possess a true coelom, divided into compartments by septa; the coelomic fluid also acts as a hydrostatic skeleton (the body becomes hard by fluid pressure).
  • Systems — A straight alimentary canal with mouth and anus at opposite ends (a complete digestive system). The circulatory system is closed. Segmentally arranged nephridia are the excretory organs. The nervous system has a dorsal pair of cerebral ganglia and a ventral double ganglionated nerve cord. Gaseous exchange is through the skin. Muscles with the hydrostatic skeleton help in locomotion. Chitinous chaetae or setae are the locomotory organs in the earthworm, while Nereis has parapodia; the leech has no locomotory organs.
  • Reproduction — Most annelids are bisexual (e.g. leeches, earthworm), some are unisexual (Nereis). Development is either direct or indirect through the trochophore larva. They also exhibit regeneration.
  • Economic importance — Earthworms burrow in the soil, which permits great penetration of air into the soil, improves the drainage capacity of the soil, makes the soil soft and increases fertility. Many worms are used as food by fishes.

11.10 Phylum Arthropoda — Joint-Footed Animals

Arthropoda (Greek: arthron = jointed, pous = foot). The name was given by Ernst Von Siebold in 1845.

  • Habit and habitat — Free-living or parasitic, found in almost all habitats. It is the biggest phylum, comprising about 75% of the animal kingdom.
  • Body — (i) A segmented body, the segments attached to one another by a thin, flexible cuticle. (ii) Several pairs of jointed limbs (appendages). (iii) The body is usually divided into head, thorax and abdomen. (iv) The body is covered with a chitinous cuticle. The reduced coelom contains blood and is called the haemocoel, connected with an open blood vascular system.
  • Systems — The digestive system is well developed, with mouth and anus or cloaca. The nervous system consists of paired ganglia forming a simple brain and a central ganglionated nerve cord. Sensory receptors, especially eyes, are present, along with cuticular hairs and antennae. Uric acid and guanine are the nitrogenous wastes, removed through unique excretory organs called Malpighian tubules or green glands. Respiration is through tracheae, gills or book lungs. The blood circulatory system is of the open type; the blood is colourless, without haemoglobin, but haemocyanin (a copper-containing protein) is present. A chitinous exoskeleton is present for the attachment of muscles.
  • Reproduction and metamorphosis — All are unisexual; fertilization is internal or external. Development is mostly indirect, accompanied by metamorphosis of two types: (a) Incomplete metamorphosis — the larval stage, called a nymph, is similar to the adult, e.g. cockroach. (b) Complete metamorphosis — through egg, larva, pupa and adult, e.g. butterfly. The periodic shedding of the exoskeleton during metamorphosis is called ecdysis or moulting.
  • Examples — Wasp, scorpion, centipede, crab, millipede.
  • Why arthropods are successful — They possess jointed feet and a segmented body, which provides great mobility. The chitinous exoskeleton protects the body and makes it light. Internal fertilization and development within an egg case (cocoon) help them, and appendages perform various functions such as quick movement, defence and offence, so they live in a variety of habitats — for example, the legs and mouth parts of the cockroach.

11.11 Economic Importance of Arthropods

  • Crustaceans — Provide food directly and indirectly to humans (prawn, crab, lobster). Some are harmful because they act as intermediate hosts for human parasites (larvae of nematodes are carried by Cyclops).
  • Beneficial insects — Help in pollination (bee, butterfly, ants); used as food in some parts of the world (grasshopper, cricket); many are scavengers. Commercial substances such as honey, beeswax, silk and shellac are produced by honey bees, silkworms and lac insects. Some insects eat other harmful insects, e.g. the dragonfly feeds on mosquitoes. Several insects are used for scientific studies, such as cockroach, fruit fly and grasshopper.
  • Harmful insects — Destroy stored foods and grains (ants, weevils); carry parasitic diseases (mosquito: malaria; tsetse fly: sleeping sickness); damage crops, fruit and timber trees (grasshoppers, locusts, beetles); damage books (silverfish) and furniture (white ants); some sting (bee) or suck blood (louse).
  • Arachnida — Poisonous arachnids like the scorpion and certain spiders sting humans; ticks and mites are parasitic disease carriers, and mites also destroy crops. Beneficial arachnids like scorpions and spiders feed on injurious insects.

Key Points

  • Annelids show true metamerism and a true coelom; nephridia are their excretory organs and setae or parapodia help in locomotion.
  • Earthworms improve soil aeration, drainage and fertility.
  • Arthropods are the largest phylum (about 75% of the animal kingdom): jointed legs, segmented body, chitinous exoskeleton shed by ecdysis.
  • Arthropods are both useful (pollination, honey, silk, food) and harmful (crop pests and disease carriers such as the mosquito).

lessons.title: Echinodermata, Hemichordata and Phylum Chordata
lessons.notes_html:
The echinoderms are spiny-skinned marine deuterostomes with a water vascular system. The hemichordates stand between invertebrates and chordates, and the chordates are defined by three basic characters: a notochord, a dorsal hollow nervous system and pharyngeal gill slits.

11.12 Phylum Echinodermata — Spiny-Skinned Animals

Echinodermata (Greek: echinos = spine, derma = skin). The phylum name was given by Leuckert in 1847.

  • Habit and habitat — Mostly free-living, some attached to the substratum; exclusively marine. More than 5,000 known species are recorded.
  • Body — Triploblastic and coelomate. The adult is radially symmetrical while the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. A delicate epidermis covers a firm mesodermal calcareous exoskeleton. The mouth is on the lower (oral) surface and the anus on the upper (aboral) surface. Arms radiate from a central disc; the body may be biscuit-shaped (cake urchin), star-shaped (starfish, brittle star), globular (sea urchin) or elongated (sea cucumber).
  • Water vascular system (ambulacral canal) — Water circulates through coelomic channels, entering through a sieve-like plate called the madreporite on the aboral body surface. It is a system of complex tubes and spaces surrounding the mouth and passing into the arms and tube feet. Locomotion occurs through the tube feet.
  • Other systems — The digestive and reproductive systems are well developed. There are no specialized organs for respiration or excretion. The nervous system is poorly developed and consists only of a pharyngeal nerve ring; the circulatory system is also less developed.
  • Reproduction — Mostly sexual; fertilization is external and the animals are unisexual. Development is indirect, through complex, bilaterally symmetrical larvae named Bipinnaria and Brachiolaria. Echinoderms also exhibit regeneration.
  • Examples and importance — Starfish, sea cucumber, sea lily, brittle star and sea urchin. Many are used as food; starfish act as scavengers and clean sea water; dried skeletons are used as fertilizer (rich in calcium and nitrogenous compounds). Some are poisonous (sea urchin stings humans) and they damage oyster beds.

11.13 Phylum Hemichordata — the Tongue Worms

Hemichordates resemble both echinoderms and chordates, because only these three groups are deuterostomes. Only 70 species are recorded. They were earlier placed in the chordates, but are now a separate phylum: they have some chordate-like characters (deuterostome development, pharyngeal gill slits, a dorsal nerve cord that is sometimes hollow), but lack a complete notochord, and their dorsal heart and epidermal nervous system are non-chordate characters.

  • The body is soft, unsegmented and mostly worm-like, distinguished into proboscis, collar and trunk.
  • The epidermis contains mucus-secreting cells; the animals are bilaterally symmetrical and triploblastic.
  • Gills are the respiratory organs; the blood is colourless and without cells; a dorsal heart has invertebrate-like blood vessels.
  • The excretory system is well developed (a glomerulus is present in the proboscis, where the excretory pore also opens); the nervous system is epidermal.
  • They are either unisexual or bisexual; fertilization is external and development indirect. They are marine, solitary or colonial, free-living or sessile, and feed on microliving things. Examples: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus.

11.14 Phylum Chordata: Basic and General Characteristics

All chordates possess three basic or fundamental characteristics, during some stage or in the whole of life:

  • Notochord — An unjointed, solid skeleton placed above the alimentary canal and below the dorsal body wall and central nervous system; it appears in the embryo of all chordates. In lower chordates it is present throughout life, but in vertebrate chordates it is replaced by the vertebral column; in vertebrates it serves as the axial endoskeleton and gives support to the body.
  • Dorsal hollow nervous system — The central nervous system is dorsally placed, located above the notochord; the nerve cord is hollow, fluid-filled and non-ganglionated.
  • Pharyngeal gill slits and gill pouches — Paired openings in the pharyngeal region. In aquatic chordates they persist and function as respiratory organs, while in terrestrial vertebrates they are replaced by the Eustachian or auditory tube, parathyroid, tonsils and thymus.
