General characteristics: bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic body; coelomate body cavity; a complete digestive system with digestive glands; a closed blood vascular system with a ventral heart; a well developed hepatic portal system; organ-system level of organization; a post-anal tail in most chordates; and kidneys (proto-, meso- or meta-nephric) as excretory organs.

The basic characteristics of chordates: dorsal hollow nerve cord, notochord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail.

Acrania and Craniata

Phylum Chordata has two groups. (i) Acrania (invertebrate chordates) — "without skull": no brain or cranium, no jaws, RBCs or paired appendages, and the notochord never changes into a vertebral column. Its two subphyla are: Urochordata — the notochord is present only in the tail of the larva and disappears in the adult, as does the nerve cord (only a dorsal ganglion remains); larvae are free-swimming, adults non-motile, and the body is covered with a tunic, so they are called tunicates, e.g. Ascidia, Herdmania, Molgula; and Cephalochordata — the notochord runs mid-dorsally through the body and persists, with the nerve cord, throughout life, e.g. Amphioxus (Branchiostoma). (ii) Craniata (vertebrate chordates) — one subphylum, Vertebrata: the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column; they have a brain and cranium, paired appendages, teeth, jaws and RBCs, and kidneys. So all vertebrates are chordates, but all chordates are not vertebrates.

Key Points

  • Echinoderms are marine, radially symmetrical as adults, with a water vascular system entering through the madreporite and locomotion by tube feet.
  • Hemichordates (Balanoglossus) have proboscis, collar and trunk, with some chordate-like and some non-chordate characters.
  • Every chordate has, at some stage, a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits.
  • Acrania (Urochordata and Cephalochordata) have no skull; Craniata (Vertebrata) replace the notochord with a vertebral column.

lessons.title: Vertebrate Classes: Fishes, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds and Mammals
lessons.notes_html:
The vertebrate chordates (Craniata) are divided into two superclasses: Agnatha, without true jaws and paired appendages, and Gnathostomata, with true jaws and paired appendages. Gnathostomata has six classes: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. The two fish classes are sometimes together placed in a division known as Pisces.

Superclass Agnatha: Class Cyclostomata

Cyclostomata (cyclo = circular, stoma = mouth, because their mouth is circular). These fishes are without true jaws and form the most primitive group of living vertebrates. The body is eel-shaped, scales are absent, the skin is smooth and soft, the skeleton is cartilaginous and the mouth is suctorial; there are no paired appendages. The heart is a two-chambered venous heart with many aortic arches; the digestive system lacks a stomach; there are 6–14 pairs of gills for respiration. They are unisexual (lamprey) or bisexual (hagfish), with a single testis or a single ovary and no accessory ducts; fertilization is external, and development is direct or indirect (the lamprey has a prolonged larval period). Examples: Myxine (hagfish) and Lamprey (Petromyzon).

Class Chondrichthyes — Cartilaginous Fishes

  • Habit and habitat — Exclusively marine and free-living.
  • Body — Spindle-shaped; the mouth is ventral and semi-circular, and the nasal sacs do not open into the oral cavity. The skin is tough, covered with sandpaper-like placoid scales. Respiration is through 5–7 pairs of gills, not covered by an operculum (lid). The endoskeleton is completely cartilaginous and the swim bladder is absent.
  • Systems and reproduction — The digestive system has a cloaca (a common opening acting as the urinogenital opening) and a J-shaped stomach. The heart is a venous, single-circuit heart with a single auricle and a single ventricle, and 5–7 pairs of aortic arches. Sexes are separate with paired gonads; fertilization is internal; oviparous or ovoviviparous. The largest of all fishes, the whale shark (30–50 feet long), belongs to this group. Examples: skate, rays, sting ray, electric ray and dog fish (sharks).
  • Economic importance — Beneficial: a great source of food; shark liver oil is a source of vitamin A and D; shark skin leather is used for bags and shoes. Harmful: sharks feed on sea food used by humans, like prawn, crab and lobster. In fishes, gills take oxygen from water and fins give balance, steering and propulsion.

Class Osteichthyes — Bony Fishes

  • Habit and body — They live in both marine and fresh water. The body is spindle-shaped and the mouth is terminal. Most have dermal, non-placoid scales: ganoid, cycloid or ctenoid. There are four pairs of gills, supported by bony arches and covered with a lid called the operculum. The endoskeleton is mostly bony, and a swim bladder is usually present, which helps in buoyancy (staying at a chosen depth without spending energy).
  • Systems and reproduction — The heart has two chambers (an auricle and a ventricle) and four pairs of aortic arches; the brain has ten pairs of cranial nerves. Sexes are separate with paired gonads; fertilization is mostly external; most are oviparous, some ovoviviparous. Examples: trout, cod, carp and catfish.
  • Economic importance — Fresh water and marine bony fishes are an important food source (cod, herring, salmon, trout, carp, catfish, mullet). Fish oil, fish meat and liquid glue are made from bony fish, and cod liver oil is the source of vitamin A and D.

Class Amphibia — the First Land Vertebrates

Amphibia (Greek: amphi = both, bios = life) are the first land vertebrates, i.e. the transition from aquatic to land habitat; they probably originated from Dipnoi, the lobe-finned lung fishes.

  • Body — The skin is smooth, scaleless and with many mucus glands (some also have poisonous glands and chromatophores). The body is divided into head, trunk, and tail or no tail. There are usually two pairs of legs, but some are legless (caecilians). Larvae respire through gills; adults mostly through lungs and skin. The heart has right and left auricles and a single ventricle, with sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus.
  • Reproduction — Unisexual, with paired sex organs; fertilization is usually external. Most are oviparous and show indirect development through metamorphosis. They are anamniotes (the embryo lacks a protective membrane) and poikilothermic (cold-blooded), so they hibernate in winter. Examples: frogs and toads (tailless), salamanders (tailed), caecilians (limbless).

Class Reptilia

Reptilia (Latin: repere = to crawl) are the first successful terrestrial group.

  • Skin and body — Dry, non-glandular, scaly skin (snakes and lizards) or bony plates (tortoise and crocodile). The body is divided into head, trunk and tail; appendages are tetrapod and pentadactyl, but some reptiles are legless (snakes). The skull has one occipital condyle. All are cold-blooded, so they hibernate in winter.
  • Heart and reproduction — The heart has right and left auricles and a partly divided ventricle, except in the crocodile, which has completely divided ventricles and atria. Fertilization is internal; mostly oviparous, laying amniotic, large, yolky, shelled eggs. They respire through lungs. Examples: snakes (cobra), lizards (wall lizard), turtles, tortoises and crocodiles.

Class Aves — Birds

Aves (Latin: avis = bird). Birds evolved from ancient running reptiles; the Jurassic (144–208 million years ago) birds Archaeopteryx (preserved in the British Museum, London) and Archaeornis (preserved in Berlin Museum, Germany) provided evidence of a connecting link between birds and reptiles.

  • Diagnostic characters — The body is streamlined, covered with feathers, and the forelimbs are modified into wings. The mouth contains a beak without teeth, and the sternum is modified into a keel. They have a single occipital condyle and are warm-blooded (homeothermic). The body is divided into head, neck, trunk and tail. Locomotion is bipedal; the hind limbs are modified for perching and bear scales and claws. The endoskeleton is light and hollow.
  • Systems — A four-chambered heart (two auricles and two ventricles); only the right aorta is present. The lungs are supplemented with air sacs and show double respiration. The voice box is the syrinx. There is a pair of kidneys but no urinary bladder (to reduce weight); the nitrogenous waste is uric acid, removed as crystals through the faeces. The gizzard is the grinding organ.
  • Reproduction — All are unisexual; fertilization is internal; birds lay eggs (oviparous); the left ovary is functional. These are the flight adaptations of birds: streamlined body, wings, hollow bones, keeled sternum, air sacs, beak and no urinary bladder. Some birds have lost flight and are called running birds (kiwi, ostrich, emu, rhea, cassowary); flying birds include parrot, crow, pigeon, sparrow and kite. The penguin is an aquatic bird whose forelimbs are modified into paddles.

Class Mammalia

The name Mammalia was given by Linnaeus. The diagnostic character of mammals is the presence of mammary glands, by which females nurse their young ones.

  • General characters — The body is mostly covered with hairs or fur. The central nervous system is highly developed; the lungs possess numerous alveoli and bronchioles. The diaphragm is a muscular partition between the chest and abdomen. Most have external ears (pinnae), and sweat and sebaceous (oil) glands. Mammals are warm-blooded (homeotherms, like birds; reptiles and amphibians are poikilotherms). They have two pairs of pentadactyl limbs, two occipital condyles and a large cranium. The buccal cavity has two sets of teeth in the life span (milk teeth and permanent teeth); dentition is heterodont. The heart has two atria and two ventricles, with one left aorta. Mature RBCs are non-nucleated. Fertilization is internal and they are mostly viviparous.
  • Subclass Prototheria (egg-laying mammals) — A connecting link between reptiles and mammals. Mammalian characters: mammary glands, hair, diaphragm and left aorta. Reptilian characters: cloaca, egg laying and some reptilian skeleton. They have one living order, the monotremes, found only in Australia. Examples: Echidna (spiny ant eater) and duck-billed platypus.
  • Subclass Metatheria (pouched mammals, marsupials) — Females possess an abdominal pouch (marsupium) in which they rear their immature young; the mammary glands are inside the pouch. Generally burrowing and herbivorous; found in Australia and America. Examples: opossum, kangaroo and Tasmanian wolf.
  • Subclass Eutheria (placental mammals) — True mammals and the largest group: the young develop inside the mother's body and are nourished through the placenta, so they are truly viviparous. The anus and urinogenital openings are completely separated. In some forms hair is modified into spines (porcupine, hedgehog) or scales (pangolin). Examples: goat, dog, horse, elephant, seal, whale, dolphin, man and monkey.

Key Points

  • Agnatha (Cyclostomata: hagfish, lamprey) have no true jaws; Gnathostomata have jaws and paired appendages.
  • Chondrichthyes have a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales and no swim bladder; Osteichthyes have a bony skeleton, an operculum and usually a swim bladder.
  • Amphibians are cold-blooded anamniotes with metamorphosis; reptiles are the first successful terrestrial group, laying shelled amniotic eggs.
  • Birds are homeothermic, feathered, with wings, hollow bones, a keeled sternum, air sacs and a syrinx.
  • Mammals have mammary glands, hair and a diaphragm: Prototheria lay eggs, Metatheria carry young in a pouch, Eutheria nourish young through a placenta.

lessons.title: Chromosomes: Structure, Types and Ultra-Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Chromosomes (Chromo — colored; soma — body) are compact coils of thread-like structure, clearly visible only during cell division. In interphase they uncoil into a fine chromatin network (DNA and proteins) and carry the information the cell needs to exist. They were first recorded by Walther Fleming in 1882 in rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae; Waldeyer assigned the name chromosome. They are linear in eukaryotes and circular in prokaryotes.

Chromosome Number and Karyotype

Number varies between species but stays constant in a species, generation after generation. Most animals and plants are diploid (two sets), many plants are polyploid (more than two sets), bryophytes and many fungi are monoploid, and haploid (half the somatic number) applies to gametes and most spores. Book examples (pairs): Penicillium 1, mosquito 3, fruit fly 4, lettuce 9, corn 10, frog 13, honey bee 16, mouse 20, human 23, monkey 24, camel 35, sugarcane 40, some ferns more than 500. The particular array of chromosomes an individual possesses is its karyotype.

Structure of a Chromosome

  • Monad and diad — A monad (unduplicated) chromosome has one strand, a chromatid; a diad (duplicated) has two sister chromatids, each a long DNA molecule tightly coiled with histone proteins.
  • Centromere (primary constriction) — The narrowed point of union. On both sides are disc-shaped proteins, the kinetochore, where spindle microtubules attach to move the chromosome during division.
  • Secondary constriction (nuclear organizer) — A second point of union on some chromosomes; it gives rise to nucleoli in interphase. The part beyond it is a knob-like satellite. DNA with useless sequences is junk DNA.
  • Telomeres — The terminal ends; they prevent chromosomes attaching to each other at their ends, and are made of repeated DNA with the sequence 5' TTAGGG-3'.

A duplicated (diad) chromosome: two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, telomeres at the ends.

Types on the Basis of Centromere Position

  • Metacentric — Centromere in the centre.
  • Submetacentric — Centromere below or above the centre.
  • Acrocentric — Arms on one side very short, on the other side very long.
  • Telocentric — Centromere at the tip, at one end.

Chemical Composition and Ultra-Structure

Chromosomes are nucleoprotein: about 60% proteins, 40% DNA and a significant amount of RNA. An average human chromosome has about 140 million nucleotides in about 5 cm of DNA. Under the electron microscope, DNA is packed in repeated nucleosomes: about 146–147 nucleotides coiled around a core of eight histones (an octamer: two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4). Histones are positively charged (rich in arginine and lysine) and are attracted to the negatively charged phosphate groups of DNA. DNA between nucleosomes is linker DNA, with linker histone H1. Packing levels: 2 nm DNA → 10 nm nucleosome string → 30 nm chromatin solenoid → 300 nm fibres → 700 nm supercoils → 1400 nm chromatid. In interphase, highly condensed heterochromatin is mostly not expressed, while less condensed euchromatin condenses during division and its genes can be expressed after division.

Key Points

  • Chromosomes are DNA coiled with histones, visible only during division; number is fixed for each species.
  • Diad = two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, with kinetochore, satellite and telomeres.
  • Four types by centromere position: metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
  • Nucleosome = 146–147 nucleotides around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4 x 2).

lessons.title: DNA as the Hereditary Material: Griffith, Avery and Hershey–Chase
lessons.notes_html:
Chromosomes contain both DNA and protein, so it was not confirmed which one carries hereditary information. Three classic experiments settled the question.

Griffith's Experiment (1928)

Fredrick Griffith gave the first evidence while working with Streptococcus pneumoniae: the S-type has a polysaccharide capsule, smooth and shiny colonies, and is virulent; the R-type has no capsule, rough colonies, and is non-virulent. S-type killed mice by blood poisoning; R-type caused no ill effects. Heat-killed S-type alone left mice healthy, but a mixture of dead S-type and live R-type — each harmless alone — killed the mice, and live virulent S-type bacteria were recovered from their blood. The information for the coat had passed from dead S-type to live R-type, permanently transforming it. This transfer of genetic material that alters the recipient cell is called transformation.

Avery, Macleod and McCarty (1944)

Oswald Avery, with Colin Macleod and Maclyn McCarty, identified the transforming principle. To mixtures of dead S- and live R-Streptococcus they added proteinase, RNase and DNase in separate tubes. Proteinase and RNase did not affect transformation — S-cells appeared. DNase destroyed all transforming activity and no S-cells appeared. They confirmed DNA is the hereditary material, while protein and RNA have no hereditary role.

Hershey and Chase Experiment (1952)

Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used bacteriophage T₂, which infects Escherichia coli and, like a chromosome, is made of DNA and protein only (linear double-stranded DNA). They labelled phage DNA with radioactive 32P in one experiment and the protein coats with radioactive 35S (present only in protein) in another. Separate bacterial cultures were exposed to each type, then agitated violently in a blender to remove the protein coats from the bacterial surfaces. Bacteria lost nearly all the 35S label, because it stayed in the coats outside; the 32P label was found inside the bacteria. When new viruses were released, those from the 32P culture were labelled and those from the 35S culture were unlabelled — proving the hereditary information injected into bacteria was DNA, not protein.

Key Points

  • Griffith (1928): dead S + live R killed mice — transformation showed a hereditary principle passes between cells.
  • Avery, Macleod and McCarty (1944): only DNase destroyed transformation, so the principle is DNA.
  • Hershey and Chase (1952): 32P (DNA) entered bacteria and labelled the next phage generation; 35S (protein) stayed outside.

lessons.title: DNA Replication: Models, Meselson–Stahl and the Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
DNA replication copies a double-stranded DNA molecule to produce two identical molecules, so that daughter cells get the same genetic information as the parent cell. It occurs in the S-phase of interphase.

Three Models of Replication

  • Conservative — Both parental strands stay intact: one daughter molecule is wholly parental, the other wholly new.
  • Dispersive — Both daughter molecules are mixtures; each strand is a patchwork of original and new DNA.
  • Semiconservative — Parental strands separate, each is a template for a new strand; each daughter has one original and one new strand.

Meselson and Stahl Experiment (1958)

Mathew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in heavy nitrogen (15N) so the DNA became fully labelled, then shifted them to light nitrogen (14N). Samples after each replication round were centrifuged in cesium chloride (CsCl); heavier DNA settled lower. After the first generation in 14N the DNA was intermediate (hybrid) density, 14N–15N, rejecting the conservative model. After the second generation two bands appeared, one light and one hybrid — proving semiconservative replication.

Mechanism of Replication

  • 1. Initiation — Begins at origins of replication, forming replication bubbles and a Y-shaped replication fork. Helicase unwinds the helix; topoisomerase relieves tension ahead of the fork by cutting and rejoining strands; single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) stop the strands re-annealing; primase synthesizes a short RNA primer (a few nucleotides) as the starting point for DNA polymerase.
  • 2. Elongation — DNA polymerase III (prokaryotes; similar enzymes in eukaryotes) adds complementary nucleotides to the 3' end of the primer. The leading strand is made continuously, 5' to 3', toward the fork. The lagging strand is made discontinuously away from the fork in Okazaki fragments, each needing a new primer. A subunit of polymerase III also does proof reading, removing mismatched nucleotides.
  • 3. Termination — DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and replaces them with DNA; DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments. Replication ends when forks meet, or at termination sequences (especially in prokaryotes).

Replication at a fork: the leading strand grows continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments away from it.

Stability and Variability of DNA

Stability depends on hydrogen bonds between bases and water molecules and base-stacking interactions between adjacent bases, plus accurate replication and repair systems; DNA polymerase adds about 1000 nucleotides per second. Genetic variation is the difference in DNA sequences between individuals, in germ cells (sperm and egg) and somatic cells. It creates new alleles and occurs mostly by random mating, random fertilization, mutation, recombination between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, and genetic drift — change in allelic frequencies of a small population by chance.

Key Points

  • Replication is semiconservative (S-phase); Meselson and Stahl proved it with 15N/14N and CsCl centrifugation.
  • Helicase unwinds, topoisomerase relieves tension, SSBs hold strands apart, primase lays an RNA primer.
  • Leading strand continuous toward the fork; lagging strand in Okazaki fragments; polymerase I replaces primers, ligase seals gaps.

lessons.title: Genetic Code, Codons and Transcription
lessons.notes_html:
A gene is the specific sequence of nucleotides in DNA which determines the amino acid sequence of a protein. The genetic code is the combination of three nucleotides which specifies a particular amino acid.

Code, Codon and Anticodon

The code lies on the sense or coding strand of DNA (5' to 3'); the other strand is the antisense / non-coding / template strand (3' to 5'). The alphabet is four nucleotides — A, G, C, T — arranged in code words of three bases. In transcription the codes pass to mRNA as codons. Of 64 codons, 61 are sense codons and 3 are stop (non-sense) codons: UGA, UAG, UAA. AUG is the start codon (methionine). The triplet on DNA is the code, its complement on mRNA the codon, and its complement on tRNA the anticodon (book example: codon GGU = glycine; DNA code CCA; anticodon CCA). Mitochondrial DNA is an exception to universality: there UGA codes tryptophan, AUA codes methionine, and AGA, AGG act as stop codons.

Characteristics of Codons

  • Triplet — Three nucleotides code for one amino acid.
  • Degenerate — Some amino acids have one codon (AUG = methionine, UGG = tryptophan); others have several, e.g. isoleucine (AUU, AUC, AUA) and leucine (six codons). This is degeneracy.
  • Universal — The same in most organisms, e.g. AUU for isoleucine, UUU for phenylalanine.
  • No punctuation — No punctuation between successive codons on mRNA.
  • Non-overlapping — AUGGUAGCG is read as AUG/GUA/GCG, not AUG/UGG/GUA.

Transcription

Gene expression is DNA to RNA (transcription) and RNA to protein (translation). Transcription copies a gene's DNA sequence into RNA by RNA polymerase, during interphase (G₁, G₀, G₂), in three phases:

  • Initiation — RNA polymerase binds the promoter (the gene's regulatory region) and synthesizes RNA 5' to 3'. Prokaryotes have one RNA polymerase for all RNAs; eukaryotes have three: polymerase-I for rRNA, polymerase-II for mRNA, polymerase-III for tRNA. The bacterial core enzyme (two alpha, one beta, one beta prime subunits) plus the sigma factor makes the holoenzyme; sigma is removed after binding. Binding sites: prokaryotes TATAAT (-10), TTGACA (-35); eukaryotes TATA box (-25), CAAT box (-70). Binding forms a transcription bubble.
  • Elongation — The core enzyme extends the RNA chain from ribonucleoside triphosphates, moving 5' to 3' toward the terminator and copying the DNA accurately.
  • Termination — The terminator has a series of GC pairs followed by AT pairs; the mRNA forms a GC hairpin followed by a poly U tail, and the hairpin makes RNA polymerase stop.

Transcription differs in eukaryotes: three polymerases (not one) and starts from many points, forming many transcription bubbles.

Post-Transcriptional Modification of mRNA

Newly made primary (immature) mRNA is changed into mature (functional) mRNA. Prokaryotes need no such process (no introns, no nucleus). In eukaryotes a cap — GTP (7-methyl triphosphate guanosine), linked 5' to 5' — and a poly A tail (about 30–500 adenine nucleotides at the 3' end) are added, keeping the mRNA stable against nucleases and phosphatases on its journey to the ribosomes. Primary mRNA contains non-coding introns and coding exons; in RNA splicing the spliceosome (small nuclear RNAs and about 80 proteins) removes introns and RNA ligase joins the exons — so the mature mRNA is shorter than the primary transcript.

Key Points

  • Genetic code: triplet, degenerate, universal, non-overlapping, no punctuation; AUG start, UAA/UAG/UGA stop.
  • Code on DNA, codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA.
  • Transcription: promoter binding, 5' to 3' elongation, GC hairpin termination.
  • Eukaryotic mRNA is capped, tailed and spliced, so it shortens before translation.

lessons.title: Translation: Protein Synthesis, Prokaryote–Eukaryote Differences and Uses of Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Translation is the formation of protein with the help of RNA — the second stage of gene expression. The ribosome decodes mRNA to produce a polypeptide that folds into an active protein. In prokaryotes it occurs freely in the cytoplasm; in eukaryotes across the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. It has four phases.

Phases of Translation

  • i) Activation — Inactive cytoplasmic amino acids are activated by aminoacyl tRNA synthetase with ATP: AA + ATP + Enzyme → AA.AMP.Enzyme Complex + 2Pi. The enzyme then attaches the amino acid to its specific tRNA at the 3' end, forming aminoacyl-tRNA.
  • ii) Initiation — The ribosomal subunits separate; mRNA binds an rRNA in the small subunit with initiation factor IF₃. A tRNA carrying N-formyl methionine binds at the P-site (peptidyl site), controlled by IF₁ and IF₂. The A-site (aminoacyl site) receives successive amino-acid tRNAs and the E-site (exit site) lets empty tRNA exit. The large subunit binds, exposing the codon next to AUG, and IF₁, IF₂, IF₃ are released.
  • iii) Elongation — Elongation factors bring the tRNA with the matching anticodon to the A-site codon. The large subunit catalyses a peptide bond: the first amino acid is released from its tRNA and attached to the second, in the presence of peptidyl synthetase. The ribosome then translocates three nucleotides along mRNA (5' to 3'): the empty tRNA moves to the E-site and leaves, the growing chain moves to the P-site, and the next codon is exposed at the A-site. The cycle repeats.
  • iv) Termination — When a non-sense (stop) codon reaches the A-site, no tRNA binds it; releasing factors (RF/TF) terminate translation, the polypeptide and tRNA are released, and the ribosomal subunits separate from the mRNA.

Protein Synthesis: Prokaryotes vs Eukaryotes

FeatureProkaryotesEukaryotes
Ribosomes70S (30S + 50S)80S (40S + 60S)
SiteCytosolCytosol, RER and outer nuclear membrane
Initiating amino acidN-formyl methionineMethionine
mRNAPolycistronic (many proteins)Monocistronic (one protein)
Initiation factorsSingle (as printed)More than one
Releasing factorsTwoOnly one

Uses of Synthesized Proteins

Proteins made in ribosomes are processed in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies and packed in lysosomes. They work inside the cell (respiratory proteins; enzymes like DNase, RNase) or outside the cell (antibodies in blood, digestive enzymes in the digestive tract, many hormones in blood), and also give structural support, movement and enzymatic activity — their functions are as varied as their amino acid sequences and three-dimensional structures.

Key Points

  • Translation: activation, initiation (P, A, E sites), elongation (peptide bonds, translocation), termination (releasing factors).
  • Prokaryotes: 70S ribosomes, N-formyl methionine, polycistronic mRNA. Eukaryotes: 80S, methionine, monocistronic mRNA.
  • Proteins work inside cells (enzymes) or outside them (antibodies, digestive enzymes, hormones).

lessons.title: Regulation of Gene Expression and the Lac Operon
lessons.notes_html:
Regulation of gene expression is the control of the amount and timing of appearance of a gene (genotype to phenotype). Genes turn on or off in response to internal or external signals. An adult human has more than 37 trillion cells with the same genome, yet only some genes are on in each cell, giving about 200 types of cells by differential gene expression.

Importance

Regulation increases the adaptability and versatility of prokaryotes and eukaryotes, helps cells fulfil their protein needs, and drives differentiation, morphogenesis (shaping of the organism by differentiation of cells, tissues and organs according to the genetic blueprint and environment) and physiology. If regulation is disturbed, serious diseases such as cancer may occur.

Positive and Negative Control

  • Positive regulation — Gene expression is increased by activator proteins.
  • Negative regulation — Gene expression is stopped by a repressor protein.

The Lac Operon

In bacteria and viruses, a cluster of genes with related functions regulated as a unit is an operon: structural genes (direct synthesis of related enzymes), a promoter (starting point for transcription) and an operator (an on/off switch within or overlapping the promoter). In E. coli, without lactose the bacterium has very few lactose enzymes; fed lactose, it quickly makes them. The lac operon has three genes: lac-Z encodes beta-galactosidase (breaks lactose into glucose and galactose), lac-Y encodes lactose permease (transports lactose into the cell), and lac-A encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase (detoxification of lactose metabolism byproducts).

Negative and Positive Control of the Lac Operon

Negative control: the operon is on until switched off. The lac repressor, produced by a regulatory site, fits the operator like a key in a lock and blocks RNA polymerase from attaching to the promoter, so transcription cannot occur. When lactose is present, it binds the repressor and changes its shape; the repressor can no longer bind the operator, and the lactose enzymes are produced. Positive control: some operons must be switched on by activators such as catabolic activator protein (CAP), which bind at or within the promoter and stimulate transcription. Operons with both activators and repressors have both controls; regulatory sites code for both kinds of protein.

Regulation Through Introns and Exons (Eukaryotes)

In eukaryotes, primary mRNA is processed in the nucleus before mature mRNA is exported, giving regulation opportunities not available in prokaryotes — for example alternative RNA splicing, in which different mRNAs are produced from the same primary transcript depending on which segments are treated as exons and which as introns. Cell-type-specific regulatory proteins control this intron–exon choice by binding regulatory sequences in the primary transcript.

Key Points

  • One genome in all cells; differential expression makes about 200 cell types; disturbed regulation can cause cancer.
  • Activators = positive control; repressors = negative control.
  • Lac operon: lac-Z, lac-Y, lac-A; the repressor blocks the operator until lactose removes it; CAP activates.
  • Eukaryotes also regulate gene expression by alternative RNA splicing.

lessons.title: Mutation: Types, Chromosomal Disorders and Gene Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Mutation is an alteration in the genetic material (genome) that can be transmitted to descendants, from a single nucleotide change to a whole set of chromosomes. Agents causing it are mutagens; the organism carrying it is a mutant. Mutagenesis is the formation of a mutation.

Causes of Mutation

  • Physical mutagens — UV, gamma rays, X-rays, radioactive radiation and high temperature, which damage DNA structure and break its bonds.
  • Chemical mutagens — Nitrosomethylurea, nitrous gas, mustard gas, pesticides, food preservatives, acridine orange, colchicines, caffeine, nicotine and radioactive isotopes; most resemble DNA bases.
  • Biological mutagens — Viruses, bacteria, and transposons (jumping DNA) that jump to a new place and influence the gene, plus errors in meiosis or replication.

Types of Mutation

  • Spontaneous (natural) — Occurs naturally from internal or external factors, e.g. replication errors. Induced — Caused by external factors (ionizing radiation, UV, base analogs, transposing) and used to establish new varieties.
  • Point mutation — Change of one or a few nucleotides (a base replaced by the same type or the opposite type), e.g. sickle cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria (enzyme deficiency; urine turns black in air).
  • Frameshift mutation — One or more nucleotides inserted or deleted, giving a completely new codon sequence and a non-functional protein; thus fatal.
  • Chromosomal structure changes — Deletion (loss of a segment), duplication (segment repeated, in excess), inversion (segment inverted; genetic map altered), translocation (segment transferred to a non-homologous chromosome), insertion (segment reinserted into another chromosome or another region of the same one).
  • Chromosome number changes — From non-disjunction in meiosis. Aneuploidy: monosomy (2n - 1, Turner's), nullisomy (2n - 2, fatal), trisomy (2n + 1, Down's, Klinefelter's), tetrasomy (2n + 2, fatal). Euploidy: whole sets change (monoploidy, triploidy, tetraploidy, pentaploidy); favourable in plants, rare in animals.

Harmful Aspects and Evolution

Harmful mutations decrease fitness and cause cancer, cleft palate, microcephaly, the syndromes below, sickle cell anaemia and haemophilia, reducing survival or fertility. But mutation is also fundamental to evolution as a primary source of genetic variation; accumulated mutations may lead to evolution. Only germline mutations (in eggs and sperms) pass to offspring.

Chromosomal Disorders

  • Down's syndrome (mongolism) — Extra autosome 21 (trisomy, 2n + 1; 47 chromosomes), described by J. Langdon Down in 1866; cause is non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in gamete formation. Symptoms: short stature, poor muscle tone, mental retardation, protruding tongue, flat broad face, small ears and mouth, short hands and fingers, squint eyes; book life expectancy about 16 years. No cure; managed by regular check-up and screening, medications, surgery, counselling and support.
  • Klinefelter's syndrome — Sex chromosome non-disjunction in males only (XXY), described by Dr Henry Klinefelter in 1942, about 1/600 male births. Sterile male with some female characters (breasts, high pitched voice), small testes with no sperm, poorly developed male secondary characters, wide hips, tallness, long legs; some have lower intelligence. Treatment: Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT) from puberty, continued for life; it does not restore fertility. Other trisomies: XYY, XXX.
  • Turner's syndrome — Monosomy in females, 2n - 1 (44 + XO), 45 chromosomes, described by Henry Turner in 1938; cause is non-disjunction of the sex pair in meiosis. Most such pregnancies abort; survivors have short stature, webbed neck, no ovaries (infertility), low hairline, abnormal bone development, many moles, and oedema of hands and feet. Treatments: growth hormone (best started early) and Estrogen Replacement Treatment (ERT) from about age 12–13.

Gene (Point) Mutation Disorders

  • Sickle cell anaemia (Hb SS) — Autosomal recessive point mutation: the 6th amino acid of the haemoglobin beta chain, glutamic acid, is replaced by valine. Abnormal HbS loses oxygen binding capacity; red cells become sickle shaped and deliver less oxygen. Symptoms: painful crises (back, long bones, chest) lasting hours to days; fatigue, fever, paleness, jaundice, organ damage, shortness of breath. Treatment: manage crises with medicines and fluids, blood transfusions (also to prevent stroke), folic acid supplements; bone marrow or stem cell transplant can cure.
  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) — Autosomal recessive point mutation: the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is defective, so phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine and toxic phenyl-ketones damage the central nervous system. Symptoms: lighter skin, hair and eyes, delayed mental and social skills, small head, hyperactivity, seizures, skin rashes, tremors. Treatment: a diet extremely low in phenylalanine (avoid milk, eggs), with the special formula Lofenalac usable throughout life.

DNA in Society (STS)

Any two people share 99.9% of their DNA, yet the 3 million differing base pairs (of 3 billion per cell) identify a person uniquely. Forensic scientists scan 13 variable DNA loci to make a DNA profile (fingerprint) from hair, blood, saliva or semen — to identify suspects, exonerate the wrongly accused, identify disaster victims and establish paternity. Harmful mutations are eradicated by natural selection: harmful traits disappear through premature death or reduced reproductive success.

Key Points

  • Mutagens are physical, chemical or biological; mutations may be spontaneous or induced, point or frameshift, structural or numerical.
  • Down's = trisomy 21; Klinefelter's = XXY; Turner's = 45, XO.
  • Sickle cell anaemia and PKU are autosomal recessive point mutations.
  • Most mutations are harmful, but mutation is the primary source of variation for evolution.

lessons.title: Evolution: Variation and Selection Pressure
lessons.notes_html:
Evolution is the process by which living organisms change over a long period of time. It explains how all life today has developed from earlier, simpler forms. According to the Big Bang theory, the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, and the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. The oldest known fossils are about 3.7 billion years old. Life has been in the process of transformation since its origin.

Scientists Who Built the Idea of Evolution

  • Jean Baptiste Lamarck was the first to suggest that organisms could change during their lifetime and pass these changes to their offspring. His idea was proved incorrect later by the experimental work of August Weismann.
  • Charles Darwin proposed the correct idea of natural selection, in which organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully.
  • Alfred Russell Wallace, around the same time, also thought of natural selection independently; their work together made natural selection the main explanation of evolution.
  • Gregor Mendel discovered how traits are inherited through genes, which later helped scientists to understand how variations appear and are passed on during evolution.

The history of the Earth can be compressed into a 24-hour clock to make it easier to understand: midnight represents the starting point of evolutionary time (the origin of the Earth, 4.5 billion years ago), noon is roughly halfway through Earth history (about 2.25 billion years ago), life originated at about 3.4–3.8 billion years ago, and modern humans (Homo sapiens) appear only about 2 seconds before midnight at the end of the clock.

13.1 Variations and Selection Pressure

Evolution happens because organisms show variation, meaning they are different from each other. The difference can be in size, colour, speed, strength or many other traits. Variation usually comes from random mutations and from the mixing of genes during reproduction.

At the same time, organisms face selection pressures like predators, diseases, competition for food, and changes in the environment. These pressures challenge their survival. Because of variation, some individuals are better suited to survive and reproduce. They pass their favourable traits to the next generation. Over many generations these small changes add up, leading to evolution: a gradual change in the species. The central idea of biological evolution is that all life on Earth shares a common ancestor, and the force that initiates evolution is variation, arising from mutation.

Key Points

  • Evolution is the change of living organisms over a long time, from earlier simpler forms; Earth is about 4.5 billion years old and the oldest fossils about 3.7 billion years old.
  • Lamarck first suggested change during a lifetime; Darwin (and Wallace independently) gave natural selection; Mendel explained inheritance through genes.
  • Variation comes from random mutations and the mixing of genes during reproduction.
  • Selection pressures — predators, disease, competition and environmental change — favour the best-suited individuals, whose traits pass to the next generation.

lessons.title: Evidence of Evolution from Biogeography
lessons.notes_html:
The evidences to support the theory of evolution are provided by many sources: the fossil record, morphology, biogeography, comparative anatomy, embryology and molecular biology all provide evidence for evolution. This lesson covers the evidence from biogeography.

13.2 What is Biogeography?

The study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living organisms (species) is called biogeography. A comparison of recently formed fossil types with living organisms in the same geographic area shows that new organisms arise in an area where similar forms already lived. Closely related species are usually found in close physical proximity to one another, and the fossils from these regions resemble modern organisms — this suggests that these species share a common lineage.

Armadillos and Glyptodonts

Armadillos (a type of mammal) appeared in North and South America, where glyptodonts (extinct giant, heavily armored armadillos) lived in the past. The glyptodont is the extinct relative of the living armadillo, and armadillos live only in the Americas. They evolved in South America millions of years ago, when it was separated from other continents. Because of continental drift and natural barriers like oceans, armadillos could not easily spread to other parts of the world. Later, when North and South America connected, some armadillos moved to North America.

Kangaroos of Australia

Modern kangaroos appeared only in Australia, where they evolved from an extinct giant kangaroo. Millions of years ago Australia was separated from other continents, so kangaroos evolved in isolation. Due to the unique environment of Australia and the absence of predators, kangaroos thrived. Kangaroos are restricted to Australia because of their evolutionary history and geographical isolation. In the same way, the unique marsupials of Australia suggest they evolved there in isolation from a common ancestor.

Darwin Finches of the Galapagos Islands

Darwin found 14 species of finches in the Galapagos Islands, famous for unique plants and animals found nowhere else in the world. These finches are not found anywhere else on Earth. He concluded that the finches had evolved from a common ancestral group that probably reached the island many generations earlier. In the isolation of the Galapagos Islands, the original finches probably evolved into the 14 species. The beaks of the Darwin finches were different because each species adopted to eat different types of food on the Galapagos Islands: some finches had long, sharp beaks for eating insects, while others had short, strong beaks for cracking seeds.

Barriers Explain Absence Too

Darwin also noticed that rabbits were not recorded in South America, even though the climate was very suitable for them. He concluded that rabbits originated somewhere else and could not reach South America because of some kind of barriers (desert, mountain, ocean and harsh climate). So biogeography works both ways: related forms occur together in one region, and suitable but unreachable regions lack a species.

Key Points

  • Biogeography is the study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living species.
  • Armadillos live only in the Americas, where their extinct relatives, the glyptodonts, also lived — evidence of common descent in one region.
  • Kangaroos evolved in isolated Australia from an extinct giant kangaroo.
  • The 14 Galapagos finch species evolved from a common ancestor, their beaks adapted to different foods.

lessons.title: Evidence from Molecular Biology and Vestigial Structures
lessons.notes_html:
Some of the strongest evidence for evolution comes from molecules shared by all living things, and from vestigial structures — reduced organs that show what an animal's ancestors were like. Inside some whales and dolphins there are small limb bones which show that they once had back legs and that their ancestors walked on land; these occasionally reappear as tiny rear flippers. Some snakes have hip bones, which show they once had four legs like lizards, their close cousins.

13.3 Shared Molecules in All Organisms

  • There are certain key molecules and biochemical mechanisms shared by different organisms. All organisms use DNA and RNA for their genetic codes. The DNA in all organisms is composed of 4 types of nucleotides, i.e. Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Thymine.
  • The ATP molecule is the common energy currency in all organisms.
  • The processes of photosynthesis, cellular respiration, transcription and translation are all identical or very similar in various types of organisms.
  • The ribosomal RNA (rRNA) molecules used in protein synthesis are highly conserved across all life forms. By comparing the sequence of rRNA in different organisms, scientists can trace the similarities among different species: the greater the similarities in rRNA sequences, the more closely the species are related.
  • Similarly, cytochrome c, an electron carrier in the electron transport chain, is found in all aerobic organisms (it is the respiratory protein found in all aerobic organisms). The differences in its sequence are proportional to the evolutionary distance between species.

These molecules make sense as important molecules present in most organisms. However, it would not make sense if each of these molecules had appeared independently in each species. These shared biochemical molecules and pathways provide strong evidence for common descent and evolution: all organisms share the same genetic code and basic biochemistry because they descended from a common ancestor.

Vestigial Structures in Man

Human vestigial organs are those organs that have lost all or most of their original functions through evolution. There are about 90 such structures present in our body, some of which are:

  • Vermiform appendix — A vestige of the caecum (functional in herbivores).
  • Coccyx or tailbone — The remnant of a lost tail.
  • Wisdom teeth — Vestigial third molars that human ancestors used to help in grinding down plant tissue.
  • Ear muscles — Minimally developed and non-functional in humans, but some people are able to move their ears in various directions.
  • Tonsils — Listed in the book among the structures removed from the human body.
  • The small finger of the foot has no function in the foot.

Vestigial structures are evidence of divergent evolution and common ancestry: an organ that was useful in an ancestor remains in a reduced, useless form in its descendants. Other evidences of evolution listed in the book are the fossil record (simpler organisms in older rocks, more complex ones in younger rocks, and transitional forms such as Archaeopteryx between reptiles and birds), comparative anatomy (homologous and analogous structures) and embryology (early embryos of vertebrates look very similar).

Key Points

  • All organisms share DNA and RNA with the same 4 nucleotides, ATP as energy currency, and similar photosynthesis, respiration, transcription and translation.
  • rRNA sequences and cytochrome c are highly conserved; greater similarity means closer relationship.
  • Shared molecules are best explained by common descent, not by independent origin in each species.
  • Vestigial structures — appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth — are reduced remains of organs useful in ancestors; whales keep small limb bones and some snakes keep hip bones.

lessons.title: Convergent and Divergent Evolution
lessons.notes_html:
Evolution can bring unrelated animals to look alike, or make related animals grow different. These two opposite patterns are convergent evolution and divergent evolution, and each leaves its own kind of structure as evidence.

13.4 Convergent Evolution and Analogous Structures

Convergent evolution happens when species from different evolutionary backgrounds evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures or ecological niches. In convergent evolution, species do not share a recent common ancestor but develop analogous structures. These structures have similar functions but different origins, e.g. the wings of a bird and the wings of a bat are analogous in the book's example of flying structures; more exactly, analogous organs are anatomically different but functioning similarly.

  • The wings of birds and insects both serve the same function, i.e. flying, but they have different evolutionary origins: bird wings evolved from forelimbs, while insect wings are not limbs at all.
  • Other examples from the solved exercises: the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins, and the eyes of the octopus and humans — same function, different origin.

Thus, due to similar environmental pressures, organisms independently evolve similar features, resulting in analogous structures. Convergent evolution is therefore directly related to analogous structures.

Divergent Evolution and Homologous Structures

Divergent evolution takes place when two or more related species become more different over time, usually because they adapt to different environments. In divergent evolution, species share a common ancestor and have homologous structures. These structures are similar in origin and basic structure but have diverged to perform different roles, e.g. the forelimbs of a human, a cat, a bat and a whale are homologous: they have a similar bone structure (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals and phalanges) but have evolved to perform different functions — grasping, walking, flying and swimming respectively.

As species evolve from a common ancestor, they modify their structures to adapt to different environments, leading to the development of homologous structures.

Convergent EvolutionDivergent Evolution
Unrelated species, no recent common ancestor.Related species from a common ancestor.
Similar environments or niches produce similar traits.Different environments produce different traits.
Produces analogous structures: different origin and structure, same function.Produces homologous structures: same origin and basic structure, different functions.
Example: wings of birds and insects; bodies of shark and dolphin.Example: forelimbs of human, cat, bat and whale.

Divergent evolution gives homologous structures; convergent evolution gives analogous structures.

Key Points

  • Convergent evolution: unrelated species in similar environments develop similar traits — analogous structures.
  • Divergent evolution: related species from a common ancestor become different in different environments — homologous structures.
  • Homologous organs have the same basic structure and origin but may perform different functions.
  • Analogous organs have the same function but different structure and origin.

lessons.title: Endosymbiotic Theory: Evolution of Eukaryotes
lessons.notes_html:
Fossil records indicate that eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes somewhere between 1.9 and 2.1 billion years ago (about 2 billion years ago). Two hypotheses have been proposed to describe the evolution of eukaryotes: the membrane invagination theory and the endosymbiotic theory. The endosymbiont hypothesis explains the origin of eukaryotes.

13.5 The Endosymbiotic Theory

The endosymbiotic theory states that some of the organelles in today's eukaryotic cells were once prokaryotic ancestors. The research conducted by Lynn Margulis supports the hypothesis that two separate, mutually beneficial invasions of a prokaryote cell produced the modern-day mitochondria and chloroplasts as eukaryotic organelles.

  • First invasion — mitochondria — Ancestral mitochondria were small, aerobic, heterotrophic cells (bacteria) capable of using oxygen to perform cellular respiration and thereby create useful energy. They became part of a large prokaryotic pseudopodial cell (bacteria) either by direct invasion as an internal parasite or as an indigestible food source. Instead of being digested, the aerobic bacterium survived inside the host and became the mitochondrion.
  • Second invasion — chloroplasts — A later, second invasion brought ancestral chloroplasts, which are thought to be small photosynthetic cyanobacteria. The engulfed cyanobacterium became the chloroplast, so the host cell could make its own food.
  • Flagella and cilia may have derived through the ingestion of spirochete bacteria.

Evidence for Endosymbiosis

  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the same size as an average bacterial cell.
  • Both are double membrane organelles containing their own small circular DNA and RNA, and 70S ribosomes.
  • Both organelles are self-replicating and divide by binary fission, independent of the host's cell cycle.
  • They therefore appear to be more similar to prokaryotes than to eukaryotes.
  • Several primitive eukaryotes (protozoans) have a nuclear membrane but no mitochondria, as expected for early stages.
  • Flagella and cilia are similar to spirochete bacteria.

Endosymbiosis: a host prokaryote engulfed an aerobic bacterium (→ mitochondrion) and a cyanobacterium (→ chloroplast).

Key Points

  • Eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes about 1.9–2.1 billion years ago.
  • Margulis proposed that mitochondria came from engulfed aerobic bacteria and chloroplasts from engulfed photosynthetic cyanobacteria.
  • Both organelles have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by binary fission like bacteria.
  • The endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of eukaryotes.

lessons.title: Lamarckism: Inheritance of Acquired Characters and Its Drawbacks
lessons.notes_html:
Jean Baptiste de Lamarck (August 1, 1744 – December 28, 1829) was a French naturalist and an early proponent of the idea that evolution (descent with modification) occurred and proceeded in accordance with natural laws. Lamarck, however, is remembered today mainly in connection with his now rejected theory of heredity, the inheritance of acquired traits. He was regarded as a premier authority on plants and invertebrate zoology, was well known as a toponymist (an expert in the study of place names), and wrote the book Philosophie Zoologique (Zoological Philosophy) in 1809.

13.6 Lamarck's Theory of Evolution (Lamarckism)

The theory about evolution presented by Lamarck is called Lamarckism. It involved two ideas:

  • (i) Use and disuse of organs — An organ which is used more and more by an organism becomes bigger and stronger, and one that is not used becomes weak and eventually disappears.
  • (ii) Inheritance of acquired characters — Any feature of an organism that is improved through use is passed to its offspring. So changes acquired during the lifetime of an organism are inherited by the next generation.

Examples Given to Support Lamarck's Theory

  • Evolution of the giraffe — According to Lamarck, the ancestors of the giraffe looked like horses, with a small neck and forelimbs. They lived in areas where there was rare ground vegetation, so they had to stretch their neck and forelimbs to eat leaves from tall plants. Consequently, these parts got elongated. This acquired trait was transmitted in the successive generations, producing the long-necked giraffe of today.
  • Extinction of limbs in snakes — Snakes are believed to have evolved from lizard-like ancestors that had two pairs of limbs. Due to disuse of the limbs, the limbs got weaker and shorter and eventually disappeared, and this loss was inherited.
  • Flightless birds — It is believed that the ancestors of birds such as the ostrich were able to fly. Due to some environmental changes, they had a lot of food and were well protected. They did not use their wings, and as a result the wings became vestigial.

13.7 Drawbacks of Lamarckism

Lamarck's theory of acquired characters could not gain popularity and acceptance due to the following drawbacks:

  • (i) There is no experimental proof of his theory.
  • (ii) New organs are not formed in organisms by requirement.
  • (iii) It is not necessary that an acquired character transmits into a new generation.
  • (iv) There is no genetic basis of this theory, because bodily characteristics which came due to the environment cannot be inherited to the next generation.

Moreover, the German biologist August Weismann, in the 1880s, disproved Lamarck's theory of inheritance by giving experimental proof. He removed the tails of 68 mice, repeatedly for many generations, and reported that no mice were born without a tail or even with a shorter tail. This rejects the theory of inheritance of acquired characters: a change acquired in the body during life is not passed to the offspring. Modern biology explains the giraffe's long neck and the snake's lost limbs by natural selection, not by use and disuse.

Key Points

  • Lamarck (Philosophie Zoologique, 1809) gave two ideas: use and disuse of organs, and inheritance of acquired characters.
  • His examples: giraffes stretched their necks longer, snakes lost limbs by disuse, and flightless birds lost used wings.
  • Drawbacks: no experimental proof, no genetic basis, and acquired characters are not necessarily inherited.
  • Weismann cut off the tails of 68 mice for many generations; all offspring were born with tails, disproving Lamarckism.

lessons.title: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection and Radiometric Dating
lessons.notes_html:
Darwin's theory of evolution (given in detail in the book's Additional Information) states that various types of plants, animals and other living things on Earth have their origin in other pre-existing types, and that the distinguishable differences are due to modifications in successive generations.

The Two Main Points of Darwin's Theory

  • Descent with modification — Passing on the traits from parent organisms to their offspring, with changes. According to Charles Darwin, all species descended from only a few life forms that had been modified over time. This descent with modification, as he called it, forms the backbone of his theory of evolution.
  • Natural selection — The process in nature by which organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more than those less adapted to their environment.

The Four Observations About Natural Selection

  • (a) Overproduction — Each species has the capacity to produce more offspring than can possibly obtain food for survival. If all offspring of any species remained alive and reproduced, they would soon overcrowd the Earth and could destroy all other species. For example: if each breeding pair of elephants produces six offspring during its 90-year lifespan, in 750 years a single pair of elephants will give rise to a population of 19 million — yet elephants have not overrun the planet. A salmon fish produces more than 2.5 million eggs in one season. A grasshopper lays more than 200 eggs at a time; however, only a few of these offspring reach reproductive age, because all eggs do not find suitable conditions.
  • (b) Struggle for existence — Individuals increase enormously in number, but the space and food available remain almost constant, so there is always active competition. This three-fold struggle to ensure living, to obtain the maximum amount of food and a better place, results in natural selection. The struggle for existence may be: (1) Intraspecific — competition among the organisms of the same species; (2) Interspecific — competition among the organisms of different species living together; (3) Environmental struggle — struggle against various environmental conditions. Human populations grow faster than the resources they depend on; when populations become too large, famine and disease break out, and in the end this keeps populations in check by killing off the weakest members.
  • (c) Variations — The individuals in a population exhibit variation in their traits. Variation is an inherited trait which makes an individual unique from other members of the species. Some of these traits improve the chances of an individual's survival and reproductive success, whereas other traits do not. Variation necessary for evolution by natural selection can result from permanent changes, or mutation, in an organism's genes; the variations in skin, colour and body structure of humans must be heritable.
  • (d) Survival of the fittest — As a result of competition among the organisms, the stronger win and survive (variant), while the weaker, less variant are rooted out. For example, if there is a flood, only those organisms that can swim or respire in water have a better chance to survive and others will die. Darwin called it natural selection; it is also called survival of the fittest. The process of natural selection thus causes an increase in favourable alleles and a decrease in unfavourable alleles within the population. Over succeeding generations, individual members become better adapted to local conditions, thus leading to the evolution of new species.

Note: "use and disuse of organs" is Lamarck's idea, not one of Darwin's observations. Darwin's four observations are overproduction, struggle for existence, variation and survival of the fittest.

Natural selection: overproduction leads to struggle; favourable variations survive and reproduce.

Radiometric Dating of Fossils (Science, Technology and Society)

Geologists and palaeontologists use several techniques to determine the actual ages of rocks and the fossils they contain. The most common method is radiometric dating (radioactive dating), based on the fact that living organisms contain certain radioactive isotopes in certain ratios. For example, living organisms have the same constant ratio of carbon-14, a radioactive isotope, to carbon-12, a stable isotope, as does the Earth's atmosphere. However, when an organism dies, its ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 starts to drop, because carbon-14 decays to other chemical elements and the organism no longer obtains any carbon-14 from the atmosphere.

Each radioactive isotope has a fixed rate of decay known as its half-life: the amount of time it takes for one half of the initial amount of the parent radioactive isotope to decay to the daughter isotope. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5600 years. Knowing both the half-life of a radioactive isotope and the ratio of radioactive to stable isotope in a fossil enables us to tell how old the fossil is: a fossil with a carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio half that of the atmosphere is about 5600 years old, and a fossil with one-fourth the atmosphere's ratio is about 11,200 years old.

Key Points

  • Darwin's two main points are descent with modification and natural selection.
  • Four observations: overproduction, struggle for existence (intraspecific, interspecific, environmental), heritable variation, and survival of the fittest.
  • Natural selection increases favourable alleles and decreases unfavourable ones, producing better adapted populations and new species.
  • Radiometric dating uses half-life: carbon-14 has a half-life of 5600 years, so a fossil with half the atmospheric ratio is about 5600 years old.

lessons.title: Species, Population, Community, Ecosystem and Modes of Nutrition
lessons.notes_html:
Ecology (environmental biology) is the branch of biology which deals with the relationship between organisms and their environment. The term was introduced by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, from two Greek words: Oikos — house or living place, and Logos — study or discussion. Every organism lives under a specific set of conditions called its environment.

14.1 Species, Population, Community and Ecosystem

  • Species — A group of similar organisms which can interbreed naturally and produce fertile offsprings, e.g., cow, man, rose, mango.
  • Population — A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time, e.g., all the grasses in a lawn make up the grass population.
  • Community — A group of different populations living and interacting together within the same area, e.g., in a pond there are populations of plants, insects, frogs and fish. Members interact with their own species and with other species, e.g., predation, symbiosis, grazing.
  • Ecosystem — A community along with its environment. It has two components: abiotic (non-living) components, e.g., water, air, light, and biotic (living) components, e.g., plants, animals, micro-organisms.

14.2 Various Modes of Nutrition

Nutrition is the process by which living organisms take in and utilize food substances. On this basis organisms are of two types:

  • Autotrophs — Green plants with chlorophyll in their leaves. They prepare their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis from simple inorganic substances (CO₂, H₂O). They are also called producers, and all other organisms directly or indirectly depend upon them.
  • Heterotrophs — Organisms which cannot prepare their own food and depend upon autotrophs. All animals and fungi are heterotrophs. They are of three main types:
  • Parasites — Get food from living organisms called hosts, living on or inside the host; they may be beneficial, harmful or harmless, and may be plants or animals, e.g., Plasmodium spreads malaria in human beings; Cuscuta is a parasitic plant which absorbs water and nutrients from other plants.
  • Saprobes — Get food from dead bodies or decaying matter, e.g., fungi and bacteria.
  • Holozoic — Food is taken into the body and digested inside, e.g., human, cat, lion.

14.3 Plants as Producers

Green plants prepare food by photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight, using water and CO₂. The light energy of the sun is converted into chemical energy in the form of carbohydrates (especially glucose), so life on earth depends upon photosynthesis. Plants are called producers because they provide the basic food for living things and form the basis of the food chain. Their chemical energy passes through the trophic levels — plants are eaten by herbivores, herbivores by carnivores, and from both the energy is supplied to decomposers (bacteria and fungi).

Key Points

  • Ecology (Haeckel, 1866) studies organisms and their environment: Oikos (house) + Logos (study).
  • Species → population → community → ecosystem (community + environment, with abiotic and biotic components).
  • Autotrophs (producers) make food by photosynthesis; heterotrophs are parasites, saprobes or holozoic.
  • Plants convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose) and form the basis of every food chain.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels and Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels
lessons.notes_html:
In an ecosystem, each stage of the food chain is called a trophic level. The organisms are arranged in different feeding levels which indicate the positions of organisms in a food chain, and also the source of energy and nutrients of different organisms.

14.4 The Five Trophic Levels

LevelGroupExamples
T1Autotrophs (producers) — produce organic food through photosynthesisPlants, algae
T2Herbivores or primary consumers — feed directly on autotrophsGoat, deer
T3Carnivores or secondary consumers — feed on herbivoresWolf, snakes
T4Secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers — feed on other carnivoresLion, big fish like tuna
T5Apex predators or quaternary consumers — top predators, not normally preyed uponSharks, eagles

Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) do not occupy a specific trophic level; they are considered a part of all trophic levels, because they can feed at any trophic level in an ecosystem.

The five trophic levels, from producers (T1) at the base to apex predators (T5) at the top.

14.5 Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels

Energy decreases as it moves from one trophic level to another: not all the energy produced in one level is transferred to the next. On average, about 10% of the net energy production at one trophic level is passed to the next — this is called the 10% rule. The remaining 90% is lost. The book's energy-flow figure shows this: of 1,000,000 J of sunlight, primary producers fix 10,000 J (1%), primary consumers receive 1,000 J, secondary consumers 100 J and tertiary consumers only 10 J.

Reasons for the loss:

  • A large amount of energy is used in life processes like digestion, growth, movement, reproduction and production of wastes.
  • Organisms do not eat every part of another organism, e.g., bones and fur are not eaten by carnivores.
  • A large amount of energy is lost as heat during respiration.
  • Some parts of food are not digested, e.g., cellulose in plants is not easily digested by herbivores.
  • When organisms die, decomposers decompose their bodies and the energy is lost as heat; the nutrients are released into the soil and taken in by producers, but the energy is not available for the next trophic level.

Key Points

  • Trophic levels: T1 producers, T2 herbivores, T3 carnivores, T4 tertiary consumers, T5 apex predators.
  • Decomposers have no fixed trophic level — they feed at every level.
  • 10% rule: only about 10% of energy passes to the next level; about 90% is lost, mainly as heat, in undigested food and in life processes.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect, Acid Rain, Global Warming and Ocean Acidification
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities have badly affected the natural environment through industrialization, urbanization, deforestation, mining and burning of fossil fuels. This lesson covers four linked problems: the greenhouse effect, acid rain, global warming and ocean acidification.

14.6 Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process in which gases in the earth's atmosphere trap heat and warm the planet. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground and plants; this energy is released as heat, but the heat cannot escape back into space easily because gases like CO₂, methane (CH₄), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrous oxide trap it. These are called greenhouse gases: they let sunlight in but stop some heat from going out.

The main cause is carbon dioxide. Its concentration has increased due to urbanization, deforestation, industrialization and burning of fuels in factories, furnaces and vehicles. About half of this CO₂ is absorbed by plants and oceans; the rest forms a thick layer in the lower atmosphere which allows sunlight to pass and heat the earth but does not allow the heat to radiate out. This layer acts like the glass of a greenhouse, so the atmospheric temperature increases.

Harmful Effects of Greenhouse Gases

Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, NO₂, O₃, SO₂, etc.) keep the earth warm — without them the temperature would be too low for life to survive. But at too high levels they harm the environment and life:

  • They cause air pollution, leading to breathing problems and other health issues in people and animals.
  • They damage the ozone (O₃) layer, so more ultraviolet (UV) rays reach the earth; UV rays are harmful for ecosystems, micro-organisms, plants and animals.
  • Too much CO₂ leads to ocean acidification, harming the marine ecosystem and marine life.
  • They are the main cause of global warming: loss of biodiversity, sea level rise from melting glaciers and ice caps, climate change, human health effects (heat stroke, dehydration) and disturbed quality and quantity of crop yield.

14.7 Acid Rain

Precipitation with acidic components that falls on the ground from the atmosphere is called acid rain. It may occur as wet deposition (rain, snow, hail or fog) or as dry deposition (dry gases or dust). It occurs when pollutants like sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrogen oxides (NO₂), which come mainly from burning fuel in vehicles, factories and power plants, mix with water vapours in the atmosphere.

Water is neutral, with a pH of 7, and normal rain water is slightly acidic due to its reaction with CO₂. When SO₂ and NO₂ dissolve in water vapours, sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃) are formed; the acidity increases (pH becomes low) and the acids return to the ground along with rain water. Acid rain often falls hundreds or thousands of kilometres away from its source.

Effects: it kills decomposers and micro-organisms; destroys crops; increases acidity in water, affecting aquatic life, and increases soil acidity; causes stone cancer by its corrosive effect on stones; affects the colours of houses and automobiles; makes plants poisoned and weak; and forests suffer when it weakens trees and washes away nutrients from the soil.

14.8 Global Warming

The long-term rise in the earth's average temperature is called global warming. It is primarily caused by the increase of greenhouse gases (especially CO₂) due to human activities: burning fossil fuels (coal, petrol, natural gas) produces CO₂, greenhouse gases are also produced by industrial processes, and deforestation increases the amount of CO₂. Some greenhouse gases are also produced by natural processes, i.e., decomposition of dead bodies and volcanic eruptions.

Effects: ecosystems are disturbed, so wildlife and biodiversity are affected; with the increase in heat waves, the risks of heatstroke and dehydration have increased; agriculture patterns are changing, affecting food production; floods, wildfires and storms have damaged buildings and roads, affecting the economy; the increased temperature has contributed to climate change and extreme weather like hurricanes and droughts; glaciers and ice caps are melting, so sea level is rising — dangerous for coastal areas, with increased danger of flooding from rivers; and increased temperature damages and destroys crops and forests and causes danger to life.

14.9 Ocean Acidification

Ocean acidification is the phenomenon in which ocean water becomes acidic due to the absorption of CO₂ from the atmosphere. The CO₂ dissolves in sea water and forms carbonic acid: H₂O + CO₂ → H₂CO₃, so the pH of the ocean decreases.

It especially affects coral reefs — massive structures in the sea built by the exoskeleton of corals, which is made of CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate). Ocean acidification reduces the availability of carbonate ions, which are necessary for the production of the CaCO₃ skeleton, so growth rates become slow and the structure of corals becomes weak; weakened corals cannot bear storms and wave action, so their bodies are damaged.

Effects of coral reefs on the aquatic ecosystem: the health of a marine ecosystem depends upon the growth of coral reefs. They provide a suitable habitat for a vast variety of marine organisms (micro-organisms, invertebrates, fish) — thousands of species can be found on one reef, so they are called the Rain Forests of the Sea. They provide a place for breeding and are the shelter house for new young ones; they are essential for nutrient cycling and an important component of the marine food web, so any decline reduces food for many marine animals and disturbs the ecosystem. Their growth is disturbed by changes in temperature, ocean acidification and pollution. Healthy coral reefs act as a natural barrier that protects coastlines from storm and erosion.

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases (mainly CO₂) trap heat like greenhouse glass; in excess they cause global warming.
  • Acid rain forms when SO₂ and nitrogen oxides dissolve in water vapour to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid; it harms crops, aquatic life, soil, forests and stone (stone cancer).
  • Global warming: melting glaciers, rising sea level, extreme weather, disturbed agriculture and health.
  • Ocean acidification (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid) weakens coral skeletons; coral reefs shelter thousands of species and protect coastlines.

lessons.title: Biogeochemical Cycles: Water Cycle and Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
A biogeochemical cycle is the flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment. Chemicals absorbed or ingested by organisms are passed through the food chain and returned to the soil, air and water as respiration, excretion and decomposition. As an element moves through the cycle, it often forms compounds with other elements, by metabolic processes in living tissues or by natural reactions in the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water) or lithosphere (the outer rigid, strong layer of the earth).

14.10 Primary Reservoirs of Nutrients

Chemicals held for long periods in one place are in a reservoir, e.g., coal deposits storing carbon for a long time. Chemicals held for only a short period are in exchange pools, e.g., plants and animals. Plants absorb minerals and nutrients from the soil and store them in their bodies, along with carbohydrates produced in photosynthesis; these pass to herbivores. Animals also store nutrients (minerals, vitamins, proteins, fats) in their tissues; carnivores obtain them from other animals and omnivores from both plants and animals. Generally reservoirs are abiotic factors, and carbon is held for a relatively short time in plants and animals in comparison to coal deposits. The period for which a chemical is held in one place is called its residence time.

14.11 Water Cycle

There is as much water today as there was thousands of years ago, because of the water cycle. The ocean is the major source, containing about 97% of the total water. The cycle is driven by solar energy, which evaporates water, and by gravity, which draws water back to earth as precipitation, i.e., rain, snow, dew or hail.

Water in the environment: some water evaporates from the soil, lakes and streams, and a portion runs off the land back to the oceans. Some rain water sinks or percolates into the ground and saturates the earth to a certain level; the top of the saturation zone is called the water table. Water in basins appears at the level of the water table as lakes and ponds, and water in channels is called streams or rivers. Sometimes ground water is located in underground rivers called aquifers.

Water in living bodies: the bodies of living things contain roughly 70% water. Water is absorbed by the roots of plants, and much of it is evaporated back to the atmosphere from their leaves. A small amount is combined with carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to produce high-energy molecules, which are broken down during cellular respiration, releasing water back to the environment. Heterotrophs get water from their food or by drinking, and some is released back by vaporization.

14.12 Water Table and Aquifers

The water table is the upper surface of the saturation zone; it describes the boundary between water-saturated ground and unsaturated ground. Below the water table, rocks and soil are full of water. An aquifer is an underground layer where the material contains water; aquifers are the sources of wells, springs, etc.

14.13 Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen is the necessary element of organic molecules such as amino acids, nucleic acids and proteins. The nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen between the earth and the atmosphere, converting nitrogen gas into organic substances and returning them to nitrogen in the atmosphere.
